1. The startup concept

Think of the product as:

“Create → Review → Approve → Negotiate → Sign → Store → Monitor → Renew → Analyze”

all in one system.

A company should be able to say:

“I need an agreement with ABC Pvt Ltd for a software development project.”

Your system should then guide them through:

Identify agreement type
Collect required information
Generate a draft
Check missing clauses
Detect risks
Send for internal approval
Send to the other company
Negotiate
Track versions
Sign electronically
Generate final immutable copy
Store the agreement
Extract obligations
Monitor deadlines
Notify responsible people
Handle amendments/renewals/termination
Analyze the company's entire contract portfolio

That is much more valuable than “DocuSign but cheaper.”

2. The most important principle

Your platform should never assume that every agreement can be treated the same way.

For example:

NDA

needs confidentiality definitions, permitted disclosure, exclusions, duration, return/destruction, remedies, etc.

Employment Agreement

needs employment terms, compensation, duties, leave, termination, IP, confidentiality, statutory requirements, etc.

Software Development Agreement

needs scope, milestones, acceptance criteria, IP ownership, source code, warranties, maintenance, support, payment, etc.

Shareholders Agreement

needs voting, transfers, reserved matters, board rights, dividends, deadlock, tag/drag rights, exit mechanisms, etc.

So your architecture should have an Agreement Type Engine.

For debt that can potentially convert into equity.

For formal corporate approvals.

4. Commercial agreements

This will probably be your largest category.

8. Master Services Agreement — MSA

Long-term relationship between two businesses.

Example:

Company A provides software development services to Company B.

The MSA establishes the general legal framework.

9. Statement of Work — SOW

Defines a specific project under the MSA.

Should contain:

project
scope
deliverables
milestones
deadlines
price
acceptance criteria
dependencies
assumptions
responsibilities

This distinction is extremely important.

Your system should understand:

MSA

↓

SOW #001

↓

SOW #002

↓

SOW #003

rather than treating each PDF as unrelated.

10. Service Agreement

For recurring services.

Examples:

marketing
consulting
accounting
IT
maintenance
security
logistics
11. Service Level Agreement — SLA

Defines service performance.

Examples:

uptime
response time
resolution time
support hours
severity levels
service credits
escalation

Your system should automatically monitor SLA obligations.

12. Vendor Agreement

Company ↔ supplier/vendor.

13. Supplier Agreement

For procurement and supply relationships.

14. Purchase Agreement

17. Partnership Agreement

For sales agents and representatives.

5. Confidentiality agreements
21. NDA — Non-Disclosure Agreement

One of the first templates you should build.

Variants:

One-way NDA

A → B

Only A discloses confidential information.

Mutual NDA

A ↔ B

Both disclose confidential information.

Your system should ask:

Who will disclose confidential information?

and automatically choose the appropriate structure.

Important fields:

confidential information definition
exclusions
permitted use
permitted disclosure
security obligations
duration
return/destruction
compelled disclosure
remedies
governing law

33. API Agreement

For companies consuming/providing APIs.

34. Data Processing Agreement — DPA

Extremely important if businesses process personal data.

Sri Lanka's Personal Data Protection Act is particularly relevant to your product because your platform itself will process substantial quantities of personal and business information. The DPA states that the PDPA applies to processing in Sri Lanka and, in certain circumstances, to organizations outside Sri Lanka offering services to or monitoring people in Sri Lanka.

These require special attention because certain transactions involving immovable property can have formal execution requirements. For example, Sri Lankan law has historically imposed specific notarial and witness requirements for certain transactions concerning land and immovable property.

Therefore your application should never simply say “e-signing is valid for everything.”

14. The agreement creation engine

This is where your startup becomes interesting.

Don't give the user:

“Choose a template.”

Give them:

“What are you trying to accomplish?”

For example:

User:

I want to hire ABC Technologies to develop our mobile application for Rs. 2.5 million.

The system determines:

Intent
   ↓
Software Development
   ↓
Commercial Relationship
   ↓
Company ↔ Company
   ↓
Likely Agreement
   ↓
Software Development Agreement
   +
SOW
   +
NDA (if required)
   +
DPA (if personal data involved)

Then it asks targeted questions.

15. Dynamic questionnaire

Instead of showing 100 fields:

Basic

Who are the parties?

Company A
Company B

What is the purpose?

Develop mobile application.

Then dynamically ask:

Commercial
Total value?
Currency?
Payment schedule?
Milestones?
Taxes?
Late payment?
Project
Deliverables?
Acceptance criteria?
Deadline?
Support period?
IP

Who owns the source code?

Options:

Client
Developer
Joint ownership
License to client
Confidentiality

Will confidential information be exchanged?

Yes → NDA provisions.

Personal data

Will the supplier process customer/employee personal data?

Yes → DPA/data-processing provisions.

This makes the system adaptive rather than template-driven.

18. AI contract review

The AI should answer questions like:

“What happens if we terminate this contract?”

“When does this contract automatically renew?”

“What is our maximum liability?”

“Who owns the source code?”

“Are there unusual payment penalties?”

“Does this contract contain an exclusivity obligation?”

“What clauses are missing?”

19. VERY important: don't let AI invent law

This should be one of your fundamental architecture rules.

The AI shouldn't say:

“This contract is legally valid.”

Instead:

“Based on the configured jurisdiction and the rules available to the system, these issues require review.”

Then:

AI Finding
     ↓
Legal Source
     ↓
Jurisdiction
     ↓
Confidence
     ↓
Human/legal review

Your system needs a Legal Knowledge / Authority Layer.

20. Jurisdiction engine

This is essential.

A contract could involve:

Sri Lanka
India
Singapore
UK
USA
UAE
Australia
EU

The system should know:

Agreement
   ↓
Governing Law
   ↓
Jurisdiction
   ↓
Applicable Rules
   ↓
Required Execution Method
   ↓
Risk Rules

For Sri Lanka, your platform needs to account for the Electronic Transactions Act and its amendments. Sri Lanka gives legal recognition to electronic signatures, including digital certificates, but that does not mean every type of transaction has identical execution requirements.

21. Signature architecture

This is probably your biggest technical/legal component.

You need:

Document
   ↓
Hash
   ↓
Signer authentication
   ↓
Signature
   ↓
Timestamp
   ↓
Audit event
   ↓
Final document

Record:

Who signed
Email
Phone
Authentication method
IP
Timestamp
Document hash
Signature event
Consent
User agent
Document version

The goal is to create a strong evidence trail.

Sri Lanka's Electronic Transactions Act provides legal recognition for electronic signatures, and ICTA describes digital certificates as providing mechanisms for proving origin, receipt and integrity.

22. Never modify a signed agreement

This rule should be built directly into your database.

Draft v1
    ↓
Draft v2
    ↓
Negotiation v3
    ↓
Approved v4
    ↓
SIGNED v4

Once signed:

SIGNED v4
     ↓
IMMUTABLE

If someone wants to change it:

Amendment
    ↓
New Version
    ↓
Approval
    ↓
Signature

29. Company identity system

This is extremely important.

Don't treat a company as merely:

company_name
email

You need:

Legal Entity
├── Legal Name
├── Registration Number
├── Registered Address
├── Country
├── Tax Information
├── Directors
├── Authorized Signatories
├── Departments
├── Users
├── Roles
└── Authority Rules

Sri Lanka's Companies Act contains provisions concerning how companies enter obligations and who can act under company authority, so your platform should model signatory authority rather than merely letting any user click “Sign.”

30. Signatory authority engine

Imagine:

CFO wants to sign Rs. 50M contract.

Your system checks:

Contract Value
      ↓
Company Policy
      ↓
User Role
      ↓
Signing Authority
      ↓
Approval Required?

Result:

❌ CFO cannot directly execute this agreement.

✅ Board approval required.

That is much more valuable than basic e-signature.

31. Company policy engine

Allow companies to configure rules.

Example:

IF contract_value > 10,000,000
THEN CFO + CEO approval

IF liability_cap = unlimited
THEN legal approval

IF contract_term > 5 years
THEN director approval

IF personal_data = true
THEN privacy review

IF foreign_jurisdiction = true
THEN legal review

This becomes a Contract Governance Engine.

32. Data protection

This platform will contain extremely sensitive information:

employee information
contracts
salaries
customer information
bank/payment information
signatures
addresses
IDs
confidential business information
intellectual property

Therefore security cannot be an afterthought.

For Sri Lanka, your design needs to account for the PDPA and its amendments/current regulatory requirements. The Data Protection Authority identifies itself as the regulator for personal-data processing and publishes the Act, amendment and related guidance.

34. Multi-tenancy

This is a SaaS product.

Therefore:

Tenant A
 ├── Users
 ├── Contracts
 ├── Documents
 └── Audit

Tenant B
 ├── Users
 ├── Contracts
 ├── Documents
 └── Audit

Tenant A must never be able to access Tenant B's data.

This deserves architectural attention from day one.

35. The killer feature: Contract Risk Graph

Eventually you can build:

Company
   │
   ├── Supplier
   │      ├── MSA
   │      ├── SOW
   │      └── SLA
   │
   ├── Customer
   │      ├── Service Agreement
   │      └── DPA
   │
   └── Employee
          └── Employment Agreement

Then AI understands relationships between agreements.

For example:

“If we terminate the MSA with ABC, which SOWs and obligations are affected?”

That's considerably more advanced than document management.

45. One extremely important business decision

You need to decide whether your company is:

A. Document/e-signature company

Easy to understand, but extremely competitive.

OR

B. Contract intelligence + CLM company

Much more defensible.

I strongly recommend B.

The signature is merely one step in the lifecycle.

19. Legal source registry

Your AI should be able to say:

rather than inventing authority.

For Sri Lanka, official ICTA material identifies the Electronic Transactions Act No. 19 of 2006 and its 2017 amendment as the principal electronic-transactions framework, including legal recognition of electronic signatures.

                 ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                 │            │            │

21. AI should have separate jobs

Don't give one giant prompt 15 responsibilities.

Use specialized capabilities.

Extraction

Contract → risk findings
Comparison
Version A ↔ Version B
Drafting assistance
Structured requirements → draft
Q&A
Question → grounded answer
22. AI grounding

Answer
+

+

+

+

Agreement v4
Section 12.2
Page 17

This dramatically reduces hallucination risk.

36. Amendment system

Don't edit an executed agreement.

Create:

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

“What are the current payment terms after all amendments?”

That's a killer feature.

37. Contract effective-state engine

This is more advanced.

Suppose:

Original:
Payment = $10,000

Amendment 1:
Payment = $12,000

Amendment 2:
Payment = $15,000

The system computes:

CURRENT PAYMENT
= $15,000

while preserving every historical version.

39. Risk scoring

+

+

The rules engine calculates the score.

55. Data protection architecture

The platform itself becomes a processor/controller depending on the specific processing relationship.

You need:

Access requests

Export
Breach response
Processing records
Subprocessor management
Cross-border transfer controls

Sri Lanka's DPA currently publishes the PDPA and 2025 amendment along with regulatory/gazette materials, so your compliance module should be designed to consume changing official requirements rather than assuming the 2022 Act alone is the final rule set.

66. Agreement state machine

Implement explicitly:

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

Then:

 ├── AMENDED
 ├── RENEWED
 └── TERMINATED

Avoid random status strings throughout the application.

67. State-transition rules

For example:

DRAFT → SENT

should be allowed only if:

+

+
document generated

Similarly:

READY_FOR_SIGNATURE → EXECUTED

only after:

70. AI must distinguish facts from assumptions

Internally:

USER_PROVIDED
EXTRACTED
INFERRED
SYSTEM_DEFAULT
LEGAL_REQUIREMENT

Warranty period is missing.

71. No hardcoded business data

Since you've emphasized this in your Aariya architecture work, apply the same principle here.

Do not build:

company_name = "ABC Pvt Ltd"
currency = "LKR"
payment = 500000

The system gets them from:

organization profile
agreement input
integrations
verified sources
user input
72. No synthetic contract data in production

Development can use isolated test fixtures, but the production system must distinguish:

TEST
STAGING
PRODUCTION

and never mix test contracts with production legal records.

For your actual production workflow, contract data should originate from:

real user input
real uploaded documents
real organization data
authorized external integrations
verified legal sources
73. AI training strategy

Do not automatically train a model on every customer contract.

That creates serious privacy/IP issues.

Instead:

Customer Data
     ↓
Operational AI
     ↓
Customer-specific results

For improving models:

Explicitly authorized datasets
+
proper anonymization
+
privacy controls
+
retention rules

Prefer RAG/configuration/model evaluation over indiscriminate training.

76. Contract quality engine

✓

✓

77. Undefined-term detector

Example:

Contract says:

“Supplier shall meet the SLA.”

But no SLA exists.

System:

⚠️ “SLA” is referenced but no SLA schedule is attached.

This is extremely useful.

78. Cross-reference validator

Detect:

Section 12 → Section 17
Schedule A → missing
Annex B → missing
Definition → missing

This catches real document errors.

79. Numerical consistency engine

Check:

Total = milestone 1 + milestone 2 + milestone 3

Example:

30% + 40% + 40%

System:

⚠️ Payment percentages total 110%.

This is a simple but valuable feature.

80. Date consistency engine

Detect:

Effective date > expiry date

or:

SOW ends after MSA

or:

Renewal notice date occurs after expiry
81. Party consistency engine

Check:

Agreement party
≠
Signature party

Example:

Agreement:

ABC Software (Private) Limited

Signer:

ABC Holdings Ltd.

System flags:

⚠️ Signing entity differs from contracting entity.

82. Signature authority check

Before signing:

Signer
 ↓
Organization
 ↓

# Mutual NDA Generator — MVP Technical Spec

**Scope:** One template (Mutual NDA), Sri Lanka jurisdiction, English only.
**Stack:** FastAPI + PostgreSQL (backend), React (web client), S3-compatible object storage for PDFs.
**Multi-tenancy:** `tenant_id` on every table from day one, not retrofitted.

---

## 1. Data model

```sql
-- Tenancy & identity
CREATE TABLE tenants (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name            TEXT NOT NULL,
    country         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'LK',
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE users (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    email           TEXT NOT NULL,
    hashed_password TEXT NOT NULL,
    role            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member', -- owner | admin | member
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)
);

-- Agreement core
CREATE TABLE agreements (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    template_key    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'mutual_nda_lk_v1',
    status          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'DRAFT',
    created_by      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Every edit produces a new immutable version; current draft = latest version
CREATE TABLE agreement_versions (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    agreement_id    UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES agreements(id),
    version_number  INT NOT NULL,
    answers_json    JSONB NOT NULL,      -- wizard questionnaire answers
    rendered_text   TEXT,                -- generated clause text, cached
    document_hash   TEXT,                -- SHA-256 of the final PDF, set at EXECUTED
    created_by      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (agreement_id, version_number)
);

-- Counterparty (external party, no account required to review)
CREATE TABLE parties (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    agreement_id    UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES agreements(id),
    role            TEXT NOT NULL,       -- 'disclosing_and_receiving' (mutual → both)
    company_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
    signatory_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    signatory_email TEXT NOT NULL,
    access_token    TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, -- opaque token for tokenized review link
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE signatures (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    agreement_id    UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES agreements(id),
    party_id        UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES parties(id),
    signed_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    ip_address      TEXT NOT NULL,
    user_agent      TEXT,
    consent_text    TEXT NOT NULL,       -- click-to-sign disclosure shown at signing
    signature_hash  TEXT NOT NULL        -- hash binding signer+doc_hash+timestamp
);

-- Immutable, append-only
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    agreement_id    UUID REFERENCES agreements(id),
    actor_id        UUID,                -- null for external-party actions
    actor_type      TEXT NOT NULL,       -- 'user' | 'external_party' | 'system'
    action          TEXT NOT NULL,       -- 'CREATED' | 'SENT' | 'VIEWED' | 'SIGNED' ...
    metadata_json   JSONB,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

**Notes:**
- `agreement_versions` is append-only — editing a draft creates version N+1, never mutates version N. This gives you free version history without a separate diff engine.
- `document_hash` and `signature_hash` are what make "never modify a signed agreement" enforceable — once `EXECUTED`, the PDF is generated once, hashed, and stored; any future access serves that exact file.
- `access_token` on `parties` is how the external party experience works without forcing account creation (per your doc's section 38) — a long random token embedded in the review link, scoped to that one agreement.

---

## 2. State machine

```
DRAFT → INTERNAL_REVIEW → SENT → VIEWED → NEGOTIATION → APPROVED → SIGNING → EXECUTED
                                     ↑___________________|
                              (external party requests change)
```

For the MVP, collapse the full 12-state machine from your doc down to 8 states — skip `APPROVAL` as a separate gate (no policy engine yet) and skip `ACTIVE`/`EXPIRING`/`RENEWED` (no obligation tracking yet for a single-use NDA):

| State | Meaning | Who can act |
|---|---|---|
| `DRAFT` | Wizard in progress, editable | Creator (internal) |
| `INTERNAL_REVIEW` | Optional: another internal user reviews before sending | Internal users |
| `SENT` | Emailed to counterparty with review link | — |
| `VIEWED` | Counterparty opened the link | — |
| `NEGOTIATION` | Counterparty requested a text change | Internal + external |
| `APPROVED` | Both sides accepted current version | — |
| `SIGNING` | Signature capture in progress | Both parties |
| `EXECUTED` | Both signatures captured, PDF hashed and locked | Read-only |

Transitions are enforced server-side in a single `transition(agreement, new_state, actor)` function — never let the client set `status` directly. Each transition writes one `audit_log` row.

---

## 3. API routes (FastAPI)

```
POST   /agreements                          create draft (template_key fixed to mutual_nda_lk_v1)
GET    /agreements/{id}                     fetch current state + latest version
PATCH  /agreements/{id}/answers             update questionnaire answers → new version, stays DRAFT
POST   /agreements/{id}/parties             add counterparty (company, signatory, email)
POST   /agreements/{id}/render              generate rendered_text + preview PDF from latest version
POST   /agreements/{id}/submit-review       DRAFT → INTERNAL_REVIEW
POST   /agreements/{id}/send                INTERNAL_REVIEW → SENT, emails party, generates access_token
GET    /agreements/{id}/audit               list audit_log entries (internal users only)

# External party endpoints (auth via access_token, not session)
GET    /review/{access_token}               fetch agreement for counterparty view; transitions SENT → VIEWED
POST   /review/{access_token}/comment       request a clause change → NEGOTIATION
POST   /review/{access_token}/accept        counterparty accepts current version
POST   /review/{access_token}/sign          capture signature → SIGNING/EXECUTED

POST   /agreements/{id}/documents/final     (system-triggered on EXECUTED) render final PDF, hash, store
```

**Auth:** internal routes use normal session/JWT auth scoped by `tenant_id` (every query filters on it — this is your tenant isolation boundary). External routes use the opaque `access_token` only, no password, no account.

---

## 4. Clause engine (MVP version)

Don't build a general rule engine yet — for one template, a single Jinja2 template with conditional blocks driven by `answers_json` is enough:

```python
# templates/mutual_nda_lk_v1.txt.jinja2
MUTUAL NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT

This Agreement is made on {{ effective_date }} between
{{ party_a_name }} ("Party A") and {{ party_b_name }} ("Party B").

1. Definition of Confidential Information
...
{% if includes_technical_info %}
Confidential Information includes technical specifications, source code, ...
{% endif %}

2. Duration
This Agreement remains in effect for {{ duration_years }} years from the Effective Date.
...
```

`POST /render` renders this template against `answers_json`, stores the result in `rendered_text`, and converts to PDF (WeasyPrint or similar). This gets you a working draft→PDF pipeline without building the "Clause Engine" as a separate service — that refactor can happen once you have a second template.

---

## 5. What's deliberately *not* in this MVP

- No AI risk scoring, clause suggestions, or comparison — pure template + wizard.
- No approval policy engine — internal review is a single optional step, not configurable rules.
- No renewal/obligation tracking — an NDA here is generate-sign-store, not monitor-over-time.
- No jurisdiction engine — Sri Lanka is hardcoded, not a selectable parameter.
- Signature is click-to-sign + hash + audit trail, not a full cryptographic e-signature provider integration.

Every one of these is a real Phase 2 item from the original plan — the point of this spec is to get one template fully working end-to-end (including the boring parts: tenant isolation, audit trail, immutability after signing) before any of them are worth building.

---

## 6. Suggested build order

1. `tenants`, `users`, auth, tenant-scoped queries
2. `agreements` + `agreement_versions` CRUD, wizard UI → `answers_json`
3. Jinja2 render → PDF preview
4. `parties` + external review link (`access_token`) + read-only view
5. State machine transitions + audit log
6. Click-to-sign flow + final hash + locked PDF
7. Email notifications (send, viewed, signed) — can be stubbed/logged initially

This order gets you a demoable product (steps 1–3) within the first working session, and a fully closed loop (steps 1–6) before you touch anything AI-related.

2. Configuration

backend/app/core/config.py

from functools import lru_cache

from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    app_name: str = "Contract Platform"
    environment: str = "development"

    database_url: str

    jwt_secret_key: SecretStr
    jwt_algorithm: str = "HS256"

    access_token_expire_minutes: int = 15
    refresh_token_expire_days: int = 30

    cors_origins: str

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        extra="ignore",
    )


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()


settings = get_settings()

Notice that the database credentials and JWT secret do not exist in source code.

4. Database engine

backend/app/core/database.py

from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import (
    AsyncSession,
    async_sessionmaker,
    create_async_engine,
)

from app.core.config import settings


engine = create_async_engine(
    settings.database_url,
    pool_pre_ping=True,
    pool_recycle=1800,
    echo=False,
)

AsyncSessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    class_=AsyncSession,
    expire_on_commit=False,
)


async def get_db() -> AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]:
    async with AsyncSessionLocal() as session:
        yield session
5. Base model

backend/app/models/base.py

import uuid
from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import DateTime, func
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin:
    id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid.uuid4,
    )


class TimestampMixin:
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        server_default=func.now(),
        nullable=False,
    )

    updated_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        server_default=func.now(),
        onupdate=func.now(),
        nullable=False,
    )

UUIDs are used for public identifiers instead of sequential IDs.

6. Organization model

backend/app/models/organization.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import String, Text
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    TimestampMixin,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
)


class Organization(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "organizations"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
    )

    slug: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        unique=True,
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    country: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(2),
        nullable=False,
    )

    timezone: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(30),
        nullable=False,
        default="active",
    )

    users = relationship(
        "OrganizationMember",
        back_populates="organization",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )

    legal_entities = relationship(
        "LegalEntity",
        back_populates="organization",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )

    agreements = relationship(
        "Agreement",
        back_populates="organization",
    )

8. RBAC

backend/app/models/rbac.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String, UniqueConstraint
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
)


class Permission(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "permissions"

    key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(150),
        unique=True,
        nullable=False,
    )

    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        String(500),
        nullable=True,
    )


class Role(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "roles"

    organization_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("organizations.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    permissions = relationship(
        "RolePermission",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "organization_id",
            "name",
            name="uq_role_organization_name",
        ),
    )


class RolePermission(Base):
    __tablename__ = "role_permissions"

    role_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("roles.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    permission_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("permissions.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        primary_key=True,
    )


class OrganizationMember(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "organization_members"

    organization_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("organizations.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
    )

    user_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
    )

    role_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("roles.id"),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(30),
        nullable=False,
        default="active",
    )

    organization = relationship(
        "Organization",
        back_populates="users",
    )

    user = relationship(
        "User",
        back_populates="memberships",
    )

    role = relationship("Role")

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "organization_id",
            "user_id",
            name="uq_organization_member",
        ),
    )

This gives us:

Organization
     │
     ├── Members
     │      │
     │      └── Role
     │             │
     │             └── Permissions
     │
     ├── Legal Entities
     │
     └── Agreements

10. Agreement types

backend/app/models/agreement_type.py

        nullable=False,

The important part is:

schema: Mapped[dict]

This is what eventually allows us to have dynamically defined agreements instead of hardcoding:

if agreement_type == "NDA":
    ...
elif agreement_type == "MSA":
    ...

We will remove that kind of architecture entirely.

16. Critical architecture decision

At this point we establish a rule that will remain throughout the entire platform:

Never trust a client-provided organization ID for authorization.

Bad:

organization_id = request.organization_id

The user could simply change it.

Instead:

JWT
 ↓
authenticated user
 ↓
organization membership
 ↓
role
 ↓
permission
 ↓
authorized resource

For example:

User A
   │
   ├── Organization X ✓
   │       │
   │       └── Agreement 123 ✓
   │
   └── Organization Y ✗
           │
           └── Agreement 999 ✗

This tenant boundary is one of the most important security controls in the entire system.

17. What comes next

The next step is authentication + tenant authorization, including:

Registration
     ↓
Email verification
     ↓
Password hashing
     ↓
Login
     ↓
Access JWT
     ↓
Refresh-token rotation
     ↓
Authenticated request
     ↓
Organization membership
     ↓
RBAC permission check
     ↓
Tenant-scoped database query

We'll also add the first real API endpoints so the system can create actual organizations and users from the application, rather than inserting anything manually.
1. Agreement access must be explicitly scoped

Every agreement gets its own Agreement Access Group.

AGREEMENT
│
├── Party A
│   ├── Authorized representatives
│   ├── Employees/team members explicitly added
│   └── Party A lawyers
│
├── Party B
│   ├── Authorized representatives
│   ├── Employees/team members explicitly added
│   └── Party B lawyers
│
└── Platform/System
    ├── Workflow engine
    ├── Notification engine
    ├── Audit engine
    └── Document/version engine

Nobody should automatically gain access merely because they belong to the same company.

For example:

Company A
├── CEO                 → Agreement ✓
├── CFO                 → Agreement ✗
├── Employee 1          → Agreement ✗
├── Lawyer A            → Agreement ✓
└── Lawyer B            → Agreement ✗

Unless explicitly authorized for that agreement.

2. Add people to a particular agreement

The agreement should have an Access & Participants section.

Something like:

Agreement: Software Development MSA

PARTY A
────────────────────────
ABC Technologies Ltd

Participants
✓ CEO — Signatory
✓ Legal Counsel — Lawyer
✓ Procurement Manager — Reviewer

PARTY B
────────────────────────
XYZ Software Ltd

Participants
✓ Managing Director — Signatory
✓ External Counsel — Lawyer
✓ Finance Manager — Reviewer

The creator can add people according to their permissions.

Each participant receives an agreement-specific role.

For example:

SIGNATORY
LAWYER
LEGAL_REVIEWER
BUSINESS_REVIEWER
FINANCE_REVIEWER
OBSERVER
APPROVER
NEGOTIATOR

These roles should be database/configuration driven, not hardcoded.

3. Lawyers must be attached to their representing party

This is important.

Don't simply have:

Agreement → Lawyer

Instead:

Agreement
    │
    ├── Party A
    │      │
    │      └── Lawyer A
    │
    └── Party B
           │
           └── Lawyer B

The system knows:

Lawyer A represents Party A.

and:

Lawyer B represents Party B.

Therefore Lawyer A cannot accidentally approve something on behalf of Party B.

4. Generation workflow

When the system generates the initial agreement:

Party A provides information
             ↓
Agreement requirements collected
             ↓
Agreement type selected
             ↓
Applicable clauses determined
             ↓
Draft generated
             ↓
Validation / legal-risk checks
             ↓
Party A's assigned lawyer notified
             ↓
Party B's assigned lawyer notified

But there is an important distinction:

The system should NOT automatically declare the agreement legally valid.

It should say something like:

DRAFT GENERATED

Status:
Pending Legal Review

Party A Legal Review: Pending
Party B Legal Review: Pending

The lawyers remain responsible for their legal review.

5. Lawyer gets the complete agreement

The assigned lawyer should receive:

New Agreement Ready for Legal Review

Agreement:
Software Development MSA

Representing:
ABC Technologies Ltd

Version:
1.0

Status:
Legal Review Required

They can open the agreement inside the platform.

6. Lawyer editing

The lawyer should be able to:

Add
+ Add Clause
Remove
Remove Clause
Modify
Edit Clause
Propose alternatives
Replace Clause
Add legal terms
Add Legal Provision

But every change creates a new immutable version.

Never overwrite the previous agreement.

7. Version system

For example:

Version 1.0
System-generated
       ↓
Lawyer A changes Clause 7
       ↓
Version 1.1
       ↓
Lawyer B changes Clause 12
       ↓
Version 1.2
       ↓
Lawyer A responds
       ↓
Version 1.3

Previous versions remain accessible to authorized participants.

8. Explicit clause-change display

This is especially important.

The system shouldn't simply show:

Agreement updated.

It should show exactly what changed.

For example:

CLAUSE 7 — LIMITATION OF LIABILITY

Party A Lawyer — Proposed Change

REMOVED:

"Neither party shall be liable for indirect damages."

ADDED:

"Neither party shall be liable for indirect, incidental,
special, consequential, or punitive damages."

────────────────────────────

Change Status:
🟡 Proposed

Changed by:
Party A Legal Counsel

Version:
1.3

The agreement viewer should support:

Original
   ↓
Proposed
   ↓
Current

and a proper redline/diff view.

9. Every change gets a reason

I'd add:

Change requested:
☐ Clause modification
☐ Clause removal
☐ New clause
☐ Legal correction
☐ Commercial correction
☐ Compliance requirement
☐ Other

and:

Explanation:
[Lawyer's explanation...]

This becomes part of the negotiation record.

10. Back-and-forth negotiation

This is where your idea becomes powerful.

The workflow should be:

                 SYSTEM GENERATES
                        │
                        ▼
             ┌────────────────────┐
             │ Party A Lawyer     │
             │ Legal Review       │
             └─────────┬──────────┘
                       │
                 changes proposed
                       │
                       ▼
             ┌────────────────────┐
             │ Party A confirms   │
             │ lawyer position    │
             └─────────┬──────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
             ┌────────────────────┐
             │ Party B Lawyer     │
             │ Legal Review       │
             └─────────┬──────────┘
                       │
                 changes proposed
                       │
                       ▼
             ┌────────────────────┐
             │ Party B confirms   │
             │ lawyer position    │
             └─────────┬──────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
                BOTH SIDES AGREE
                       │
                       ▼
                PARTY APPROVAL
                       │
                       ▼
                  EXECUTION

But there's an important improvement.

Don't treat "lawyer confirmed" as "party accepted."

They are different states.

For example:

Party A Lawyer
      ↓
LEGAL REVIEW COMPLETE

Party A Authorized Representative
      ↓
PARTY APPROVAL

Party B Lawyer
      ↓
LEGAL REVIEW COMPLETE

Party B Authorized Representative
      ↓
PARTY APPROVAL

Both parties approved
      ↓
READY FOR SIGNATURE

This protects against a lawyer's internal review accidentally becoming the company's contractual acceptance.

11. Negotiation rounds

We should explicitly model negotiation rounds.

Example:

Negotiation Round 1

Party A → Party B
Version 1.1
3 changes

Party B → Party A
Version 1.2
5 changes

Party A → Party B
Version 1.3
2 changes

Party B → Party A
Version 1.4
No changes

Round 1 → Resolved

The system can show:

ROUND 1
──────────────
12 changes proposed
10 accepted
2 rejected

ROUND 2
──────────────
4 changes proposed
4 accepted

CURRENT
──────────────
All tracked changes resolved
12. Notifications

The notification system should be event-driven.

Not:

if clause_changed:
    send_email()

Instead:

Agreement Event
       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓
Email
In-app

SMS (optional)

13. Who gets notified?

This must be calculated from agreement participants and event permissions.

Suppose Party A's lawyer changes Clause 8.

The system sends:

Party A Lawyer
      ↓
Change saved

Affected:
✓ Party A assigned legal team
✓ Party A authorized agreement participants
✓ Party B assigned legal team
✓ Party B authorized agreement participants

But not:

✗ Random Party A employees
✗ Random Party B employees
✗ Other company lawyers
✗ Other agreements' participants
✗ Platform users without agreement access

And the notification itself must not leak confidential agreement content.

For example, a user without agreement access should never receive:

"Party A changed the indemnification clause..."

They shouldn't even know that agreement exists.

14. Confidential notification design

Instead of putting sensitive information into email:

Agreement ABC-123 has been updated.

You have an action pending.

Open the secure agreement workspace.

The actual details stay behind authentication and authorization.

15. Party confirmation

After lawyers finish:

LEGAL REVIEW
─────────────────

Party A Lawyer
✓ Complete

Party B Lawyer
✓ Complete

Then:

PARTY APPROVAL
─────────────────

Party A Authorized Representative
🟡 Pending

Party B Authorized Representative
🟡 Pending

Party A approves:

Party A
✓ Approved

Party B approves:

Party B
✓ Approved

Then:

Agreement
    ↓
Both parties approved
    ↓
Execution requirements evaluated
    ↓
Signature workflow
    ↓
All required signatures
    ↓
Agreement ACTIVE
16. Agreement activation

Do not automatically activate merely because two people clicked "approve."

The system should evaluate:

Required parties?
✓

Required approvals?
✓

Required signatories?
✓

Required signatures?
✓

Required execution formalities?
✓

Required documents/annexures?
✓

Required legal workflow?
✓

Then:

STATUS = ACTIVE

This is particularly important because some agreements can have special execution/formality requirements depending on jurisdiction and subject matter.

For Sri Lanka, for example, electronic transactions have statutory recognition under the Electronic Transactions Act, but not every category of legal instrument should be treated as having identical execution requirements. The platform therefore needs an execution-requirements layer rather than assuming "e-sign = valid for everything."

✓ Assigned legal team

✓ Assigned legal team
18. Agreement termination system

This should be a state machine, not a simple database field.

For example:

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

And amendments:

   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

19. Automatic expiry monitoring

The system should have a background scheduler.

Example:

365 days before expiry
      ↓

      ↓
Notification

      ↓
Notification

      ↓
Renewal decision required

14 days
      ↓

7 days
      ↓
Urgent notification

1 day
      ↓

      ↓

But these intervals should not be hardcoded.

They belong in agreement/workflow configuration:

21. Termination must check obligations

This is another important part.

Before termination:

Outstanding obligations
────────────────────────────
Payment          $12,000       🟡
Deliverables     2              🟡
Confidentiality  Continuing     ✓
IP obligations   Continuing     ✓
Data deletion    Required       🟡
Equipment return Required       🟡

The system shouldn't simply flip:

ACTIVE → TERMINATED

without checking the agreement's configured termination obligations.

So I would expand our previous database with these entities:

This is much stronger than simply adding a lawyer_id column.

23. Most important security rule

Your requirement:

people who aren't included shouldn't know anything about the agreement

means we need agreement-level authorization, not merely organization-level authorization.

The authorization hierarchy becomes:

PLATFORM
   ↓
ORGANIZATION
   ↓
LEGAL ENTITY
   ↓
AGREEMENT
   ↓
PARTY
   ↓
PARTICIPANT
   ↓
ROLE
   ↓
PERMISSION

So a user must satisfy all relevant checks before seeing an agreement.

For example:

Can user see agreement?
        │
        ├── authenticated?       ✓
        ├── organization member? ✓
        ├── agreement participant? ✓
        ├── participant active?  ✓
        └── permission allows view? ✓
                    │
                    ▼
                  ALLOW

Otherwise:

403 Forbidden

And importantly, APIs should avoid revealing whether an inaccessible agreement exists.

24. One more thing I strongly recommend

Add a "Legal Workspace" for each side.

                 AGREEMENT
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
          │                     │
     PARTY A                PARTY B
     LEGAL WORKSPACE         LEGAL WORKSPACE
          │                     │
      Lawyers                Lawyers
      Reviewers               Reviewers
      Approvers               Approvers

Each lawyer gets:

Agreement
├── Overview
├── Current Draft
├── Redline
├── Clause Changes
├── Comments
├── Negotiation
├── Legal Issues
├── Approvals
├── Versions
├── Obligations
└── Audit Trail

That gives you a proper CLM negotiation environment, rather than merely a document editor.


Milestone 1.3 — Agreement Participants, Lawyers & Fine-Grained Access

We're going to implement the access-control layer we just designed.

The key rule is:

Being a member of a company does NOT automatically grant access to an agreement.

Access must be explicitly granted to that particular agreement.

1. Final access architecture

We'll use:

Organization
    │
    ├── Legal Entity A
    │      │
    │      └── Party A on Agreement
    │             │
    │             ├── Lawyer A
    │             ├── CEO
    │             └── Finance Reviewer
    │
    └── Legal Entity B
           │
           └── Party B on Agreement
                  │
                  ├── Lawyer B
                  ├── Director
                  └── Procurement Reviewer

The actual permission chain becomes:

User
 ↓
Organization Membership
 ↓
Agreement Participant
 ↓
Participant Role
 ↓

 ↓

6. Why this matters

Suppose:

ABC Ltd

has 15 employees and 3 lawyers.

Only:

CEO
Lawyer A
Finance Manager

are added to Agreement #123.

Then:

CEO             → sees Agreement #123
Lawyer A        → sees Agreement #123
Finance Manager → sees Agreement #123

Employee 4      → DOES NOT see it
Employee 5      → DOES NOT see it
Lawyer B        → DOES NOT see it

Even though all of them belong to ABC Ltd.

9. Agreement access dependency

Create:

backend/app/dependencies/agreement_access.py

import uuid

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.core.database import get_db
from app.models.agreement_access import AgreementParticipant
from app.models.user import User
from app.dependencies.auth import get_current_user


def require_agreement_permission(permission: str):

    async def dependency(
        agreement_id: uuid.UUID,
        current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user),
        db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    ):
        permission_map = {
            "agreement.view": AgreementParticipant.can_view,
            "agreement.comment": AgreementParticipant.can_comment,
            "agreement.propose_change":
                AgreementParticipant.can_propose_changes,
            "agreement.approve":
                AgreementParticipant.can_approve,
            "agreement.sign":
                AgreementParticipant.can_sign,
        }

        column = permission_map.get(permission)

        if column is None:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                detail="Unsupported agreement permission",
            )

        query = (
            select(AgreementParticipant)
            .where(
                AgreementParticipant.agreement_id == agreement_id,
                AgreementParticipant.user_id == current_user.id,
                AgreementParticipant.status == "active",
                column.is_(True),
            )
        )

        result = await db.execute(query)

        participant = result.scalar_one_or_none()

        if participant is None:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN,
                detail="Agreement access denied",
            )

        return participant

    return dependency

This is the foundation.

10. Agreement endpoint

For example:

@router.get("/{agreement_id}")
async def get_agreement(
    agreement_id: UUID,
    participant=Depends(
        require_agreement_permission(
            "agreement.view"
        )
    ),
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
):
    ...

The endpoint won't execute unless the user has agreement access.

11. But there's a security improvement

We shouldn't expose:

Agreement does not exist

versus:

Agreement exists but you're forbidden

to unauthorized users.

For sensitive agreement systems, this can leak information.

So eventually our authorization layer should deliberately return an indistinguishable response for inaccessible agreement resources where appropriate.

Requester

The client cannot simply grant itself permissions.

17. Never modify an executed version

This is a hard rule.

Version 1
   ↓
immutable

Version 2
   ↓
immutable

Version 3
   ↓
immutable

If somebody changes Clause 7:

Version 3
   ↓
proposed modification
   ↓
Version 4

Never:

Version 3
   ↓
overwrite Clause 7

This is critical for auditability and dispute resolution.

20. Lawyer approval ≠ party approval

We will explicitly model these as separate actions.

LEGAL_REVIEW_COMPLETE

is different from:

PARTY_APPROVED

and different again from:

SIGNED

So:

Lawyer A ✓
Lawyer B ✓

Party A ✗
Party B ✗

Agreement cannot be signed.

Even:

Lawyer A ✓
Lawyer B ✓
Party A ✓
Party B ✓

doesn't necessarily mean:

ACTIVE

because the signature/execution workflow still has to complete.

22. Notification engine

The event should trigger notification resolution:

AgreementEvent
      ↓
Notification Resolver
      ↓

      ↓
Check agreement participants
      ↓
Check participant permissions
      ↓
Create notification
      ↓
Delivery workers
      ├── Email
      ├── Web
      └── Mobile

This means later we can add:

Slack
Microsoft Teams
SMS
Webhook

without rewriting agreement logic.

23. One very important privacy rule

Do not put this in a normal email to somebody who isn't authorized:

"Party A changed Clause 8 concerning indemnification..."

Instead:

"An agreement requiring your attention has been updated.
Sign in to review the changes."

And only after authentication and authorization can the person see the actual change.

                           │

                           │

And importantly:

Party A cannot see Party B's private internal legal workspace unless the agreement's configured permissions explicitly allow it.

Likewise, Party B cannot see Party A's internal lawyer comments or private legal notes.

That distinction will become very important when we build the negotiation UI.
Milestone 1.4 — Private Legal Workspaces + Redline Negotiation

Now we build the actual negotiation layer.

The critical design decision is that an agreement has three different visibility levels:

1. PRIVATE
   Lawyer/client internal notes
   Only that party's authorized internal users

2. NEGOTIATION
   Changes/comments explicitly sent to the other side
   Visible to the authorized opposing participants

3. AGREEMENT
   The actual contractual document/version
   Visible according to agreement access permissions

This prevents a lawyer's internal strategy from accidentally being exposed to the other party.

                         AGREEMENT

       │             │               │             │
    Lawyers       Business        Lawyers       Business
       │           Users             │           Users

       ▼                             ▼

cannot accidentally become visible to:

Party B

6. Clause-level redlines

We already created:

agreement_changes
agreement_change_items

Now make each change explicit.

A change can be:

ADD
REMOVE
MODIFY
MOVE
REPLACE

Example:

{
  "clause_identifier": "liability.12",
  "change_type": "modify",
  "old_content": "Liability shall not exceed...",
  "new_content": "Liability shall not exceed two times...",
  "reason": "Proposed liability cap revision"
}

The server creates a new version.

7. Never trust the submitted old content

This is important.

The client must not be allowed to tell the server:

{
  "old_content": "whatever"
}

and have the server accept it.

Instead:

Client
 ↓
base_version_id
 ↓
Server loads immutable version
 ↓
Server finds clause
 ↓
Server calculates old content
 ↓
Server validates proposed modification
 ↓
Server creates new version

The database is the source of truth.

8. Version creation service

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_versioning.py

import hashlib
import uuid

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement import (
    Agreement,
    AgreementVersion,
)


def calculate_hash(content: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(
        content.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()


async def create_version(
    db: AsyncSession,
    agreement: Agreement,
    content: str,
    created_by: uuid.UUID,
) -> AgreementVersion:

    result = await db.execute(
        select(AgreementVersion.version_number)
        .where(
            AgreementVersion.agreement_id
            == agreement.id
        )
        .order_by(
            AgreementVersion.version_number.desc()
        )
        .limit(1)
    )

    latest = result.scalar_one_or_none()

    next_version = 1 if latest is None else latest + 1

    version = AgreementVersion(
        agreement_id=agreement.id,
        version_number=next_version,
        content=content,
        content_hash=calculate_hash(content),
        status="draft",
        created_by=created_by,
    )

    db.add(version)

    await db.flush()

    return version

This means every new proposal gets a new version.

9. Change proposal service

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_changes.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement_changes import (
    AgreementChange,
    AgreementChangeItem,
)
from app.models.agreement import Agreement


async def create_change(
    db: AsyncSession,
    agreement: Agreement,
    base_version_id: uuid.UUID,
    proposed_version_id: uuid.UUID,
    proposed_by: uuid.UUID,
    change_type: str,
    explanation: str | None,
    items: list[dict],
):
    change = AgreementChange(
        agreement_id=agreement.id,
        base_version_id=base_version_id,
        proposed_version_id=proposed_version_id,
        proposed_by=proposed_by,
        change_type=change_type,
        explanation=explanation,
        status="proposed",
    )

    db.add(change)

    await db.flush()

    for item in items:
        change_item = AgreementChangeItem(
            change_id=change.id,
            clause_identifier=item["clause_identifier"],
            change_type=item["change_type"],
            old_content=item.get("old_content"),
            new_content=item.get("new_content"),
            reason=item.get("reason"),
            status="proposed",
        )

        db.add(change_item)

    await db.flush()

    return change

Later we'll make this service perform server-side clause validation and actual structural document diffing.

11. Example negotiation

Suppose the initial system-generated version is:

VERSION 1.0

Party A lawyer changes Clause 8:

VERSION 1.1

Clause 8
MODIFIED

Party A lawyer submits:

PROPOSED

Party B receives:

🔔 New legal proposal

Clause 8
Modified by Party A Legal Counsel

[View changes]

Party B lawyer opens the redline:

Original:
────────────
Liability shall not exceed $50,000.

Proposed:
────────────
Liability shall not exceed $100,000.

They can:

[Accept]
[Reject]
[Counter-propose]
12. Counter proposal

If Party B chooses:

COUNTER-PROPOSE

they create:

VERSION 1.2

The history becomes:

1.0
 │
 └── Party A
       │
       ▼
      1.1
       │
       └── Party B
             │
             ▼
            1.2

Party A now receives the counter-proposal.

13. Clause status

Every changed clause should have a state:

UNCHANGED
PROPOSED
COUNTER_PROPOSED
ACCEPTED
REJECTED
WITHDRAWN
CONFLICT

Example:

Clause 1    ✓ Agreed
Clause 2    ✓ Agreed
Clause 3    🟡 Party B proposal
Clause 4    ✓ Agreed
Clause 5    🔴 Conflict
Clause 6    ✓ Agreed

The agreement cannot proceed to final approval while unresolved mandatory changes remain.

14. Change acceptance

We should never simply do:

change.status = "accepted"

without checking who is performing it.

The service should verify:

Current user
      ↓
Agreement participant
      ↓
Active
      ↓
Represents correct party
      ↓
Has agreement.accept_change permission
      ↓
Change belongs to this agreement
      ↓
Change was proposed by opposing side
      ↓
Change still unresolved

Only then:

ACCEPTED
15. Conflict prevention

Consider:

Party A changes Clause 7
       ↓
Version 1.4

while Party B is still editing an older:

Version 1.2

Party B cannot blindly submit its changes.

The server detects:

BASE VERSION = 1.2
CURRENT VERSION = 1.4

Therefore:

⚠ Version conflict

The agreement changed after you began editing.

Review the newer changes before submitting.

This prevents one lawyer from accidentally overwriting another lawyer's work.

16. Optimistic locking

Add to AgreementVersion:

revision: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
    nullable=False,
    default=1,
)

And every update/proposal references the base version.

The server verifies the expected version before accepting the operation.

For higher concurrency, PostgreSQL transactions and row locks can be used around final state transitions.

17. Lawyer → Client confirmation

This is the workflow you specifically requested.

Party A lawyer:

LEGAL REVIEW
       ↓
Changes proposed
       ↓
Submit to Party A

Party A sees:

LAWYER RECOMMENDATION

Your legal counsel has reviewed the agreement.

3 changes proposed.

[Review]

[Confirm lawyer's position]

[Request discussion]

If Party A confirms:

PARTY A CONFIRMED

Only then can the proposal be formally transmitted to the opposing side.

18. Why this distinction matters

We now have:

LAWYER_PROPOSED

and:

CLIENT_CONFIRMED

separately.

So:

Lawyer:
"I recommend changing Clause 9."

Client:
"Yes, send this to the other party."

is different from:

Lawyer:
"I recommend changing Clause 9."

Client:
"Don't send it yet."

The second must remain private.

19. Opposing side receives only released changes

The transmission process becomes:

Party A Lawyer
       ↓
Internal Draft
       ↓
Party A Confirmation
       ↓
RELEASE TO PARTY B
       ↓
Party B Lawyer Notification

This is much safer than notifying the other side immediately whenever a lawyer types something.

22. Notifications become automatic

When Party A submits a proposal:

EVENT:
CHANGE_RELEASED

The notification engine determines:

Affected Party:
Party B

Participants:
✓ Party B lawyer
✓ Party B authorized reviewers
✓ Party B authorized representative

Party A's internal notes are excluded.

When Party B counter-proposes:

EVENT:
COUNTER_PROPOSAL_RELEASED

Party A's authorized legal team gets notified.

25. Important legal/data-protection consideration

Because this platform will potentially contain personal information, employee information, legal documents, and confidential commercial information, access control isn't just a UX feature. It needs to be part of the security architecture.

For Sri Lankan deployments, the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 and its current amendments/regulatory framework need to be incorporated into the platform's data-processing, retention, access, and security design. The Sri Lankan Data Protection Authority currently publishes the applicable framework and guidance.

So we'll later add:

Data classification
↓
Purpose / processing basis
↓
Access control
↓
Encryption
↓
Retention policy
↓
Deletion/anonymization workflow
↓
Audit

27. What we have achieved

The platform can now be designed around this rule:

A lawyer can privately work with their client, prepare changes, obtain the client's confirmation, release only the intended changes to the opposing side, receive the opposing lawyer's response, negotiate through controlled versions, and eventually reach a mutually confirmed version.

And throughout the process:

Private legal information
        ≠
Negotiation information
        ≠
Final agreement information

That's the separation we need.

Milestone 1.5 — Approval & Execution State Machine

Now we make the lifecycle enforceable in the backend, rather than relying on the frontend to move an agreement from one state to another.

The important rule is:

No user can directly set an agreement status. Every transition must pass through a server-side state machine and its required authorization/evidence checks.

This also keeps your requirement of no mock, synthetic, placeholder, or hardcoded business/legal data. The state machine is application logic; the actual parties, lawyers, approvals, clauses, signatories, dates, and legal requirements come from the database and agreement configuration.

1. Define the lifecycle

Use these states:

DRAFT
   ↓
LEGAL_REVIEW
   ↓
LAWYER_CHANGES_PENDING_CLIENT
   ↓
CLIENT_CONFIRMED
   ↓
RELEASED_TO_OTHER_PARTY
   ↓
OPPOSING_LEGAL_REVIEW
   ↓
OPPOSING_CHANGES_PENDING_CLIENT
   ↓
OPPOSING_CLIENT_CONFIRMED
   ↓
FINAL_REVIEW
   ↓
EXECUTION_READY
   ↓
SIGNATURE_REQUESTED
   ↓
PARTIALLY_SIGNED
   ↓
EXECUTED
   ↓
ACTIVE
   ↓
EXPIRING
   ↓
RENEWAL_NEGOTIATION / TERMINATION_PENDING
   ↓
RENEWED / TERMINATED

There also need to be rejection/counterproposal paths.

For example:

CLIENT_CONFIRMED
       ↓
RELEASED_TO_OTHER_PARTY
       ↓
OPPOSING_LEGAL_REVIEW
       ↓
COUNTER_PROPOSAL
       ↓
OPPOSING_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION
       ↓
RELEASED_TO_OTHER_PARTY

So negotiation can continue indefinitely until the parties actually reach agreement.

2. Don't use Python enums as the source of truth

Because you want the platform to eventually support configurable workflows, don't build a massive:

if agreement_type == "NDA":
    ...
elif agreement_type == "MSA":
    ...

Instead, create database-backed workflow states and transitions.

Create:

workflow_definitions
workflow_states
workflow_transitions
workflow_transition_requirements
workflow_instances
3. Workflow models

Create:

backend/app/models/workflow.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import (
    Boolean,
    ForeignKey,
    Integer,
    String,
    Text,
    UniqueConstraint,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

from app.models.base import Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin


class WorkflowDefinition(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "workflow_definitions"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200), nullable=False)
    key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), nullable=False, unique=True)

    agreement_type_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID | None] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("agreement_types.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=True,
    )

    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Integer, nullable=False, default=1)
    is_active: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=True,
    )

    states = relationship(
        "WorkflowState",
        back_populates="workflow",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )

    transitions = relationship(
        "WorkflowTransition",
        back_populates="workflow",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )


class WorkflowState(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "workflow_states"

    workflow_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_definitions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(200),
        nullable=False,
    )

    is_initial: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=False,
    )

    is_terminal: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=False,
    )

    workflow = relationship(
        "WorkflowDefinition",
        back_populates="states",
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "workflow_id",
            "key",
            name="uq_workflow_state_key",
        ),
    )


class WorkflowTransition(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "workflow_transitions"

    workflow_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_definitions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    from_state_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_states.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    to_state_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_states.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    action_key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(200),
        nullable=False,
    )

    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        Text,
        nullable=True,
    )

    requires_confirmation: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=False,
    )

    workflow = relationship(
        "WorkflowDefinition",
        back_populates="transitions",
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "workflow_id",
            "from_state_id",
            "action_key",
            name="uq_workflow_transition_action",
        ),
    )


class WorkflowInstance(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "workflow_instances"

    agreement_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreements.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
        unique=True,
    )

    workflow_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_definitions.id",
            ondelete="RESTRICT",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    current_state_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_states.id",
            ondelete="RESTRICT",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    revision: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        Integer,
        nullable=False,
        default=0,
    )
4. Transition requirements

A transition may require multiple conditions.

For example:

READY_FOR_SIGNATURE

might require:

both_lawyers_completed
both_parties_approved
mandatory_clauses_resolved
annexures_complete
execution_requirements_complete
signatories_verified

Create:

workflow_transition_requirement.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import Boolean, ForeignKey, String
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
)


class WorkflowTransitionRequirement(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "workflow_transition_requirements"

    transition_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "workflow_transitions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    requirement_key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(150),
        nullable=False,
    )

    required: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=True,
    )

    configuration: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        default=dict,
        nullable=False,
    )

The important part is configuration.

That means the database can eventually contain things like:

{
    "minimum": 2
}

or:

{
    "party_role": "buyer"
}

instead of embedding those values into Python.

5. Workflow transition service

Create:

backend/app/services/workflow_engine.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import HTTPException
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.workflow import (
    WorkflowInstance,
    WorkflowState,
    WorkflowTransition,
)


@dataclass
class TransitionResult:
    previous_state: str
    current_state: str
    transition_id: UUID


class WorkflowEngine:

    async def transition(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        action_key: str,
        actor_id: UUID,
    ) -> TransitionResult:

        instance_result = await db.execute(
            select(WorkflowInstance)
            .where(
                WorkflowInstance.agreement_id == agreement_id
            )
            .with_for_update()
        )

        instance = instance_result.scalar_one_or_none()

        if instance is None:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=404,
                detail="Workflow instance not found",
            )

        current_state_result = await db.execute(
            select(WorkflowState)
            .where(
                WorkflowState.id == instance.current_state_id
            )
        )

        current_state = current_state_result.scalar_one()

        transition_result = await db.execute(
            select(WorkflowTransition)
            .where(
                WorkflowTransition.workflow_id == instance.workflow_id,
                WorkflowTransition.from_state_id
                == instance.current_state_id,
                WorkflowTransition.action_key
                == action_key,
            )
        )

        transition = transition_result.scalar_one_or_none()

        if transition is None:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=409,
                detail=(
                    f"Action '{action_key}' is not valid "
                    f"from state '{current_state.key}'"
                ),
            )

        await self._authorize_transition(
            db=db,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            actor_id=actor_id,
            action_key=action_key,
        )

        await self._validate_requirements(
            db=db,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            transition_id=transition.id,
        )

        next_state_result = await db.execute(
            select(WorkflowState)
            .where(
                WorkflowState.id == transition.to_state_id
            )
        )

        next_state = next_state_result.scalar_one()

        instance.current_state_id = next_state.id
        instance.revision += 1

        await db.flush()

        return TransitionResult(
            previous_state=current_state.key,
            current_state=next_state.key,
            transition_id=transition.id,
        )

    async def _authorize_transition(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        actor_id: UUID,
        action_key: str,
    ) -> None:

        # Connect this to the agreement-level authorization
        # service from the previous milestone.

        # Important:
        # Do NOT trust organization membership alone.

        authorized = await self._check_actor_permission(
            db=db,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            actor_id=actor_id,
            action_key=action_key,
        )

        if not authorized:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=403,
                detail="Actor is not authorized for this action",
            )

    async def _check_actor_permission(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        actor_id: UUID,
        action_key: str,
    ) -> bool:

        # Delegate to the centralized authorization layer.
        #
        # This method should evaluate:
        #
        # user
        # -> agreement participant
        # -> represented party
        # -> permission
        # -> action
        #
        # No frontend-controlled authorization.

        return False

    async def _validate_requirements(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        transition_id: UUID,
    ) -> None:

        # Requirement evaluation will be connected to
        # the requirement registry.
        #
        # Every required condition must return True.

        return

Notice something intentional:

return False

is not production functionality.

It is a seam that must be connected to the real authorization service before this endpoint is enabled.

We are not pretending it works.

7. Requirement interface

requirements/base.py

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession


class RequirementResult:
    def __init__(
        self,
        passed: bool,
        reason: str | None = None,
    ):
        self.passed = passed
        self.reason = reason


class WorkflowRequirement(ABC):

    key: str

    @abstractmethod
    async def evaluate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        configuration: dict,
    ) -> RequirementResult:
        raise NotImplementedError
8. Registry

requirements/registry.py

from app.services.requirements.base import WorkflowRequirement


class RequirementRegistry:

    def __init__(self):
        self._requirements: dict[
            str,
            WorkflowRequirement
        ] = {}

    def register(
        self,
        requirement: WorkflowRequirement,
    ) -> None:

        if requirement.key in self._requirements:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Requirement already registered: "
                f"{requirement.key}"
            )

        self._requirements[
            requirement.key
        ] = requirement

    def get(
        self,
        key: str,
    ) -> WorkflowRequirement:

        requirement = self._requirements.get(key)

        if requirement is None:
            raise KeyError(
                f"Unknown workflow requirement: {key}"
            )

        return requirement

Now requirements are executable capabilities, while their activation/configuration comes from the database.

9. Lawyer review requirement

requirements/lawyer_review.py

from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement_access import (
    AgreementParty,
    LegalRepresentativeAssignment,
)

from app.services.requirements.base import (
    RequirementResult,
    WorkflowRequirement,
)


class LawyersCompletedReview(
    WorkflowRequirement
):

    key = "lawyers_completed_review"

    async def evaluate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        configuration: dict,
    ) -> RequirementResult:

        result = await db.execute(
            select(AgreementParty.id)
            .where(
                AgreementParty.agreement_id == agreement_id
            )
        )

        party_ids = result.scalars().all()

        if not party_ids:
            return RequirementResult(
                False,
                "Agreement has no parties",
            )

        assignments = await db.execute(
            select(LegalRepresentativeAssignment)
            .where(
                LegalRepresentativeAssignment.agreement_id
                == agreement_id,
                LegalRepresentativeAssignment.agreement_party_id
                .in_(party_ids),
                LegalRepresentativeAssignment.status
                == "active",
            )
        )

        completed = assignments.scalars().all()

        if len(completed) < len(party_ids):

            return RequirementResult(
                False,
                "Required legal representatives have not "
                "completed their review",
            )

        return RequirementResult(True)

This should later become more precise by checking a dedicated legal_reviews table rather than assuming an assignment itself equals completed review.

That's important.

Assignment ≠ review completed.

12. Critical version rule

Suppose:

Version 8

is sent to Party A.

Party A approves Version 8.

Then Lawyer A creates:

Version 9

Version 8's approval must not automatically remain valid.

The approval belongs to:

agreement_id
party_id
version_id
approver
timestamp

Therefore Version 9 needs new approval.

This prevents a serious security/legal integrity problem.

14. Execution readiness service

This becomes the most important checkpoint before signing.

Create:

app/services/execution_readiness.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession


@dataclass
class ReadinessCheck:
    key: str
    passed: bool
    reason: str | None = None


@dataclass
class ExecutionReadiness:
    ready: bool
    checks: list[ReadinessCheck]


class ExecutionReadinessService:

    async def evaluate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ExecutionReadiness:

        checks: list[ReadinessCheck] = []

        checks.append(
            await self._check_lawyer_reviews(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        checks.append(
            await self._check_party_approvals(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        checks.append(
            await self._check_unresolved_changes(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        checks.append(
            await self._check_required_documents(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        checks.append(
            await self._check_execution_requirements(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        checks.append(
            await self._check_signatories(
                db,
                agreement_id,
            )
        )

        return ExecutionReadiness(
            ready=all(
                check.passed
                for check in checks
            ),
            checks=checks,
        )

    async def _check_lawyer_reviews(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        # Query real legal_review records.

        raise NotImplementedError

    async def _check_party_approvals(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        raise NotImplementedError

    async def _check_unresolved_changes(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        raise NotImplementedError

    async def _check_required_documents(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        raise NotImplementedError

    async def _check_execution_requirements(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        raise NotImplementedError

    async def _check_signatories(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ) -> ReadinessCheck:

        raise NotImplementedError

These NotImplementedErrors are deliberate engineering boundaries. We will fill each one from real database entities, not invented values.
