19. The final execution sequence

The backend should enforce:

                    ┌───────────────────┐
                    │ Agreement Draft   │
                    └─────────┬─────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌───────────────────┐
                    │ Lawyer Review     │
                    └─────────┬─────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────┐
                 │ Lawyer proposes edits │
                 └────────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────┐
                 │ Client confirms edits │
                 └────────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────┐
                 │ Release to other side │
                 └────────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────┐
                 │ Opposing lawyer review│
                 └────────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────┐
                 │ Opposing client checks│
                 └────────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                       ┌──────┴──────┐
                       │             │
                    Reject         Confirm
                       │             │
                       └──────┬──────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                       FINAL REVIEW
                              │
                              ▼
                   EXECUTION READINESS
                              │
                    ┌─────────┴──────────┐
                    │                    │
                 FAIL                   PASS
                    │                    │
                    ▼                    ▼
               Fix issues       SIGNATURE REQUEST
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                  SIGNATURES
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                  EVIDENCE CHECK
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                    EXECUTED
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                     ACTIVE
20. One more critical protection: immutable executed version

Once the agreement reaches:

EXECUTED

the signed version must become immutable.

Do not allow:

PUT /agreements/{id}/content

to modify it.

Instead:

Executed Agreement
       │
       ├── Amendment
       │      ↓
       │   New version
       │
       └── Renewal
              ↓
           New lifecycle

So:

Agreement #42
Version 7
EXECUTED

cannot simply become Version 8 by editing the executed document.

An amendment produces a related agreement/version chain.

21. Agreement state and workflow state should not be confused

Keep these separate.

Workflow state
LEGAL_REVIEW
CLIENT_CONFIRMATION
OPPOSING_REVIEW
EXECUTION_READY
SIGNATURE_REQUESTED
...
Agreement lifecycle state
DRAFT
NEGOTIATING
EXECUTED
ACTIVE
EXPIRED
TERMINATED
Signature state
NOT_STARTED
REQUESTED
PARTIALLY_SIGNED
COMPLETED
VOIDED
EXPIRED
Approval state
PENDING
APPROVED
REJECTED
SUPERSEDED

This prevents one giant status field from becoming an unmaintainable mess.

23. What we have now

At this point the architecture has separated:

Concern	Mechanism
Who can access agreement	Agreement participants
Who represents a party	Legal representative assignment
Lawyer review	LegalReview
Client approval	PartyApproval
Negotiation	Change/round/action models
Workflow	Workflow definition/state/transition
Requirements	Requirement registry
Signatory authority	AuthorizedSignatory
Signature process	SignatureRequest
Individual signing	SignatureRequestSigner
Signature evidence	SignatureEvidence
Executed document	Immutable agreement version
Auditability	Agreement events + audit events

And most importantly:

No frontend action can legitimately skip the approval/execution sequence.

Milestone 1.6 — Complete Authorization Engine

Now we build the layer that actually enforces the security model.

The authorization decision must be:

Authenticated User
       ↓
Organization Membership
       ↓
Agreement Participant
       ↓
Represented Party
       ↓
Participant Role
       ↓
Permission
       ↓
Workflow State
       ↓
Requested Action
       ↓
ALLOW / DENY

The frontend is never trusted to make this decision.

1. The authorization problem we're solving

For example:

Company A
 ├── Employee Alice
 ├── Lawyer Bob
 └── CFO Carol

Company B
 ├── Employee David
 └── Lawyer Eve

Agreement:

Company A ↔ Company B

Alice being an employee of Company A does not mean:

Alice → can_view(agreement)

Instead:

Alice
 ↓
organization membership
 ↓
agreement participant
 ↓
Party A
 ↓
agreement.view

If there is no agreement participant record:

DENY
2. Permission model

Don't encode permissions like:

if user.role == "lawyer":
    ...

That becomes impossible to maintain at scale.

Instead create database-driven permissions.

You already have:

roles
permissions
role_permissions

We'll extend this with agreement-level grants.

3. Add permission catalog

app/models/permission.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import String, UniqueConstraint
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
)


class Permission(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "permissions"

    key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(150),
        nullable=False,
        unique=True,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(200),
        nullable=False,
    )

    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        String(1000),
        nullable=True,
    )

    scope: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(50),
        nullable=False,
    )

Examples of database records:

agreement.view
agreement.comment
agreement.propose_change
agreement.accept_change
agreement.reject_change
agreement.approve
agreement.manage_participants
agreement.manage_lawyers
agreement.request_signature
agreement.sign
agreement.view_audit
agreement.view_versions
agreement.manage_obligations
agreement.request_termination
agreement.approve_termination

These are permission identifiers, not hardcoded business data.

4. Improve agreement access

Your previous AgreementParticipant model had boolean columns such as:

can_view
can_comment
can_propose_changes
can_approve
can_sign

That works initially, but it doesn't scale.

For example, eventually you might need:

agreement.export
agreement.download_original
agreement.view_private_legal_workspace
agreement.manage_execution
agreement.manage_renewal
agreement.view_financial_terms

Adding a database column every time is bad architecture.

Instead introduce:

AgreementParticipantPermission

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import (
    Boolean,
    ForeignKey,
    UniqueConstraint,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
)


class AgreementParticipantPermission(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "agreement_participant_permissions"

    agreement_participant_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreement_participants.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    permission_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "permissions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    granted: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=True,
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "agreement_participant_id",
            "permission_id",
            name="uq_agreement_participant_permission",
        ),
    )

Now permissions are extensible.

5. Why both role permissions and agreement permissions?

Because they solve different problems.

Organization role
CFO
Lawyer
Employee
Administrator

defines what someone generally can do inside the organization.

Agreement participant permissions

Defines what that particular person can do on that particular agreement.

For example:

Bob
Organization role = Lawyer

Agreement #123:
participant = true
party = Company A
permissions:
    view
    comment
    propose_change
    accept_change
    reject_change

But perhaps Bob cannot:

approve
sign

because those belong to the client's authority.

6. Central authorization context

Create:

app/security/authorization.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
from uuid import UUID


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AuthorizationContext:
    user_id: UUID
    organization_id: UUID
    agreement_id: UUID
    agreement_party_id: UUID | None
    participant_id: UUID | None
    permission_key: str

This makes authorization decisions explicit and auditable.

7. Authorization decision object
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AuthorizationDecision:
    allowed: bool
    reason: str
    participant_id: UUID | None = None
    party_id: UUID | None = None

Never return only:

True

for security decisions.

We want a reason internally for audit/debugging.

For example:

allowed = false
reason = "USER_NOT_AGREEMENT_PARTICIPANT"
8. Build the authorization service

Create:

app/services/authorization_service.py

from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement import Agreement
from app.models.agreement_access import (
    AgreementParticipant,
    AgreementParty,
    AgreementAccessGrant,
)
from app.models.permission import Permission
from app.models.agreement_participant_permission import (
    AgreementParticipantPermission,
)


class AuthorizationService:

    async def authorize_agreement_action(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        user_id: UUID,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        permission_key: str,
    ):
        agreement = await self._get_agreement(
            db,
            agreement_id,
        )

        if agreement is None:
            return self._deny(
                "AGREEMENT_NOT_FOUND"
            )

        participant = await self._get_participant(
            db,
            agreement_id,
            user_id,
        )

        if participant is None:
            return self._deny(
                "USER_NOT_AGREEMENT_PARTICIPANT"
            )

        if participant.status != "active":
            return self._deny(
                "AGREEMENT_PARTICIPATION_INACTIVE"
            )

        permission = await self._get_permission(
            db,
            permission_key,
        )

        if permission is None:
            return self._deny(
                "UNKNOWN_PERMISSION"
            )

        granted = await self._permission_granted(
            db,
            participant.id,
            permission.id,
        )

        if not granted:
            return self._deny(
                "PERMISSION_NOT_GRANTED"
            )

        return {
            "allowed": True,
            "reason": "AUTHORIZED",
            "participant_id": participant.id,
            "party_id": participant.agreement_party_id,
        }

    async def _get_agreement(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
    ):
        result = await db.execute(
            select(Agreement)
            .where(
                Agreement.id == agreement_id
            )
        )

        return result.scalar_one_or_none()

    async def _get_participant(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement_id: UUID,
        user_id: UUID,
    ):
        result = await db.execute(
            select(AgreementParticipant)
            .where(
                AgreementParticipant.agreement_id
                == agreement_id,
                AgreementParticipant.user_id
                == user_id,
            )
        )

        return result.scalar_one_or_none()

    async def _get_permission(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        permission_key: str,
    ):
        result = await db.execute(
            select(Permission)
            .where(
                Permission.key == permission_key
            )
        )

        return result.scalar_one_or_none()

    async def _permission_granted(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        participant_id: UUID,
        permission_id: UUID,
    ) -> bool:

        result = await db.execute(
            select(
                AgreementParticipantPermission
            )
            .where(
                AgreementParticipantPermission
                .agreement_participant_id
                == participant_id,

                AgreementParticipantPermission
                .permission_id
                == permission_id,

                AgreementParticipantPermission
                .granted.is_(True),
            )
        )

        return (
            result.scalar_one_or_none()
            is not None
        )

    def _deny(self, reason: str):
        return {
            "allowed": False,
            "reason": reason,
            "participant_id": None,
            "party_id": None,
        }
9. But there is an important missing security boundary

The previous service checks:

user → agreement participant → permission

We also need:

participant → organization → legal entity/party

Otherwise we could accidentally associate someone with the wrong party.

Add this validation.

async def validate_party_membership(
    self,
    db: AsyncSession,
    *,
    participant_id: UUID,
    organization_id: UUID,
) -> bool:

    result = await db.execute(
        select(AgreementParticipant)
        .join(
            AgreementParty,
            AgreementParty.id
            == AgreementParticipant.agreement_party_id,
        )
        .join(
            Agreement,
            Agreement.id
            == AgreementParticipant.agreement_id,
        )
        .where(
            AgreementParticipant.id == participant_id,
            Agreement.organization_id == organization_id,
        )
    )

    return result.scalar_one_or_none() is not None

Later we should replace organization ownership with a more explicit:

AgreementParty
      ↓
LegalEntity
      ↓
Organization

relationship.

10. Party isolation

This is one of the most important pieces.

Suppose:

Agreement #500

Party A
 ├── Lawyer A
 └── CFO A

Party B
 ├── Lawyer B
 └── CFO B

Lawyer A requests:

GET /agreements/500/private-comments

The query must contain:

LegalPrivateComment.agreement_party_id == lawyer_a_party_id

Never:

LegalPrivateComment.agreement_id == agreement_id

alone.

Otherwise Lawyer A could see Lawyer B's private notes.

11. Create a reusable party-scoped query

Create:

app/services/party_scope.py

from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement_access import (
    AgreementParticipant,
)


async def get_user_party_for_agreement(
    db: AsyncSession,
    *,
    user_id: UUID,
    agreement_id: UUID,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            AgreementParticipant
        )
        .where(
            AgreementParticipant.user_id == user_id,
            AgreementParticipant.agreement_id
            == agreement_id,
            AgreementParticipant.status
            == "active",
        )
    )

    return result.scalar_one_or_none()

Then:

participant = await get_user_party_for_agreement(
    db,
    user_id=current_user.id,
    agreement_id=agreement_id,
)

if participant is None:
    raise HTTPException(
        status_code=403,
        detail="Agreement access denied",
    )

party_id = participant.agreement_party_id

Every private-party endpoint uses this.

12. Authorization dependency

Now connect it to FastAPI.

app/api/dependencies/authorization.py

from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.core.database import get_db
from app.core.security import get_current_user
from app.services.authorization_service import (
    AuthorizationService,
)


def require_agreement_permission(
    permission_key: str,
):

    async def dependency(
        agreement_id: UUID,
        current_user=Depends(
            get_current_user
        ),
        db: AsyncSession = Depends(
            get_db
        ),
    ):

        service = AuthorizationService()

        decision = (
            await service
            .authorize_agreement_action(
                db=db,
                user_id=current_user.id,
                agreement_id=agreement_id,
                permission_key=permission_key,
            )
        )

        if not decision["allowed"]:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=403,
                detail="Agreement access denied",
            )

        return decision

    return dependency

Now an endpoint can do:

@router.get("/{agreement_id}")
async def get_agreement(
    agreement_id: UUID,
    authorization=Depends(
        require_agreement_permission(
            "agreement.view"
        )
    ),
):
    ...

The endpoint itself doesn't need to understand the security rules.

13. Lawyer-only actions

Some operations need additional constraints.

For example:

agreement.propose_change

should require:

participant
+
permission
+
party
+
legal representative assignment

Create:

async def require_representing_lawyer(
    db: AsyncSession,
    *,
    user_id: UUID,
    agreement_id: UUID,
    party_id: UUID,
) -> bool:

Implementation:

from sqlalchemy import select

from app.models.agreement_access import (
    LegalRepresentative,
    LegalRepresentativeAssignment,
)


async def require_representing_lawyer(
    db,
    *,
    user_id,
    agreement_id,
    party_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            LegalRepresentativeAssignment
        )
        .join(
            LegalRepresentative,
            LegalRepresentative.id
            == LegalRepresentativeAssignment
            .legal_representative_id,
        )
        .where(
            LegalRepresentativeAssignment
            .agreement_id == agreement_id,

            LegalRepresentativeAssignment
            .agreement_party_id == party_id,

            LegalRepresentative.user_id == user_id,

            LegalRepresentativeAssignment
            .status == "active",

            LegalRepresentative
            .verification_status == "verified",
        )
    )

    return (
        result.scalar_one_or_none()
        is not None
    )

This means someone cannot simply grant themselves the lawyer role through the frontend.

14. Client approval must be different

Similarly:

agreement.approve

should not automatically mean:

The system needs a participant role/authority configuration.

For example:

PARTICIPANT
LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE
BUSINESS_OWNER
AUTHORIZED_APPROVER
AUTHORIZED_SIGNATORY
OBSERVER

Those are configuration values associated with actual participants.

A lawyer can therefore:

review
comment
propose
counter

while the client can:

approve
reject

and an authorized signatory can:

sign

These responsibilities remain distinct.

15. Workflow + authorization must work together

This is where the previous milestone becomes powerful.

Suppose current state is:

OPPOSING_LEGAL_REVIEW

Lawyer A calls:

POST /agreements/123/propose-change

The backend checks:

1. Is user authenticated?
2. Is user an agreement participant?
3. Is user active?
4. Which party does user represent?
5. Is user an assigned lawyer for that party?
6. Is lawyer verified?
7. Does lawyer have agreement.propose_change?
8. Is the agreement currently in a state where PROPOSE is allowed?
9. Is the submitted base version still current?
10. Are private/public visibility rules satisfied?

Only then:

CHANGE_PROPOSED

is created.

16. Prevent stale-version attacks

This is critical.

Suppose:

Lawyer A loads Version 12

Then Lawyer B changes the agreement:

Version 13

Lawyer A tries to submit a change against Version 12.

The server must reject it.

Create:

async def ensure_current_version(
    db,
    agreement_id,
    base_version_id,
):
    ...

Implementation:

from sqlalchemy import select

from app.models.agreement import Agreement


async def ensure_current_version(
    db,
    *,
    agreement_id,
    base_version_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(Agreement.current_version_id)
        .where(
            Agreement.id == agreement_id
        )
    )

    current_version_id = (
        result.scalar_one_or_none()
    )

    if current_version_id is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "Agreement has no current version"
        )

    if current_version_id != base_version_id:
        raise ValueError(
            "Agreement version is stale"
        )

In the API this should become HTTP 409 Conflict.

17. Never trust submitted old content

This is a major correction to make to the earlier negotiation design.

Bad:

{
    "old_content": "whatever the browser says",
    "new_content": "..."
}

Good:

{
    "base_version_id": "...",
    "new_content": "..."
}

The server does:

base_version_id
       ↓
database
       ↓
immutable content
       ↓
calculate actual diff

The client cannot fabricate the original agreement text.

18. Redline generation

The backend should calculate:

DATABASE VERSION 12
        ↓
     DIFF ENGINE
        ↓
ADD
REMOVE
MODIFY
MOVE
        ↓
AgreementChange
        ↓
AgreementChangeItem

For example:

Clause: PAYMENT-TERM

OLD:
Payment due within 30 days.

NEW:
Payment due within 15 days.

The system stores:

change_type = MODIFY
clause_identifier = PAYMENT-TERM
old_content = server-derived
new_content = submitted proposal

No client-supplied fake old content.

19. Audit every authorization-sensitive action

Create an audit event whenever:

permission granted
permission revoked
participant added
participant removed
lawyer assigned
lawyer removed
approval created
approval rejected
change proposed
change released
signature requested
signatory verified
signature completed
agreement activated
agreement terminated

Example:

await audit_service.record(
    db,
    actor_id=current_user.id,
    tenant_id=agreement.organization_id,
    action="AGREEMENT_CHANGE_PROPOSED",
    resource_type="agreement",
    resource_id=agreement.id,
    metadata={
        "change_id": str(change.id),
        "base_version_id": str(
            change.base_version_id
        ),
    },
)

Do not put sensitive private clause text into the audit metadata.

20. Denial logging

For security monitoring, denied operations should also be recorded.

Example:

USER_NOT_AGREEMENT_PARTICIPANT
PERMISSION_NOT_GRANTED
WRONG_PARTY
LAWYER_NOT_ASSIGNED
LAWYER_NOT_VERIFIED
INVALID_WORKFLOW_STATE

This becomes extremely valuable later for detecting abuse.

Create:

backend/tests/security/test_agreement_authorization.py

import pytest


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_non_participant_cannot_view_agreement():

    User belongs to the organization but is not an

But don't stop there.

The important tests are:

organization member + no participant
        → DENY

participant + no view permission
        → DENY

participant + view permission
        → ALLOW

party A lawyer → party B private notes
        → DENY

party A lawyer → party A private notes
        → ALLOW

unassigned lawyer → propose change
        → DENY

assigned verified lawyer → propose change
        → ALLOW

lawyer → client approval
        → DENY unless explicitly authorized

client → signature
        → DENY unless authorized signatory

authorized signatory → signature
        → ALLOW

stale version → change
        → CONFLICT

executed agreement → direct edit
        → DENY

These tests are more important than a pretty UI.

22. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security later

Application-level authorization is necessary.

For enterprise-grade security, we'll eventually add PostgreSQL RLS as defense in depth.

Conceptually:

Application authorization
        +
PostgreSQL RLS
        +
Private object-storage authorization
        +
Audit trail

So even if a developer accidentally writes:

SELECT * FROM legal_private_comments;

the database itself can prevent cross-tenant/party access.

We should implement this after the application authorization model is stable rather than prematurely making the development environment difficult.

23. Important architectural rule

From now on, every protected resource follows:

Authentication
      ↓
Tenant isolation
      ↓
Resource existence
      ↓
Agreement participation
      ↓
Party isolation
      ↓
Role/representation
      ↓
Permission
      ↓
Workflow state
      ↓
Business/legal requirement
      ↓
Action
      ↓
Audit

Not:

JWT
 ↓
role == admin
 ↓
allow

That would be far too weak for the system you're building.

24. The complete security decision

For a lawyer proposing a change:

                 REQUEST
                    │
                    ▼
             Authenticated?
                    │
             ┌──────┴──────┐
            NO             YES
            │               │
          DENY              ▼
                    Agreement exists?
                           │
                           ▼
                    Participant?
                           │
                           ▼
                    Active participant?
                           │
                           ▼
                     Which party?
                           │
                           ▼
                  Assigned lawyer?
                           │
                           ▼
                   Lawyer verified?
                           │
                           ▼
                 Permission granted?
                           │
                           ▼
                  Correct workflow state?
                           │
                           ▼
                   Current version?
                           │
                           ▼
                  Requirements pass?
                           │
                           ▼
                    CREATE CHANGE
                           │
                           ▼
                     AUDIT EVENT
                           │
                           ▼
                       SUCCESS

That's the authorization model we want.

25. What Milestone 1.6 gives Aariya/ContractOS

You now have the foundation for:

strict agreement-level access
party-level isolation
lawyer representation
permission-based authorization
client approval separation
signatory separation
workflow-aware permissions
stale-version protection
private legal workspace protection
immutable executed versions
auditability
future PostgreSQL RLS
future SSO/SCIM/enterprise RBAC
future API/service-to-service authorization

And importantly, the authorization model doesn't need to know whether the agreement is an NDA, MSA, employment agreement, SaaS agreement, JV agreement, SAFE, or something else.

That stays in the dynamic agreement/workflow configuration layer.

Milestone 1.7 — Dynamic Agreement Type Engine

Now we remove another major source of hardcoding.

The platform should not have separate Python code such as:

if agreement_type == "nda":
    ...
elif agreement_type == "msa":
    ...
elif agreement_type == "employment":
    ...

Instead, the database defines the structure of each agreement type, while the engine interprets that configuration.

The architecture becomes:

Agreement Type
      ↓
Schema Definition
      ↓
Sections
      ↓
Fields
      ↓
Party Requirements
      ↓
Clause Requirements
      ↓
Execution Requirements
      ↓
Workflow
      ↓
Validation
      ↓
Draft
      ↓
Version
      ↓
Document
1. The data model

We already have:

agreement_types

Now add:

agreement_type_versions
agreement_type_sections
agreement_type_fields
agreement_type_requirements
agreement_type_clause_bindings
agreement_type_execution_requirements

This gives us versioned agreement-type definitions.

2. Agreement type versions

An agreement type itself should not be modified destructively.

For example:

NDA
 ├── Definition v1
 ├── Definition v2
 └── Definition v3

Existing agreements continue referencing the definition version they were created against.

Create:

app/models/agreement_type_version.py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import (
    Boolean,
    ForeignKey,
    Integer,
    String,
    Text,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
)


class AgreementTypeVersion(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "agreement_type_versions"

    agreement_type_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreement_types.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        Integer,
        nullable=False,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(200),
        nullable=False,
    )

    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        Text,
        nullable=True,
    )

    schema_version: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(50),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(50),
        nullable=False,
    )

    is_current: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=False,
    )

import uuid

    Boolean,

    Integer,
    String,

from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,

class AgreementTypeSection(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,

    __tablename__ = "agreement_type_sections"

    agreement_type_version_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreement_type_versions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,

5. Why configuration matters

Suppose a field is:

payment_currency

Its configuration could come from the database:

{
    "source": "supported_currencies"
}

Or:

payment_frequency

could use:

{
    "source": "payment_frequencies"
}

The application doesn't need:

if field.key == "payment_currency":

Instead:

field.configuration
       ↓
data source
       ↓
available values

This is the direction we want.

6. Don't store executable rules in the database

There is an important boundary.

Do not put arbitrary Python:

eval(...)
exec(...)
lambda ...

inside configuration.

Likewise, don't allow administrators to upload arbitrary executable JavaScript/Python as "workflow rules."

Instead define a safe rule language.

For example:

{
    "all": [
        {
            "field": "payment.amount",
            "operator": "greater_than",
            "value": 0
        },
        {
            "field": "payment.currency",
            "operator": "exists"
        }
    ]
}

The engine interprets the operators.

7. Rule engine

Create:

app/services/rules/engine.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class RuleResult:
    passed: bool
    reason: str | None = None


class RuleEngine:

    def evaluate(
        self,
        rule: dict[str, Any],
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> RuleResult:

        if "all" in rule:
            results = [
                self.evaluate(
                    child,
                    data,
                )
                for child in rule["all"]
            ]

            failed = [
                result
                for result in results
                if not result.passed
            ]

            if failed:
                return failed[0]

            return RuleResult(True)

        if "any" in rule:
            results = [
                self.evaluate(
                    child,
                    data,
                )
                for child in rule["any"]
            ]

            if any(
                result.passed
                for result in results
            ):
                return RuleResult(True)

            return RuleResult(
                False,
                "None of the required conditions passed",
            )

        return self._evaluate_condition(
            rule,
            data,
        )

    def _evaluate_condition(
        self,
        condition: dict,
        data: dict,
    ) -> RuleResult:

        field = condition["field"]
        operator = condition["operator"]

        value = self._get_value(
            data,
            field,
        )

        if operator == "exists":
            return RuleResult(
                value is not None,
                f"{field} is required",
            )

        if operator == "equals":
            passed = value == condition.get("value")
            return RuleResult(
                passed,
                None if passed
                else f"{field} has an invalid value",
            )

        if operator == "not_equals":
            passed = value != condition.get("value")
            return RuleResult(
                passed,
                None if passed
                else f"{field} has a prohibited value",
            )

        if operator == "greater_than":
            passed = (
                value is not None
                and value > condition["value"]
            )

            return RuleResult(
                passed,
                None if passed
                else f"{field} must be greater than "
                     f"{condition['value']}",
            )

        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported rule operator: {operator}"
        )

    @staticmethod
    def _get_value(
        data: dict,
        path: str,
    ):
        current = data

        for part in path.split("."):
            if not isinstance(current, dict):
                return None

            current = current.get(part)

            if current is None:
                return None

        return current

This is intentionally a small deterministic interpreter, not an arbitrary code executor.

We will expand its supported operators carefully.

11. Dynamic agreement validation

Create:

app/services/agreement_validator.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement_type_requirement import (
    AgreementTypeRequirement,
)
from app.models.agreement_type_version import (
    AgreementTypeVersion,
)

from app.services.rules.engine import (
    RuleEngine,
)


@dataclass
class ValidationIssue:
    requirement_key: str
    message: str


@dataclass
class AgreementValidationResult:
    valid: bool
    issues: list[ValidationIssue]


class AgreementValidator:

    def __init__(
        self,
        rule_engine: RuleEngine,
    ):
        self.rule_engine = rule_engine

    async def validate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_type_version_id: UUID,
        data: dict,
    ) -> AgreementValidationResult:

        result = await db.execute(
            select(
                AgreementTypeRequirement
            )
            .where(
                AgreementTypeRequirement
                .agreement_type_version_id
                == agreement_type_version_id
            )
        )

        requirements = result.scalars().all()

        issues = []

        for requirement in requirements:

            if (
                requirement.requirement_type
                != "rule"
            ):
                continue

            rule = requirement.configuration.get(
                "rule"
            )

            if not rule:
                issues.append(
                    ValidationIssue(
                        requirement_key=(
                            requirement.requirement_key
                        ),
                        message=(
                            "Requirement has no rule configuration"
                        ),
                    )
                )
                continue

            evaluation = self.rule_engine.evaluate(
                rule,
                data,
            )

            if not evaluation.passed:
                issues.append(
                    ValidationIssue(
                        requirement_key=(
                            requirement.requirement_key
                        ),
                        message=(
                            evaluation.reason
                            or "Requirement failed"
                        ),
                    )
                )

        return AgreementValidationResult(
            valid=len(issues) == 0,
            issues=issues,
        )
12. Agreement creation must snapshot the type definition

This is another important integrity rule.

Suppose:

Agreement Type: MSA
Definition v4

is used to create Agreement #100.

Later an administrator publishes:

MSA Definition v5

Agreement #100 must not silently change.

Therefore the agreement stores:

agreement_type_id
agreement_type_version_id

Add this field to Agreement:

agreement_type_version_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
    UUID(as_uuid=True),
    ForeignKey(
        "agreement_type_versions.id",
        ondelete="RESTRICT",
    ),
    nullable=False,
)

Now:

Agreement #100
       ↓
MSA
       ↓
Definition v4

remains stable.

14. Schema endpoint

Create:

app/api/agreement_types.py

from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.core.database import get_db
from app.models.agreement_type_version import (
    AgreementTypeVersion,
)
from app.models.agreement_type_section import (
    AgreementTypeSection,
)
from app.models.agreement_type_field import (
    AgreementTypeField,
)


router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/agreement-types",
    tags=["agreement-types"],
)


@router.get(
    "/{agreement_type_id}/versions/{version_id}/schema"
)
async def get_agreement_type_schema(
    agreement_type_id: UUID,
    version_id: UUID,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
):

    version_result = await db.execute(
        select(AgreementTypeVersion)
        .where(
            AgreementTypeVersion.id == version_id,
            AgreementTypeVersion.agreement_type_id
            == agreement_type_id,
        )
    )

    version = version_result.scalar_one_or_none()

    if version is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=404,
            detail="Agreement type version not found",
        )

    sections_result = await db.execute(
        select(AgreementTypeSection)
        .where(
            AgreementTypeSection
            .agreement_type_version_id
            == version.id
        )
        .order_by(
            AgreementTypeSection.display_order
        )
    )

    sections = sections_result.scalars().all()

    response_sections = []

    for section in sections:

        fields_result = await db.execute(
            select(AgreementTypeField)
            .where(
                AgreementTypeField.section_id
                == section.id
            )
            .order_by(
                AgreementTypeField.display_order
            )
        )

        fields = fields_result.scalars().all()

        response_sections.append({
            "id": str(section.id),
            "key": section.key,
            "name": section.name,
            "required": section.required,
            "fields": [
                {
                    "id": str(field.id),
                    "key": field.key,
                    "label": field.label,
                    "field_type": field.field_type,
                    "required": field.required,
                    "configuration": field.configuration,
                }
                for field in fields
            ],
        })

    return {
        "agreement_type_id": str(
            agreement_type_id
        ),
        "version_id": str(version.id),
        "version": version.version,
        "schema_version": version.schema_version,
        "sections": response_sections,
    }

This is now a real schema-driven API.

16. Critical: schema validation

The user can submit:

{
    "unexpected_field": "abc"
}

The server must not blindly accept it.

Validation should verify:

field exists
field type correct
required field exists
nested structure correct
allowed values valid
conditional requirements satisfied

We can implement a JSON Schema layer next.

The existing AgreementType.schema field should eventually contain a formal schema identifier/version rather than being a dumping ground for arbitrary configuration.

17. Clause library architecture

Now we need to make the clause engine equally dynamic.

The structure should become:

clauses
    ↓
clause_versions
    ↓
jurisdiction applicability
    ↓
agreement-type bindings
    ↓
conditions
    ↓
selected clause versions

A clause should have:

identifier
title
category
status

and its versions:

version
content
variables
status
effective_from
effective_to

This lets us later connect authoritative legal research without overwriting historical clauses.

18. Don't let AI directly invent legal clauses

This will matter later.

The AI layer should not be allowed to silently create:

"legally compliant clause"

and put it into an executed agreement.

Instead:

Legal knowledge
       ↓
Authoritative sources
       ↓
Reviewed/approved clause
       ↓
Clause library
       ↓
Agreement type binding
       ↓
Draft

AI can assist with:

drafting
comparison
explanation
risk identification
research
suggestions

but the provenance of legal content must remain traceable.

19. Execution requirements also become dynamic

Remember our earlier execution architecture.

Agreement types can specify:

execution requirement

For example:

signature_required
signatory_authority_required
identity_verification_required
witness_required
notarization_required
physical_execution_required
specific_certificate_required

But these should not be blindly attached to agreement types without jurisdictional context.

The eventual resolution should be:

Agreement Type
      +
Jurisdiction
      +
Parties
      +
Transaction characteristics
      ↓
Applicable legal/execution requirements

This is where the legal knowledge layer from a later milestone comes in.

1.8.1 Database model

Create:

backend/app/models/clause.py
import uuid
from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import (
    Boolean,
    DateTime,
    ForeignKey,
    Integer,
    String,
    Text,
    UniqueConstraint,
    JSON,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

from app.models.base import Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin


class Clause(Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin):
    __tablename__ = "clauses"

    key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(150),
        nullable=False,
        unique=True,
        index=True,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
    )

    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        Text,
        nullable=True,
    )

    category: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=True,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(30),
        nullable=False,
        default="active",
        index=True,
    )

    versions = relationship(
        "ClauseVersion",
        back_populates="clause",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )


class ClauseVersion(Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin):
    __tablename__ = "clause_versions"

    clause_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("clauses.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    version_number: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        Integer,
        nullable=False,
    )

    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
    )

    content: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        Text,
        nullable=False,
    )

    content_hash: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(64),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(30),
        nullable=False,
        default="draft",
        index=True,
    )

    effective_from: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    effective_until: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    provenance: Mapped[dict | None] = mapped_column(
        JSON,
        nullable=True,
    )

    approved_by: Mapped[uuid.UUID | None] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    approved_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    clause = relationship(
        "Clause",
        back_populates="versions",
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "clause_id",
            "version_number",
            name="uq_clause_version_number",
        ),
    )
Important

ClauseVersion.content is immutable once approved.

You don't edit:

Clause v1

into v2.

You create:

Clause v1
Clause v2
Clause v3

This is essential for legal traceability.

1.8.3 Clause conditions

A clause may only apply under certain conditions.

For example:

IF transaction.requires_data_processing == true
THEN include data-processing clause

But do not use Python eval().

Create:

backend/app/models/clause_condition.py
import uuid

from sqlalchemy import (
    ForeignKey,
    Integer,
    JSON,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin


class ClauseCondition(Base, UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin, TimestampMixin):
    __tablename__ = "clause_conditions"

    clause_version_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("clause_versions.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    condition: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSON,
        nullable=False,
    )

    display_order: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        Integer,
        nullable=False,
        default=0,
    )

The condition is stored as data.

Example structure:

{
  "all": [
    {
      "path": "transaction.contains_personal_data",
      "operator": "equals",
      "value": true
    }
  ]
}

That is configuration, not executable code.

1.8.7 Hash every clause version

import hashlib


def calculate_clause_hash(content: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(
        content.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()

1.8.8 Clause version selection

Now create:

backend/app/services/clause_selector.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.clause import ClauseVersion


class ClauseSelector:

    async def select_current_approved_version(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        clause_id,
        effective_at: datetime | None = None,
    ) -> ClauseVersion | None:

        effective_at = effective_at or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

        result = await db.execute(
            select(ClauseVersion)
            .where(
                ClauseVersion.clause_id == clause_id,
                ClauseVersion.status == "approved",
                ClauseVersion.effective_from.is_not(None),
                ClauseVersion.effective_from <= effective_at,
            )
            .where(
                (ClauseVersion.effective_until.is_(None))
                | (ClauseVersion.effective_until > effective_at)
            )
            .order_by(
                ClauseVersion.version_number.desc()
            )
            .limit(1)
        )

        return result.scalar_one_or_none()

Notice what isn't here:

if clause == "NDA":

No agreement-type-specific legal assumptions.

1.8.9 Safe condition evaluator

We already created a rule engine in Milestone 1.7.

We should reuse the same deterministic rule language rather than creating multiple incompatible rule engines.

Create:

backend/app/services/clause_condition_engine.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class ConditionResult:
    matched: bool
    reason: str | None = None


class ClauseConditionEngine:

    def evaluate(
        self,
        condition: dict,
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> ConditionResult:

        if "all" in condition:
            results = [
                self.evaluate(item, data)
                for item in condition["all"]
            ]

            if all(result.matched for result in results):
                return ConditionResult(True)

            return ConditionResult(
                False,
                "Not all conditions matched",
            )

        if "any" in condition:
            results = [
                self.evaluate(item, data)
                for item in condition["any"]
            ]

            if any(result.matched for result in results):
                return ConditionResult(True)

            return ConditionResult(
                False,
                "No condition matched",
            )

        path = condition.get("path")
        operator = condition.get("operator")

        actual = self._get_value(data, path)

        if operator == "exists":
            expected = condition.get("value", True)

            return ConditionResult(
                (actual is not None) == expected
            )

        if operator == "equals":
            return ConditionResult(
                actual == condition.get("value")
            )

        if operator == "not_equals":
            return ConditionResult(
                actual != condition.get("value")
            )

        if operator == "greater_than":
            return ConditionResult(
                actual is not None
                and actual > condition["value"]
            )

        if operator == "less_than":
            return ConditionResult(
                actual is not None
                and actual < condition["value"]
            )

        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported clause condition operator: {operator}"
        )

    def _get_value(
        self,
        data: dict[str, Any],
        path: str | None,
    ) -> Any:

        if not path:
            return None

        current: Any = data

        for part in path.split("."):
            if not isinstance(current, dict):
                return None

            current = current.get(part)

            if current is None:
                return None

        return current

Later, this should probably be unified with the Milestone 1.7 RuleEngine so you have one policy/rule evaluation framework.

1.8.10 Clause applicability service

Now combine:

agreement type
clause binding
jurisdiction
conditions
effective dates
approved version

Create:

backend/app/services/clause_applicability.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.clause import ClauseVersion
from app.models.clause_condition import ClauseCondition
from app.models.clause_jurisdiction import ClauseJurisdiction
from app.services.clause_condition_engine import (
    ClauseConditionEngine,
)
from app.services.clause_selector import ClauseSelector


@dataclass
class ApplicableClause:
    clause_version: ClauseVersion
    reason: str


class ClauseApplicabilityService:

    def __init__(self):
        self.selector = ClauseSelector()
        self.condition_engine = ClauseConditionEngine()

    async def resolve_clause(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        clause_id,
        jurisdiction_id,
        agreement_data: dict,
        effective_at: datetime | None = None,
    ) -> ApplicableClause | None:

        effective_at = (
            effective_at or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        )

        clause_version = (
            await self.selector.select_current_approved_version(
                db,
                clause_id=clause_id,
                effective_at=effective_at,
            )
        )

        if clause_version is None:
            return None

        jurisdiction_result = await db.execute(
            select(ClauseJurisdiction)
            .where(
                ClauseJurisdiction.clause_version_id
                == clause_version.id,
                ClauseJurisdiction.jurisdiction_id
                == jurisdiction_id,
            )
        )

        jurisdiction_binding = (
            jurisdiction_result.scalar_one_or_none()
        )

        if (
            jurisdiction_binding is not None
            and not jurisdiction_binding.applicable
        ):
            return None

        condition_result = await db.execute(
            select(ClauseCondition)
            .where(
                ClauseCondition.clause_version_id
                == clause_version.id
            )
            .order_by(
                ClauseCondition.display_order
            )
        )

        conditions = condition_result.scalars().all()

        for condition in conditions:
            result = self.condition_engine.evaluate(
                condition.condition,
                agreement_data,
            )

            if not result.matched:
                return None

        return ApplicableClause(
            clause_version=clause_version,
            reason="Applicable approved clause version",
        )

This gives us the core:

Should this clause be included?

without embedding legal assumptions in Python.

1.8.11 Variable resolution

Now resolve:

{{party_a.legal_name}}

against actual data.

Create:

backend/app/services/clause_renderer.py
import re
from typing import Any


VARIABLE_PATTERN = re.compile(
    r"\{\{\s*([a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+)\s*\}\}"
)


class ClauseRenderer:

    def render(
        self,
        content: str,
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> str:

        missing: list[str] = []

        def replace(match: re.Match) -> str:
            path = match.group(1)

            value = self._resolve(
                data,
                path,
            )

            if value is None:
                missing.append(path)
                return match.group(0)

            return str(value)

        rendered = VARIABLE_PATTERN.sub(
            replace,
            content,
        )

        if missing:
            raise ValueError(
                "Missing required clause variables: "
                + ", ".join(sorted(set(missing)))
            )

        return rendered

    def _resolve(
        self,
        data: dict[str, Any],
        path: str,
    ) -> Any:

        current: Any = data

        for part in path.split("."):
            if not isinstance(current, dict):
                return None

            current = current.get(part)

        return current

This is deliberately strict.

If the clause requires:

{{party_a.legal_name}}

and the real database does not contain it, the system fails the draft generation.

It does not invent:

ABC Holdings Ltd.

It does not use:

[COMPANY NAME]

and it does not silently produce an incomplete legal document.

1.8.12 Draft assembly

Now create:

backend/app/services/agreement_draft_assembler.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement import Agreement
from app.models.agreement_type import (
    AgreementTypeClauseBinding,
)
from app.services.clause_applicability import (
    ClauseApplicabilityService,
)
from app.services.clause_renderer import ClauseRenderer


@dataclass
class AssembledClause:
    clause_id: object
    clause_version_id: object
    title: str
    content: str
    display_order: int


class AgreementDraftAssembler:

    def __init__(self):
        self.applicability = (
            ClauseApplicabilityService()
        )

        self.renderer = ClauseRenderer()

    async def assemble(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement: Agreement,
        agreement_data: dict,
    ) -> list[AssembledClause]:

        result = await db.execute(
            select(AgreementTypeClauseBinding)
            .where(
                AgreementTypeClauseBinding
                .agreement_type_version_id
                == agreement.agreement_type_version_id
            )
            .order_by(
                AgreementTypeClauseBinding.display_order
            )
        )

        bindings = result.scalars().all()

        assembled: list[AssembledClause] = []

        for binding in bindings:

            applicable = (
                await self.applicability.resolve_clause(
                    db,
                    clause_id=binding.clause_id,
                    jurisdiction_id=agreement.jurisdiction_id,
                    agreement_data=agreement_data,
                )
            )

            if applicable is None:

                if binding.required:
                    raise ValueError(
                        "Required clause has no applicable "
                        "approved version"
                    )

                continue

            rendered = self.renderer.render(
                applicable.clause_version.content,
                agreement_data,
            )

            assembled.append(
                AssembledClause(
                    clause_id=binding.clause_id,
                    clause_version_id=(
                        applicable.clause_version.id
                    ),
                    title=(
                        applicable.clause_version.title
                    ),
                    content=rendered,
                    display_order=binding.display_order,
                )
            )

        return assembled
1.8.13 Very important: agreement_data must come from the database

Do not allow the frontend to send arbitrary legal facts such as:

{
  "party_a": {
    "legal_name": "Whatever the browser says"
  }
}

The frontend can submit agreement input, but the backend must validate it and resolve authoritative fields from the actual entities.

For example:

agreement
   │
   ├── party A
   │      └── legal entity
   │             └── legal_name
   │
   ├── party B
   │      └── legal entity
   │             └── legal_name
   │
   ├── jurisdiction
   │
   └── agreement data

Then construct the rendering context server-side.

1.8.14 Server-side context builder

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_context.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement import Agreement
from app.models.agreement_access import AgreementParty
from app.models.legal_entity import LegalEntity


class AgreementContextBuilder:

    async def build(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        agreement: Agreement,
    ) -> dict:

        result = await db.execute(
            select(AgreementParty, LegalEntity)
            .join(
                LegalEntity,
                LegalEntity.id
                == AgreementParty.legal_entity_id,
            )
            .where(
                AgreementParty.agreement_id
                == agreement.id
            )
        )

        parties = result.all()

        context = {
            "agreement": {
                "id": str(agreement.id),
                "title": agreement.title,
                "effective_date": (
                    agreement.effective_date.isoformat()
                    if agreement.effective_date
                    else None
                ),
                "execution_date": (
                    agreement.execution_date.isoformat()
                    if agreement.execution_date
                    else None
                ),
                "expiry_date": (
                    agreement.expiry_date.isoformat()
                    if agreement.expiry_date
                    else None
                ),
                "governing_law": agreement.governing_law,
            },
            "parties": [],
        }

        for party, entity in parties:

            context["parties"].append(
                {
                    "party_id": str(party.id),
                    "role": party.party_role,
                    "legal_entity_id": str(
                        entity.id
                    ),
                    "legal_name": entity.legal_name,
                    "registration_number": (
                        entity.registration_number
                    ),
                    "registered_address": (
                        entity.registered_address
                    ),
                    "tax_identifier": (
                        entity.tax_identifier
                    ),
                }
            )

        return context

This is only the beginning.

Later we should expose convenient aliases such as:

party_a
party_b

only when their identity is determined from the actual agreement party records, not from frontend assumptions.

1.8.15 Do not make party_a and party_b arbitrary

This is important.

A contract could have:

Buyer
Seller
Guarantor
Licensor
Licensee
Employer
Employee
Lender
Borrower
Investor
Company
Founder

Therefore the better long-term representation is:

{
  "parties": {
    "buyer": {...},
    "seller": {...},
    "guarantor": {...}
  }
}

where those roles originate from the agreement type/party requirements.

So the architecture becomes:

Agreement Type
       ↓
Party Requirement
       ↓
Agreement Party
       ↓
Legal Entity
       ↓
Authoritative Data

not:

frontend says party_a = ...
1.8.16 Generate the actual agreement version

Once clauses are assembled, construct the draft content.

def assemble_document(
    clauses: list[AssembledClause],
) -> str:

    ordered = sorted(
        clauses,
        key=lambda item: item.display_order,
    )

    sections: list[str] = []

    for index, clause in enumerate(ordered, start=1):

        sections.append(
            f"{index}. {clause.title}\n\n"
            f"{clause.content}"
        )

    return "\n\n".join(sections)

Then:

from app.services.agreement_draft_assembler import (
    AgreementDraftAssembler,
)
from app.services.agreement_context import (
    AgreementContextBuilder,
)
from app.services.version_service import create_version


async def generate_draft(
    db,
    agreement,
    created_by,
):

    context_builder = AgreementContextBuilder()

    agreement_data = await context_builder.build(
        db,
        agreement,
    )

    assembler = AgreementDraftAssembler()

    clauses = await assembler.assemble(
        db,
        agreement=agreement,
        agreement_data=agreement_data,
    )

    content = assemble_document(clauses)

    version = await create_version(
        db,
        agreement,
        content,
        created_by,
    )

    return version

Now the flow is:

Real DB data
     ↓
Agreement context
     ↓
Applicable approved clauses
     ↓
Variables resolved
     ↓
Conditions evaluated
     ↓
Draft assembled
     ↓
Version created
     ↓
SHA-256 hash
     ↓
Legal review
1.8.17 Record exactly which clauses were used

This is extremely important for auditability.

Add:

AgreementVersionClause
import uuid

from sqlalchemy import (

    Integer,
    UniqueConstraint,

from app.models.base import (
    Base,

    TimestampMixin,

class AgreementVersionClause(
    Base,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,

    __tablename__ = "agreement_version_clauses"

    agreement_version_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreement_versions.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    clause_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(

            ondelete="RESTRICT",

        nullable=False,
    )

    clause_version_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(

            "clause_versions.id",

        nullable=False,

Then when generating the version:

for clause in clauses:
    db.add(
        AgreementVersionClause(
            agreement_version_id=version.id,
            clause_id=clause.clause_id,
            clause_version_id=clause.clause_version_id,
            display_order=clause.display_order,
        )
    )

Now the platform can later answer:

Which exact approved clause versions were used to generate this agreement?

Without guessing.

1.8.18 Provenance

The ClauseVersion.provenance field should hold structured provenance.

For example, conceptually:

{
  "source_type": "legal_research",
  "source_id": "...",
  "source_version": "...",
  "review_status": "approved",
  "reviewed_at": "...",
  "reviewed_by": "..."
}

But do not populate this with invented values.

If the clause came from:

an organization's approved internal clause,
an external licensed legal source,
an authoritative government source,
a lawyer-created clause,

the actual source should be recorded.

If provenance is unavailable, the system should not pretend it has provenance.

1.8.19 Clause lifecycle

Use:

DRAFT
   ↓
UNDER_REVIEW
   ↓
APPROVED
   ↓
ACTIVE
   ↓
SUPERSEDED
   ↓
RETIRED

A safer implementation is to distinguish:

Clause
    │
    ├── Version 1 → superseded
    ├── Version 2 → approved/current
    └── Version 3 → draft

An executed agreement referencing Version 1 continues referencing Version 1 even if Version 2 later becomes current.

That is non-negotiable for historical accuracy.

1.8.20 Clause changes during negotiation

Suppose the original agreement contains:

Clause Version 14

A lawyer proposes a modification.

Do not modify Clause Version 14.

Instead:

Original Agreement Version
        │
        ▼
Negotiation Change
        │
        ├── base_version_id
        ├── clause_identifier
        ├── old_content
        └── proposed new content

Then:

Client confirms
       ↓
Released to opposing party
       ↓
Opposing lawyer reviews
       ↓
Counterproposal

The underlying approved clause library remains untouched.

1.8.21 Redline generation

Your existing negotiation architecture should compare:

base agreement version
        ↓
proposed agreement version

rather than trusting client-provided old text.

The backend should calculate:

ADD
REMOVE
MODIFY
MOVE
REPLACE

and store the result in:

AgreementChangeItem

For example:

Clause: Limitation of Liability

OLD:
...

NEW:
...

Change:
MODIFY

Proposed by:
Lawyer X

Representing:
Party A

Status:
PENDING_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION

Then the client confirms.

Only then:

RELEASED_TO_OTHER_PARTY

This fits directly into the negotiation state machine we already established.

1.8.22 API endpoint

Create:

backend/app/agreements/routes.py

or your existing agreement router.

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.core.database import get_db

router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/agreements",

The actual endpoint should first use the authorization dependency:

@router.post(
    "/{agreement_id}/draft/generate",
)
async def generate_agreement_draft(
    agreement_id: str,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    current_user=Depends(
        require_agreement_permission(
            "agreement.propose_change"
        )
    ),

    ...

But don't stop there.

The endpoint must also enforce:

Authentication
→ Tenant isolation
→ Agreement participant
→ Party
→ Permission
→ Workflow state
→ Agreement type version
→ Valid schema
→ Applicable clauses
→ Required clauses
→ Required variables
→ Draft generation
→ Version creation
→ Audit event
1.8.23 One major correction to the existing authorization design

We previously allowed participant permissions such as:

agreement.propose_change

That should not automatically mean:

this user can generate an entire first draft.

Those are different capabilities.

Add permissions such as:

agreement.create_draft
agreement.edit_draft
agreement.propose_change
agreement.accept_change
agreement.reject_change
agreement.approve
agreement.request_signature
agreement.sign

And keep them database-driven.

1.8.24 Audit the generation

When a draft is generated:

await audit_service.record(
    db,
    actor_id=current_user.id,
    action="AGREEMENT_DRAFT_GENERATED",
    resource_type="agreement",
    resource_id=agreement.id,
    metadata={
        "agreement_version_id": str(version.id),
    },
)

Don't put the complete contract text into the audit event.

The immutable version/document storage is the source of the content.

1.8.25 The complete clause architecture

At this point:

                       ┌─────────────────────┐

                       └──────────┬──────────┘

                       ┌─────────────────────┐

                       ┌─────────────────────┐
                       │ Clause Bindings     │
                       └──────────┬──────────┘
                                  │
                                  ▼
                       ┌─────────────────────┐
                       │ Clause              │
                       └──────────┬──────────┘
                                  │
                                  ▼
                       ┌─────────────────────┐
                       │ Clause Version      │
                       └──────┬───────┬──────┘
                              │       │
                ┌─────────────┘       └──────────────┐
                ▼                                    ▼
       ┌─────────────────┐                  ┌─────────────────┐
       │ Jurisdiction    │                  │ Conditions      │
       │ applicability   │                  │                 │
       └────────┬────────┘                  └────────┬────────┘
                │                                    │
                └────────────────┬───────────────────┘

                       ┌─────────────────────┐
                       │ Applicability       │
