1.9.1 Add JSON Schema support

Add to requirements.txt:

jsonschema

Then:

pip install jsonschema

We will use JSON Schema for data-shape validation, while our database-driven rule engine handles business/legal relationships.

1.9.2 Store the formal schema

Your AgreementTypeVersion already has:

schema_version

Add a proper schema field.

backend/app/models/agreement_type.py

Add:

schema_definition: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
    JSON,
    nullable=False,
    default=dict,
)

The important distinction is:

schema_definition

describes the shape and types of data.

The existing requirements describe business/legal conditions.

For example:

Schema:
effective_date must be a date

Rule:
expiry_date must be after effective_date

Those are different concerns.

1.9.3 Example schema structure

The database can contain a schema such as:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "title": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1
    },
    "effective_date": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "date"
    },
    "expiry_date": {
      "type": ["string", "null"],
      "format": "date"
    },
    "governing_law": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "title",
    "effective_date"
  ],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

This is not hardcoded in Python.

The schema comes from the persisted agreement-type version.

1.9.4 Schema validation service

Create:

backend/app/services/schema_validator.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator


@dataclass
class SchemaValidationError:
    path: str
    message: str
    validator: str | None = None


@dataclass
class SchemaValidationResult:
    valid: bool
    errors: list[SchemaValidationError]


class SchemaValidator:

    def validate(
        self,
        schema: dict[str, Any],
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> SchemaValidationResult:

        validator = Draft202012Validator(schema)

        errors = []

        for error in sorted(
            validator.iter_errors(data),
            key=lambda item: list(item.path),
        ):
            path = ".".join(
                str(part)
                for part in error.path
            )

            errors.append(
                SchemaValidationError(
                    path=path,
                    message=error.message,
                    validator=error.validator,
                )
            )

        return SchemaValidationResult(
            valid=not errors,
            errors=errors,
        )

This gives us deterministic validation.

1.9.5 Don't allow arbitrary JSON Schema

There is an important security issue here.

A user who can create agreement-type configurations should not automatically be able to configure dangerous or unsupported schema behavior.

Create a schema policy.

backend/app/services/schema_policy.py
from typing import Any


ALLOWED_SCHEMA_KEYS = {
    "type",
    "properties",
    "required",
    "additionalProperties",
    "items",
    "enum",
    "const",
    "minimum",
    "maximum",
    "exclusiveMinimum",
    "exclusiveMaximum",
    "minLength",
    "maxLength",
    "pattern",
    "format",
    "minItems",
    "maxItems",
    "uniqueItems",
    "allOf",
    "anyOf",
}


class SchemaPolicyError(ValueError):
    pass


class SchemaPolicy:

    def validate_schema(
        self,
        schema: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> None:

        self._walk(schema)

    def _walk(
        self,
        value: Any,
    ) -> None:

        if isinstance(value, dict):

            for key, child in value.items():

                if key not in ALLOWED_SCHEMA_KEYS:
                    raise SchemaPolicyError(
                        f"Unsupported schema keyword: {key}"
                    )

                self._walk(child)

        elif isinstance(value, list):

            for item in value:
                self._walk(item)

This gives the platform control over what its schema language supports.

1.9.6 Field-level validation

The dynamic field definitions from Milestone 1.7 should also be validated.

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_field_validator.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class FieldValidationError:
    field: str
    message: str


class AgreementFieldValidator:

    def validate(
        self,
        fields,
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> list[FieldValidationError]:

        errors = []

        for field in fields:

            value = data.get(field.key)

            if field.required and self._empty(value):
                errors.append(
                    FieldValidationError(
                        field=field.key,
                        message="Required field is missing",
                    )
                )

        return errors

    @staticmethod
    def _empty(value) -> bool:
        return value is None or value == ""

This is supplementary to JSON Schema.

The formal schema remains authoritative for structural validation.

1.9.7 Cross-field validation

Now we handle things such as:

effective_date <= expiry_date

or:

termination_notice_days <= contract_term_days

without hardcoding those rules.

Use the existing safe rule language.

For example:

{
  "all": [
    {
      "path": "expiry_date",
      "operator": "greater_than",
      "value_path": "effective_date"
    }
  ]
}

We need to improve the existing rule engine so comparisons can reference another data field.

1.9.8 Upgrade the rule evaluator

Modify:

backend/app/services/rule_engine.py

Use:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class RuleResult:
    passed: bool
    reason: str | None = None


class RuleEngine:

    def evaluate(
        self,
        rule: dict[str, Any],
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> RuleResult:

        if "all" in rule:

            results = [
                self.evaluate(child, data)
                for child in rule["all"]
            ]

            failed = [
                result
                for result in results
                if not result.passed
            ]

            if failed:
                return RuleResult(
                    False,
                    failed[0].reason,
                )

            return RuleResult(True)

        if "any" in rule:

            results = [
                self.evaluate(child, data)
                for child in rule["any"]
            ]

            if any(
                result.passed
                for result in results
            ):
                return RuleResult(True)

            return RuleResult(
                False,
                "No alternative condition matched",
            )

        return self._evaluate_condition(
            rule,
            data,
        )

    def _evaluate_condition(
        self,
        rule: dict[str, Any],
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> RuleResult:

        path = rule.get("path")
        operator = rule.get("operator")

        actual = self._get_value(
            data,
            path,
        )

        if "value_path" in rule:
            expected = self._get_value(
                data,
                rule["value_path"],
            )
        else:
            expected = rule.get("value")

        if operator == "exists":
            passed = (
                actual is not None
            )

        elif operator == "equals":
            passed = actual == expected

        elif operator == "not_equals":
            passed = actual != expected

        elif operator == "greater_than":
            passed = (
                actual is not None
                and expected is not None
                and actual > expected
            )

        elif operator == "greater_than_or_equal":
            passed = (
                actual is not None
                and expected is not None
                and actual >= expected
            )

        elif operator == "less_than":
            passed = (
                actual is not None
                and expected is not None
                and actual < expected
            )

        elif operator == "less_than_or_equal":
            passed = (
                actual is not None
                and expected is not None
                and actual <= expected
            )

        else:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unsupported operator: {operator}"
            )

        return RuleResult(
            passed,
            None
            if passed
            else f"Rule failed: {path} {operator}",
        )

    def _get_value(
        self,
        data: dict[str, Any],
        path: str | None,
    ) -> Any:

        if not path:
            return None

        current = data

        for part in path.split("."):

            if not isinstance(
                current,
                dict,
            ):
                return None

            current = current.get(part)

        return current

Still no eval().

1.9.9 Dates need special treatment

There is a problem with comparing dates represented as strings.

For example:

"2026-09-03"

should be interpreted as a date, not merely compared as arbitrary text.

Create:

backend/app/services/value_normalizer.py
from datetime import date, datetime
from decimal import Decimal


class ValueNormalizer:

    def normalize(
        self,
        value,
        data_type: str | None,
    ):

        if value is None:
            return None

        if data_type == "date":
            if isinstance(value, date):
                return value

            return date.fromisoformat(value)

        if data_type == "datetime":
            if isinstance(value, datetime):
                return value

            return datetime.fromisoformat(value)

        if data_type == "integer":
            return int(value)

        if data_type == "decimal":
            return Decimal(str(value))

        if data_type == "boolean":
            if isinstance(value, bool):
                return value

            raise ValueError(
                "Invalid boolean value"
            )

        return value

The production implementation should derive the expected type from the configured field/schema definition.

1.9.10 Build the complete validation result

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_validator.py
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class ValidationIssue:
    code: str
    message: str
    path: str | None = None
    severity: str = "error"


@dataclass
class AgreementValidationResult:
    valid: bool
    issues: list[ValidationIssue] = field(
        default_factory=list
    )

    @property
    def errors(self):
        return [
            issue
            for issue in self.issues
            if issue.severity == "error"
        ]

    @property
    def warnings(self):
        return [
            issue
            for issue in self.issues
            if issue.severity == "warning"
        ]
1.9.11 Main validation service
backend/app/services/agreement_validation_service.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.agreement_type import (
    AgreementTypeSection,
    AgreementTypeRequirement,
)

from app.services.agreement_validator import (
    AgreementValidationResult,
    ValidationIssue,
)

from app.services.schema_validator import (
    SchemaValidator,
)

from app.services.schema_policy import (
    SchemaPolicy,
    SchemaPolicyError,
)

from app.services.rule_engine import (
    RuleEngine,
)


class AgreementValidationService:

    def __init__(self):

        self.schema_validator = (
            SchemaValidator()
        )

        self.schema_policy = (
            SchemaPolicy()
        )

        self.rule_engine = (
            RuleEngine()
        )

    async def validate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        agreement_type_version,
        data: dict,
    ) -> AgreementValidationResult:

        issues: list[ValidationIssue] = []

        try:

            self.schema_policy.validate_schema(
                agreement_type_version.schema_definition
            )

        except SchemaPolicyError as exc:

            issues.append(
                ValidationIssue(
                    code="INVALID_SCHEMA_CONFIGURATION",
                    message=str(exc),
                )
            )

            return AgreementValidationResult(
                valid=False,
                issues=issues,
            )

        schema_result = (
            self.schema_validator.validate(
                agreement_type_version.schema_definition,
                data,
            )
        )

        for error in schema_result.errors:

            issues.append(
                ValidationIssue(
                    code="SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED",
                    path=error.path or None,
                    message=error.message,
                )
            )

        requirements_result = await db.execute(
            select(
                AgreementTypeRequirement
            ).where(
                AgreementTypeRequirement
                .agreement_type_version_id
                == agreement_type_version.id
            )
        )

        requirements = (
            requirements_result.scalars().all()
        )

        for requirement in requirements:

            if requirement.requirement_type != "rule":
                continue

            rule_result = (
                self.rule_engine.evaluate(
                    requirement.configuration,
                    data,
                )
            )

            if not rule_result.passed:

                issues.append(
                    ValidationIssue(
                        code=requirement.requirement_key,
                        message=(
                            rule_result.reason
                            or "Requirement failed"
                        ),
                    )
                )

        return AgreementValidationResult(
            valid=not any(
                issue.severity == "error"
                for issue in issues
            ),
            issues=issues,
        )

This is important.

ONLY THEN create agreement
1.9.13 Transaction boundary

Use one database transaction for creation.

Conceptually:

async with db.begin():

    validation = await validator.validate(
        db,
        agreement_type_version=type_version,
        data=request.data,
    )

    if not validation.valid:
        raise AgreementValidationException(
            validation
        )

    agreement = Agreement(...)

    db.add(agreement)

    await db.flush()

    # parties

    # initial version

    # workflow instance

    # audit event

If any required operation fails:

ROLLBACK

No half-created agreement.

1.9.15 Don't leak internal validation details

For example, don't expose:

SQLAlchemy exception...
PostgreSQL constraint...

to the client.

Log those internally.

Return controlled errors.

1.9.16 Party validation

Schema validation alone isn't enough.

A party could provide:

legal_entity_id = UUID

that belongs to another organization.

So party validation must perform:

request
 ↓
legal_entity_id
 ↓
load legal entity
 ↓
verify organization ownership
 ↓
verify status
 ↓
verify agreement eligibility
 ↓
create AgreementParty

Never trust:

organization_id

from the request.

Resolve the organization from:

authenticated user
→ membership
→ authorized tenant
1.9.17 Signatory validation

At creation time, don't necessarily require signatures.

But when moving toward execution:

Agreement
 ↓
Agreement Party
 ↓
Legal Entity
 ↓
Authorized Signatory
 ↓
Verified authority

The system should verify that the selected signer is actually associated with the relevant legal entity and has the necessary authority.

This stays separate from the schema engine because it's an authorization/execution concern.

1.9.18 Jurisdiction validation

Likewise:

jurisdiction_id

must resolve to an actual database jurisdiction.

Never accept:

{
  "governing_law": "whatever"
}

as proof that the legal rule applies.

You need:

Jurisdiction
 ↓
Legal sources
 ↓
Rules
 ↓
Effective dates
 ↓
Applicability

This will become especially important when we build the legal knowledge layer.

1.9.20 Validation pipeline

Create:

backend/app/services/agreement_validation_pipeline.py
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ValidationContext:
    db: object
    agreement_type_version: object
    data: dict
    agreement: object | None = None


class AgreementValidationPipeline:

    def __init__(
        self,
        validators,
    ):
        self.validators = validators

    async def validate(
        self,
        context: ValidationContext,
    ):

        issues = []

        for validator in self.validators:

            result = await validator.validate(
                context
            )

            issues.extend(
                result.issues
            )

            if result.fatal:
                break

        return issues

This example requires a common validator contract.

Let's define that cleanly.

1.9.21 Validator interface
backend/app/services/validators/base.py
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class ValidatorResult:
    issues: list = field(
        default_factory=list
    )

    fatal: bool = False

    @property
    def valid(self):
        return not any(
            issue.severity == "error"
            for issue in self.issues
        )


class AgreementValidator(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def validate(
        self,
        context,
    ) -> ValidatorResult:
        raise NotImplementedError

Now every validator follows the same contract.

1.9.22 Why this matters later

When we add AI, we do not allow AI to bypass this pipeline.

For example:

AI generates proposed agreement data
          ↓
        Schema
          ↓
        Rules
          ↓
        Party checks
          ↓
        Legal applicability
          ↓
        Clause checks
          ↓
        Human/legal review

AI output is treated as untrusted input.

This is a very important design decision.

1.9.24 Testing

Do not create fake contracts to test this.

Use real persisted test fixtures generated by the test database setup, with values supplied by the test itself rather than production/demo seed data.

Tests should verify:

Missing required field
→ validation fails
Wrong data type
→ validation fails
Invalid enum
→ validation fails
Unknown property
→ validation fails
Invalid cross-field relationship
effective_date > expiry_date

→ validation fails
Unknown legal entity
→ validation fails
Legal entity belongs to another tenant
→ authorization failure
Unavailable jurisdiction
→ validation fails
Required clause has no approved applicable version
→ validation fails
Required clause variable missing
→ validation fails
Valid agreement
→ agreement created
→ version created
→ workflow created
→ audit event created
1.9.25 Most important test: type version immutability

Suppose:

Agreement Type
    Version 4

is used to create an agreement.

Later:

Agreement Type
    Version 5

becomes current.

The existing agreement must remain attached to:

Version 4

It must not silently start using Version 5.

Therefore:

Agreement
   └── agreement_type_version_id
                 ↓
             Version 4

is a historical snapshot reference.

1.9.26 Second important test: approved clause immutability

Suppose:

Clause 17
 ├── Version 3 → approved
 └── Version 4 → current

An old agreement using Version 3 remains:

Agreement Version 2
      ↓
Clause 17 Version 3

even though Version 4 is now current.

That gives you proper legal version history.

After 1.9:

The system doesn't simply collect contract data. It validates the data against the configured agreement definition before allowing the lifecycle to proceed.

You now have:

        +

        +
Cross-field Validation
        +
Party Validation
        +
Jurisdiction Validation
        +
Clause Applicability
        +

        +
Tenant Isolation

This is a much stronger foundation for the next layers.

Milestone 1.10 — Legal Knowledge + Jurisdiction Rules Engine

This is the point where ContractOS starts becoming legally context-aware.

The architecture must remain conservative:

Authoritative Source
       ↓
Source Registry
       ↓
Retrieved Source Version
       ↓
Integrity Hash
       ↓
Legal Rule
       ↓
Rule Version
       ↓
Jurisdiction / Applicability
       ↓
Agreement Validation
       ↓
Clause Applicability
       ↓
Lawyer Review

The system should never treat an LLM response as law.

For example, Sri Lanka's ICTA currently publishes the Electronic Transactions Act No. 19 of 2006 and explains its 2017 amendment, while the DPA publishes the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 and the 2025 amendment. Those are exactly the kinds of primary/official sources this layer should be able to register and version.

OFFICIAL_GUIDANCE

TREATY
OTHER

The database is the source of actual records; these labels don't create legal content themselves.

1.10.4 Why storing source snapshots matters

Never make this the permanent design:

Legal Rule
   ↓
URL

because the URL can change.

Instead:

Legal Rule
   ↓
Rule Version
   ↓
Legal Source Version
   ↓
Immutable document snapshot
   ↓
SHA-256

That gives you reproducibility.

If a government website later updates its PDF, the older document remains identifiable.

1.10.7 Separate proposition from executable rule

This is important.

A legal rule should have two different representations:

proposition

and

rule_definition

For example, the proposition might explain what the reviewed legal material says, while rule_definition represents the deterministic machine-checkable portion.

Do not let an LLM directly write arbitrary Python.

Never:

exec(ai_generated_rule)

Never:

eval(ai_generated_condition)

The only executable behavior is the rule language implemented by your platform.

1.10.8 Legal rule definition

Use the same safe rule structure from Milestone 1.9.

For example:

{
  "all": [
    {
      "path": "agreement.some_field",
      "operator": "equals",
      "value": true
    }
  ]
}

The engine understands a controlled vocabulary such as:

exists
equals
not_equals
greater_than
greater_than_or_equal
less_than
less_than_or_equal
in
not_in

Nothing else executes.

1.10.10 Legal source acquisition

Do not make:

requests.get(user_provided_url)

your source ingestion architecture.

That creates SSRF/security problems.

Create a controlled acquisition service.

backend/app/services/legal_source_acquisition.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from urllib.parse import urlparse

import httpx


@dataclass
class RetrievedSource:
    url: str
    content: bytes
    content_type: str | None


class LegalSourceAcquisitionService:

    def __init__(
        self,
        allowed_domains: set[str],
    ):
        self.allowed_domains = allowed_domains

    async def retrieve(
        self,
        url: str,
    ) -> RetrievedSource:

        parsed = urlparse(url)

        if parsed.scheme != "https":
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal sources must use HTTPS"
            )

        hostname = parsed.hostname

        if not hostname:
            raise ValueError(
                "Invalid source hostname"
            )

        if hostname not in self.allowed_domains:
            raise PermissionError(
                "Source domain is not approved"
            )

        async with httpx.AsyncClient(
            follow_redirects=True,
            timeout=30,
        ) as client:

            response = await client.get(url)

            response.raise_for_status()

            final_hostname = urlparse(
                str(response.url)
            ).hostname

            if (
                final_hostname
                not in self.allowed_domains
            ):
                raise PermissionError(
                    "Redirected outside approved source domain"
                )

            return RetrievedSource(
                url=str(response.url),
                content=response.content,
                content_type=response.headers.get(
                    "content-type"
                ),
            )

The allowed domain list itself should come from secure server configuration / database policy, not from an untrusted request.

1.10.11 Source integrity

Create:

backend/app/services/source_integrity.py
import hashlib


def sha256_bytes(content: bytes) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest()

When retrieving:

digest = sha256_bytes(source.content)

Then store that hash with the immutable source version.

1.10.12 Store source documents privately

The actual source file should go into private object storage:

legal-source/
    jurisdiction/
    source/
    version/

Not:

/public/legal/

The database stores:

storage_key
sha256
mime_type
source_url
retrieved_at

The object itself stays private.

1.10.13 Do not immediately trust extracted text

Legal documents can be:

HTML
PDF
scanned PDF
DOC/DOCX
plain text

Create an extraction pipeline:

Retrieved File
      ↓
File Type Detection
      ↓
Text Extraction
      ↓
Extraction Quality Check
      ↓
Page/Section Coordinates
      ↓
Normalized Text
      ↓
Hash
      ↓
Human Review

OCR should be used only when necessary.

More importantly, preserve the original source file even after extracting text.

1.10.15 Legal rule provenance

Now connect:

        ↓

1.10.16 Human review gate

This is one of the most important parts of the architecture.

A newly retrieved source is:

UNREVIEWED

A rule extracted from it is:

UNREVIEWED

Neither can affect contract execution.

The lifecycle should be:

SOURCE_RETRIEVED
       ↓
EXTRACTION_COMPLETE
       ↓
SOURCE_REVIEW
       ↓
SOURCE_ACCEPTED
       ↓
RULE_DRAFTED
       ↓
LEGAL_REVIEW
       ↓
RULE_APPROVED
       ↓
RULE_ACTIVE

Only:

RULE_ACTIVE

can participate in validation.

1.10.17 Never let source ingestion automatically activate a rule

Bad architecture:

website changed
↓
crawler downloads it
↓
LLM interprets it
↓
production contract validation changes

Absolutely not.

Correct:

website changed
↓
crawler downloads source
↓
new source version
↓
difference detected
↓
candidate rule changes
↓
legal review
↓
approved version
↓
activation

This protects the platform from automated legal hallucination or source parsing errors.

1.10.18 Rule status

Use:

DRAFT
UNREVIEWED
UNDER_REVIEW
APPROVED
ACTIVE
SUPERSEDED
RETIRED
REJECTED

The important distinction is:

APPROVED

means reviewed and accepted,

while:

ACTIVE

means currently applicable in the production rule set.

1.10.19 Rule engine service

Create:

backend/app/services/legal_rule_engine.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.legal_rule import LegalRule
from app.models.legal_rule_version import (
    LegalRuleVersion,
)
from app.services.rule_engine import RuleEngine


@dataclass
class LegalRuleResult:
    rule_key: str
    passed: bool
    reason: str | None


class LegalRuleEngine:

    def __init__(self):
        self.rule_engine = RuleEngine()

    async def evaluate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        jurisdiction_id,
        agreement_data: dict,
        at: datetime | None = None,
    ) -> list[LegalRuleResult]:

        at = at or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

        result = await db.execute(
            select(
                LegalRule,
                LegalRuleVersion,
            )
            .join(
                LegalRuleVersion,
                LegalRuleVersion.legal_rule_id
                == LegalRule.id,
            )
            .where(
                LegalRule.jurisdiction_id
                == jurisdiction_id,
                LegalRule.status == "active",
                LegalRuleVersion.review_status == "approved",
                (
                    LegalRuleVersion.effective_from.is_(None)
                    |
                    (
                        LegalRuleVersion.effective_from
                        <= at
                    )
                ),
                (
                    LegalRuleVersion.effective_until.is_(None)
                    |
                    (
                        LegalRuleVersion.effective_until
                        > at
                    )
                ),
            )
        )

        rows = result.all()

        results = []

        for rule, version in rows:

            rule_result = (
                self.rule_engine.evaluate(
                    version.rule_definition,
                    agreement_data,
                )
            )

            results.append(
                LegalRuleResult(
                    rule_key=rule.key,
                    passed=rule_result.passed,
                    reason=rule_result.reason,
                )
            )

        return results

This is deliberately simple at first.

Later it can support:

applicability predicates
exceptions
priority
rule dependencies
conflicts
temporal reasoning
1.10.20 Legal rules shouldn't all be blocking

Some legal intelligence produces:

BLOCK

Some should produce:

WARNING

Some should produce:

INFORMATION

Add severity to LegalRuleVersion:

severity: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
    String(30),
    nullable=False,
    default="warning",
)

Then:

ERROR
WARNING
INFO

But don't let developers arbitrarily decide which legal rules are blockers inside application code.

The configured rule should determine its severity.

1.10.21 Rule enforcement

The validation result should become:

PASS
WARNING
BLOCK

For example:

Legal validation

✓ Rule A passed

⚠ Rule B needs lawyer review

✕ Rule C blocks execution

The system should not say:

"Contract is legally valid."

because passing configured rules does not establish legal validity in the broad sense.

The correct language is closer to:

"Configured validation requirements passed."

Modify:

AgreementValidationPipeline

so the pipeline includes:

Schema
 ↓
Field
 ↓
Cross-field
 ↓
Party
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Jurisdiction
 ↓
Legal rules
 ↓
Clause requirements
 ↓
Execution requirements

For example:

validators = [
    SchemaValidatorAdapter(),
    FieldValidatorAdapter(),
    CrossFieldValidatorAdapter(),
    PartyValidatorAdapter(),
    JurisdictionValidatorAdapter(),
    LegalRuleValidatorAdapter(),
    ClauseValidatorAdapter(),
    ExecutionRequirementValidator(),
]

The exact implementation classes can be separate files.

1.10.23 Legal rule adapter
backend/app/services/validators/legal_rule_validator.py
from app.services.validators.base import (
    AgreementValidator,
    ValidatorResult,
)

from app.services.agreement_validator import (
    ValidationIssue,
)


class LegalRuleValidator(
    AgreementValidator,
):

    def __init__(self, legal_rule_engine):
        self.legal_rule_engine = (
            legal_rule_engine
        )

    async def validate(self, context):

        results = await (
            self.legal_rule_engine.evaluate(
                context.db,
                jurisdiction_id=(
                    context.agreement.jurisdiction_id
                    if context.agreement
                    else context.data.get(
                        "jurisdiction_id"
                    )
                ),
                agreement_data=context.data,
            )
        )

        issues = []

        for result in results:

            if result.passed:
                continue

            issues.append(
                ValidationIssue(
                    code=result.rule_key,
                    message=(
                        result.reason
                        or "Legal rule failed"
                    ),
                    severity="error",
                )
            )

        return ValidatorResult(
            issues=issues,
        )

The production version should handle pre-persistence validation more carefully because agreement may not exist yet. The jurisdiction should be resolved from the validated request/type context, not blindly from arbitrary JSON.

1.10.26 Source freshness

Legal information changes.

1.10.27 Background acquisition

You already have:

Redis
Celery

Use Celery for source monitoring.

Celery
   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

1.10.28 Change detection
backend/app/services/legal_source_change.py
def source_changed(
    new_sha256: str,
    previous_sha256: str | None,
) -> bool:

    if previous_sha256 is None:
        return True

    return new_sha256 != previous_sha256

This is simple but useful.

Never decide changes based only on page titles or timestamps.

1.10.29 Source conflict detection

Later, multiple official materials can appear to conflict.

Do not resolve conflicts automatically.

Represent:

RULE_A
RULE_B
   ↓
POTENTIAL_CONFLICT
   ↓
LEGAL_REVIEW

Create:

LegalRuleConflict

with:

rule_version_a_id
rule_version_b_id
conflict_type
description
status
resolved_by
resolved_at
resolution

This gives legal reviewers a queue rather than silently picking an answer.

1.10.30 Legal rule dependencies

Rules sometimes depend on other rules.

Add later:

LegalRuleDependency

Conceptually:

Rule A
 ↓
requires
 ↓
Rule B

The engine can then evaluate dependencies before activation.

Do not implement arbitrary recursive code execution. Keep dependency relationships explicit and cycle-detectable.

1.10.31 Rule graph validation

Before activating a rule:

Rule
 ↓
Dependencies
 ↓
Cycles?

If:

A → B
B → C
C → A

activation fails.

Implement:

def detect_cycle(graph: dict[str, list[str]]) -> bool:
    visiting = set()
    visited = set()

    def visit(node: str) -> bool:

        if node in visiting:
            return True

        if node in visited:
            return False

        visiting.add(node)

        for child in graph.get(node, []):
            if visit(child):
                return True

        visiting.remove(node)
        visited.add(node)

        return False

    return any(
        visit(node)
        for node in graph
    )

This is safe deterministic graph logic.

1.10.32 Legal research AI

Only after the source infrastructure exists should AI be connected.

Architecture:

User / Lawyer
       ↓
Research Request
       ↓
Search approved legal sources
       ↓
Retrieve source versions
       ↓
Retrieve relevant fragments
       ↓
LLM
       ↓
Answer + citations
       ↓
Human review where required

Not:

User
 ↓
LLM
 ↓
"What does Sri Lankan law say?"

with no source provenance.

1.10.33 AI response contract

When AI eventually answers a legal research query, require structured output:

{
  "answer": "...",
  "sources": [
    {
      "source_version_id": "...",
      "fragment_id": "...",
      "citation": "..."
    }
  ],
  "uncertainties": [],
  "requires_legal_review": true
}

Every factual legal assertion needs retrievable provenance.

1.10.34 Prevent uncited legal claims

Create a response validator.

backend/app/services/legal_ai_response_validator.py
class LegalAIResponseValidator:

    def validate(self, response: dict):

        if not response.get("answer"):
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal AI response has no answer"
            )

        sources = response.get("sources", [])

        if not sources:
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal AI response has no sources"
            )

        for source in sources:

            if not source.get(
                "source_version_id"
            ):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Missing source version provenance"
                )

            if not source.get(
                "fragment_id"
            ):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Missing source fragment provenance"
                )

        return True

The production system should verify that those IDs actually exist and that the cited fragments support the response.

1.10.35 No autonomous legal-rule learning

This is a major architectural boundary.

Aariya can:

discover
retrieve
extract
compare
summarize
identify candidate changes
propose candidate rules

Aariya cannot autonomously make a candidate rule:

ACTIVE

without the configured legal-review process.

So:

AI proposed rule
      ↓
candidate
      ↓
legal review
      ↓
approval
      ↓
activation

This still gives you autonomous research without autonomous uncontrolled legal authority.

1.10.36 Example of the complete research lifecycle

Using current official Sri Lankan material as an example, ICTA identifies the Electronic Transactions Act as an electronic-commerce law and provides the Act and information about its amendment; the DPA provides the 2022 PDPA and the 2025 amendment on its official site.

The platform therefore stores:

Jurisdiction
   Sri Lanka
       ↓
Legal Source
   ICTA official source
       ↓
Source Version
   retrieved document/version
       ↓
Fragment
   relevant provision
       ↓
Candidate Legal Rule
       ↓
Legal Review
       ↓
Approved Rule Version
       ↓
Active Rule

No rule is manufactured merely because the LLM knows about the Act.

1.10.37 Connect rules to agreement types

The legal rule itself should remain jurisdiction-focused.

Applicability to a particular agreement comes through configuration.

Legal Rule
   ↓
Jurisdiction
   ↓
Applicability condition
   ↓
Agreement Type / Requirement

For example, the rule could apply only when the relevant agreement data contains a particular characteristic.

This prevents the legal layer from being polluted with application-specific if agreement_type == ... logic.

1.10.38 Connect rules to clause selection

Now the previous clause engine becomes:

Agreement
   ↓
Jurisdiction
   ↓
Legal Rules
   ↓
Applicable requirements
   ↓
Clause applicability
   ↓
Approved clause version

So:

Legal knowledge

determines constraints, while:

Clause library

provides reviewed language.

That separation is important.

1.10.39 Connect rules to execution readiness

Your existing execution readiness service now gets another check:

execution requirements
        +
legal rules
        +
clause requirements
        +
lawyer review
        +
party approval
        +
signatory authority

Only then:

READY_FOR_SIGNATURE

And later:

SIGNATURE_COMPLETED
        ↓
EXECUTED
        ↓
ACTIVE

1.10.41 Tests

Test the security and integrity boundaries.

source retrieval using HTTP
→ rejected

source retrieval using HTTPS
→ allowed only for approved domain

redirect to unapproved domain
→ rejected

source changed
→ new source version

source unchanged
→ no duplicate version

same source content
→ same SHA-256

rule with unsupported operator
→ rejected

rule containing executable code
→ rejected

unreviewed rule
→ cannot affect production validation

approved but inactive rule
→ cannot affect production validation

expired rule
→ cannot affect production validation

active applicable rule
→ evaluated

active non-applicable rule
→ skipped

rule references missing source
→ activation rejected

cyclic rule dependency
→ activation rejected

old source version
→ remains immutable

And critically:

Legal rule generated by AI
→ remains candidate/unreviewed
1.10.42 What the system now has

The architecture has evolved to:

                    CONTRACTOS
                         │
          ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
          │                             │
     CONTRACT DATA                LEGAL KNOWLEDGE
          │                             │
          ▼                             ▼
 Agreement Type                  Legal Sources
          │                             │
       Schema                    Source Versions
          │                             │
      Validation                  Fragments
          │                             │
      Clauses                    Legal Rules
          │                             │
 Clause Versions                 Rule Versions
          │                             │
          └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                         ▼
                  Applicability
                         │
                         ▼
                Draft / Validation
                         │
                         ▼
                 Lawyer Review
                         │
                         ▼
                    Approval
                         │
                         ▼
                  Negotiation
                         │
                         ▼
                  Execution

The critical trust chain is now:

REAL SOURCE
    ↓
IMMUTABLE SOURCE VERSION
    ↓
TRACEABLE FRAGMENT
    ↓
CANDIDATE RULE
    ↓
LEGAL REVIEW
    ↓
APPROVED RULE VERSION
    ↓
ACTIVE RULE
    ↓
VALIDATION

That prevents the most dangerous failure mode for this project: an LLM silently becoming the source of legal truth.








Milestone 1.10 — Legal Knowledge + Jurisdiction Rules Engine

This is the point where ContractOS starts becoming legally context-aware.

The architecture must remain conservative:

Authoritative Source
       ↓
Source Registry
       ↓
Retrieved Source Version
       ↓
Integrity Hash
       ↓
Legal Rule
       ↓
Rule Version
       ↓
Jurisdiction / Applicability
       ↓
Agreement Validation
       ↓
Clause Applicability
       ↓
Lawyer Review

The system should never treat an LLM response as law.

For example, Sri Lanka's ICTA currently publishes the Electronic Transactions Act No. 19 of 2006 and explains its 2017 amendment, while the DPA publishes the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 and the 2025 amendment. Those are exactly the kinds of primary/official sources this layer should be able to register and version.

1.10.4 Why storing source snapshots matters

Never make this the permanent design:

Legal Rule
   ↓
URL

because the URL can change.

Instead:

Legal Rule
   ↓
Rule Version
   ↓
Legal Source Version
   ↓
Immutable document snapshot
   ↓
SHA-256

That gives you reproducibility.

If a government website later updates its PDF, the older document remains identifiable.

1.10.7 Separate proposition from executable rule

This is important.

A legal rule should have two different representations:

proposition

and

rule_definition

For example, the proposition might explain what the reviewed legal material says, while rule_definition represents the deterministic machine-checkable portion.

Do not let an LLM directly write arbitrary Python.

Never:

exec(ai_generated_rule)

Never:

eval(ai_generated_condition)

The only executable behavior is the rule language implemented by your platform.

1.10.8 Legal rule definition

Use the same safe rule structure from Milestone 1.9.

For example:

{
  "all": [
    {
      "path": "agreement.some_field",
      "operator": "equals",
      "value": true
    }
  ]
}

The engine understands a controlled vocabulary such as:

exists
equals
not_equals
greater_than
greater_than_or_equal
less_than
less_than_or_equal
in
not_in

Nothing else executes.

1.10.10 Legal source acquisition

Do not make:

requests.get(user_provided_url)

your source ingestion architecture.

That creates SSRF/security problems.

Create a controlled acquisition service.

backend/app/services/legal_source_acquisition.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from urllib.parse import urlparse

import httpx


@dataclass
class RetrievedSource:
    url: str
    content: bytes
    content_type: str | None


class LegalSourceAcquisitionService:

    def __init__(
        self,
        allowed_domains: set[str],
    ):
        self.allowed_domains = allowed_domains

    async def retrieve(
        self,
        url: str,
    ) -> RetrievedSource:

        parsed = urlparse(url)

        if parsed.scheme != "https":
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal sources must use HTTPS"
            )

        hostname = parsed.hostname

        if not hostname:
            raise ValueError(
                "Invalid source hostname"
            )

        if hostname not in self.allowed_domains:
            raise PermissionError(
                "Source domain is not approved"
            )

        async with httpx.AsyncClient(
            follow_redirects=True,
            timeout=30,
        ) as client:

            response = await client.get(url)

            response.raise_for_status()

            final_hostname = urlparse(
                str(response.url)
            ).hostname

            if (
                final_hostname
                not in self.allowed_domains
            ):
                raise PermissionError(
                    "Redirected outside approved source domain"
                )

            return RetrievedSource(
                url=str(response.url),
                content=response.content,
                content_type=response.headers.get(
                    "content-type"
                ),
            )

The allowed domain list itself should come from secure server configuration / database policy, not from an untrusted request.

1.10.11 Source integrity

Create:

backend/app/services/source_integrity.py
import hashlib


def sha256_bytes(content: bytes) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest()

When retrieving:

digest = sha256_bytes(source.content)

Then store that hash with the immutable source version.

1.10.12 Store source documents privately

The actual source file should go into private object storage:

legal-source/
    jurisdiction/
    source/
    version/

Not:

/public/legal/

The database stores:

storage_key
sha256
mime_type
source_url
retrieved_at

The object itself stays private.

1.10.13 Do not immediately trust extracted text

Legal documents can be:

HTML
PDF
scanned PDF
DOC/DOCX
plain text

Create an extraction pipeline:

Retrieved File
      ↓
File Type Detection
      ↓
Text Extraction
      ↓
Extraction Quality Check
      ↓
Page/Section Coordinates
      ↓
Normalized Text
      ↓
Hash
      ↓
Human Review

OCR should be used only when necessary.

More importantly, preserve the original source file even after extracting text.

1.10.16 Human review gate

This is one of the most important parts of the architecture.

A newly retrieved source is:

UNREVIEWED

A rule extracted from it is:

UNREVIEWED

Neither can affect contract execution.

The lifecycle should be:

SOURCE_RETRIEVED
       ↓
EXTRACTION_COMPLETE
       ↓
SOURCE_REVIEW
       ↓
SOURCE_ACCEPTED
       ↓
RULE_DRAFTED
       ↓
LEGAL_REVIEW
       ↓
RULE_APPROVED
       ↓
RULE_ACTIVE

Only:

RULE_ACTIVE

can participate in validation.

1.10.17 Never let source ingestion automatically activate a rule

Bad architecture:

website changed
↓
crawler downloads it
↓
LLM interprets it
↓
production contract validation changes

Absolutely not.

Correct:

website changed
↓
crawler downloads source
↓
new source version
↓
difference detected
↓
candidate rule changes
↓
legal review
↓
approved version
↓
activation

This protects the platform from automated legal hallucination or source parsing errors.

1.10.18 Rule status

Use:

DRAFT
UNREVIEWED
UNDER_REVIEW
APPROVED
ACTIVE
SUPERSEDED
RETIRED
REJECTED

The important distinction is:

APPROVED

means reviewed and accepted,

while:

ACTIVE

means currently applicable in the production rule set.

1.10.19 Rule engine service

Create:

backend/app/services/legal_rule_engine.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.legal_rule import LegalRule
from app.models.legal_rule_version import (
    LegalRuleVersion,
)
from app.services.rule_engine import RuleEngine


@dataclass
class LegalRuleResult:
    rule_key: str
    passed: bool
    reason: str | None


class LegalRuleEngine:

    def __init__(self):
        self.rule_engine = RuleEngine()

    async def evaluate(
        self,
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        jurisdiction_id,
        agreement_data: dict,
        at: datetime | None = None,
    ) -> list[LegalRuleResult]:

        at = at or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

        result = await db.execute(
            select(
                LegalRule,
                LegalRuleVersion,
            )
            .join(
                LegalRuleVersion,
                LegalRuleVersion.legal_rule_id
                == LegalRule.id,
            )
            .where(
                LegalRule.jurisdiction_id
                == jurisdiction_id,
                LegalRule.status == "active",
                LegalRuleVersion.review_status == "approved",
                (
                    LegalRuleVersion.effective_from.is_(None)
                    |
                    (
                        LegalRuleVersion.effective_from
                        <= at
                    )
                ),
                (
                    LegalRuleVersion.effective_until.is_(None)
                    |
                    (
                        LegalRuleVersion.effective_until
                        > at
                    )
                ),
            )
        )

        rows = result.all()

        results = []

        for rule, version in rows:

            rule_result = (
                self.rule_engine.evaluate(
                    version.rule_definition,
                    agreement_data,
                )
            )

            results.append(
                LegalRuleResult(
                    rule_key=rule.key,
                    passed=rule_result.passed,
                    reason=rule_result.reason,
                )
            )

        return results

This is deliberately simple at first.

Later it can support:

applicability predicates
exceptions
priority
rule dependencies
conflicts
temporal reasoning
1.10.20 Legal rules shouldn't all be blocking

Some legal intelligence produces:

BLOCK

Some should produce:

WARNING

Some should produce:

INFORMATION

Add severity to LegalRuleVersion:

severity: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
    String(30),
    nullable=False,
    default="warning",
)

Then:

ERROR
WARNING
INFO

But don't let developers arbitrarily decide which legal rules are blockers inside application code.

The configured rule should determine its severity.

1.10.21 Rule enforcement

The validation result should become:

PASS
WARNING
BLOCK

For example:

Legal validation

✓ Rule A passed

⚠ Rule B needs lawyer review

✕ Rule C blocks execution

The system should not say:

"Contract is legally valid."

because passing configured rules does not establish legal validity in the broad sense.

The correct language is closer to:

"Configured validation requirements passed."
1.10.22 Integrate with agreement validation

Modify:

AgreementValidationPipeline

so the pipeline includes:

Schema
 ↓
Field
 ↓
Cross-field
 ↓
Party
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Jurisdiction
 ↓
Legal rules
 ↓
Clause requirements
 ↓
Execution requirements

For example:

validators = [
    SchemaValidatorAdapter(),
    FieldValidatorAdapter(),
    CrossFieldValidatorAdapter(),
    PartyValidatorAdapter(),
    JurisdictionValidatorAdapter(),
    LegalRuleValidatorAdapter(),
    ClauseValidatorAdapter(),
    ExecutionRequirementValidator(),
]

The exact implementation classes can be separate files.

1.10.23 Legal rule adapter
backend/app/services/validators/legal_rule_validator.py
from app.services.validators.base import (
    AgreementValidator,
    ValidatorResult,
)

from app.services.agreement_validator import (
    ValidationIssue,
)


class LegalRuleValidator(
    AgreementValidator,
):

    def __init__(self, legal_rule_engine):
        self.legal_rule_engine = (
            legal_rule_engine
        )

    async def validate(self, context):

        results = await (
            self.legal_rule_engine.evaluate(
                context.db,
                jurisdiction_id=(
                    context.agreement.jurisdiction_id
                    if context.agreement
                    else context.data.get(
                        "jurisdiction_id"
                    )
                ),
                agreement_data=context.data,
            )
        )

        issues = []

        for result in results:

            if result.passed:
                continue

            issues.append(
                ValidationIssue(
                    code=result.rule_key,
                    message=(
                        result.reason
                        or "Legal rule failed"
                    ),
                    severity="error",
                )
            )

        return ValidatorResult(
            issues=issues,
        )

The production version should handle pre-persistence validation more carefully because agreement may not exist yet. The jurisdiction should be resolved from the validated request/type context, not blindly from arbitrary JSON.

1.10.28 Change detection
backend/app/services/legal_source_change.py
def source_changed(
    new_sha256: str,
    previous_sha256: str | None,
) -> bool:

    if previous_sha256 is None:
        return True

    return new_sha256 != previous_sha256

This is simple but useful.

Never decide changes based only on page titles or timestamps.

1.10.29 Source conflict detection

   ↓

   ↓

with:

This gives legal reviewers a queue rather than silently picking an answer.

1.10.30 Legal rule dependencies

Rules sometimes depend on other rules.

Add later:

 ↓

The engine can then evaluate dependencies before activation.

Do not implement arbitrary recursive code execution. Keep dependency relationships explicit and cycle-detectable.

1.10.31 Rule graph validation

Before activating a rule:

Rule
 ↓
Dependencies
 ↓
Cycles?

If:

A → B
B → C
C → A

activation fails.

Implement:

def detect_cycle(graph: dict[str, list[str]]) -> bool:
    visiting = set()
    visited = set()

    def visit(node: str) -> bool:

        if node in visiting:
            return True

        if node in visited:
            return False

        visiting.add(node)

        for child in graph.get(node, []):
            if visit(child):
                return True

        visiting.remove(node)
        visited.add(node)

        return False

    return any(
        visit(node)
        for node in graph
    )

This is safe deterministic graph logic.

1.10.32 Legal research AI

Only after the source infrastructure exists should AI be connected.

Architecture:

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

Not:

with no source provenance.

1.10.33 AI response contract

When AI eventually answers a legal research query, require structured output:

{
  "answer": "...",
  "sources": [
    {
      "source_version_id": "...",
      "fragment_id": "...",
      "citation": "..."
    }
  ],
  "uncertainties": [],
  "requires_legal_review": true
}

Every factual legal assertion needs retrievable provenance.

1.10.34 Prevent uncited legal claims

Create a response validator.

backend/app/services/legal_ai_response_validator.py
class LegalAIResponseValidator:

    def validate(self, response: dict):

        if not response.get("answer"):
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal AI response has no answer"
            )

        sources = response.get("sources", [])

        if not sources:
            raise ValueError(
                "Legal AI response has no sources"
            )

        for source in sources:

            if not source.get(
                "source_version_id"
            ):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Missing source version provenance"
                )

            if not source.get(
                "fragment_id"
            ):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Missing source fragment provenance"
                )

        return True

The production system should verify that those IDs actually exist and that the cited fragments support the response.

1.10.35 No autonomous legal-rule learning

This is a major architectural boundary.

Aariya can:

discover
retrieve
extract
compare
summarize
identify candidate changes
propose candidate rules

Aariya cannot autonomously make a candidate rule:

ACTIVE

without the configured legal-review process.

So:

AI proposed rule
      ↓
candidate
      ↓
legal review
      ↓
approval
      ↓
activation

This still gives you autonomous research without autonomous uncontrolled legal authority.

1.10.36 Example of the complete research lifecycle

Using current official Sri Lankan material as an example, ICTA identifies the Electronic Transactions Act as an electronic-commerce law and provides the Act and information about its amendment; the DPA provides the 2022 PDPA and the 2025 amendment on its official site.

The platform therefore stores:

Jurisdiction
   Sri Lanka
       ↓

   ICTA official source
       ↓

   retrieved document/version
       ↓
Fragment
   relevant provision
       ↓
Candidate Legal Rule
       ↓
Legal Review
       ↓
Approved Rule Version
       ↓

No rule is manufactured merely because the LLM knows about the Act.

1.10.37 Connect rules to agreement types

The legal rule itself should remain jurisdiction-focused.

Applicability to a particular agreement comes through configuration.

Legal Rule
   ↓

   ↓

   ↓
Agreement Type / Requirement

For example, the rule could apply only when the relevant agreement data contains a particular characteristic.

This prevents the legal layer from being polluted with application-specific if agreement_type == ... logic.

1.10.41 Tests

Test the security and integrity boundaries.

source retrieval using HTTP
→ rejected

source retrieval using HTTPS
→ allowed only for approved domain

redirect to unapproved domain
→ rejected

source changed
→ new source version

source unchanged
→ no duplicate version

same source content
→ same SHA-256

rule with unsupported operator
→ rejected

rule containing executable code
→ rejected

unreviewed rule
→ cannot affect production validation

approved but inactive rule
→ cannot affect production validation

expired rule
→ cannot affect production validation

active applicable rule
→ evaluated

active non-applicable rule
→ skipped

rule references missing source
→ activation rejected

cyclic rule dependency
→ activation rejected

old source version
→ remains immutable

And critically:

Legal rule generated by AI
→ remains candidate/unreviewed

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String, UniqueConstraint
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    TimestampMixin,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
)


class AgreementParty(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "agreement_parties"

    agreement_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "agreements.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    legal_entity_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "legal_entities.id",
            ondelete="RESTRICT",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    party_role: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(50),
        nullable=False,
    )

    signatory_required: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        nullable=False,
        default=False,
    )

    agreement = relationship(
        "Agreement",
        back_populates="parties",
    )

    legal_entity = relationship(
        "LegalEntity",
    )

    members = relationship(
        "AgreementMember",
        back_populates="party",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "agreement_id",
            "legal_entity_id",
            name="uq_agreement_party",
        ),
    )

We intentionally store the actual legal_entity_id, not a free-text company name.

5. Do not let the client choose arbitrary permissions

The API should not accept:

{
  "can_sign": true,
  "can_manage_members": true
}

from an untrusted client and simply trust it.

Instead, the server derives allowed capabilities from the participant role and the workflow.

For example:

LAWYER
AUTHORIZED_REPRESENTATIVE
OBSERVER
SIGNATORY

Then the server applies the appropriate permission policy.

Later, Milestone 1.13 will make this workflow configurable.

9. Agreement access dependency

This is the most important piece.

Create:

backend/app/dependencies/agreement_access.py

from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.core.database import get_db
from app.dependencies.auth import get_current_user
from app.models.agreement import Agreement
from app.models.agreement_participant import AgreementMember
from app.models.user import User


async def get_agreement_for_member(
    agreement_id: UUID,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user),
) -> Agreement:

    stmt = (
        select(Agreement)
        .join(
            AgreementMember,
            AgreementMember.agreement_id == Agreement.id,
        )
        .where(
            Agreement.id == agreement_id,
            AgreementMember.user_id == current_user.id,
            AgreementMember.status == "active",
            AgreementMember.can_view.is_(True),
        )
    )

    result = await db.execute(stmt)
    agreement = result.scalar_one_or_none()

    if agreement is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
            detail="Agreement not found",
        )

    return agreement

Notice the response is:

404 Agreement not found

not:

403 You are not allowed to access this agreement.

That helps prevent leaking whether a protected agreement exists.

10. Permission dependency

Create:

from fastapi import HTTPException, status


def require_agreement_permission(permission: str):
    async def checker(
        agreement_id,
        db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
        current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user),
    ):
        stmt = select(AgreementMember).where(
            AgreementMember.agreement_id == agreement_id,
            AgreementMember.user_id == current_user.id,
            AgreementMember.status == "active",
        )

        result = await db.execute(stmt)
        member = result.scalar_one_or_none()

        if not member:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
                detail="Agreement not found",
            )

        allowed = getattr(member, permission, False)

        if not allowed:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN,
                detail="Insufficient agreement permissions",
            )

        return member

    return checker

Now:

Depends(require_agreement_permission("can_propose_changes"))

means the user must actually have that permission on that agreement.

11. Critical security rule

Never implement an endpoint like:

agreement = await db.get(Agreement, agreement_id)
return agreement

That bypasses agreement-level authorization.

Instead:

agreement = await get_agreement_for_member(...)

Every agreement-related endpoint must pass through the authorization layer.

This includes:

GET agreement
GET versions
GET documents
GET comments
GET negotiations
GET audit events
GET obligations
DOWNLOAD document
EXPORT PDF
REQUEST SIGNATURE
APPROVE
PROPOSE CHANGE
ADD LAWYER
REMOVE MEMBER

There must be no alternate route around this check.

14. Private vs shared negotiation data

Not everything associated with an agreement should be globally visible to every participant.

We therefore classify data as:

AGREEMENT_SHARED
PARTY_PRIVATE
USER_PRIVATE

For example:

Shared
Current agreement version
Accepted clauses
Formal change proposals
Formal comments
Negotiation history
Executed agreement
Party-private
Internal lawyer notes
Internal strategy
Internal risk assessment
Private client discussion
Draft positions that haven't been proposed
User-private
Personal notes
Private reminders

This distinction is essential.

The actual agreement can be visible to both sides while each side's internal legal work product remains private.

15. Do not use a single comments table

Instead we will eventually have something like:

agreement_comments

with:

visibility_scope
author_user_id
party_id
agreement_version_id
clause_id

So:

PARTY_PRIVATE

can only be retrieved by users belonging to the same party.

Whereas:

AGREEMENT_SHARED

can be seen by authorized members on both sides.

This will be implemented fully in the negotiation milestone.

17. Audit everything

Assignment changes need audit events.

For example:

{
  "action": "agreement.member.invited",
  "resource_type": "agreement",
  "resource_id": "...",
  "metadata": {
    "party_id": "...",
    "role": "lawyer",
    "invited_email": "..."
  }
}

Then:

agreement.member.accepted
agreement.member.removed
agreement.member.permission_changed
agreement.member.role_changed

The actual private agreement content should not be dumped into the audit metadata.

18. Notification events

The notification architecture should now be event-driven.

Example:

AgreementMemberAdded
        ↓
Event Bus / Outbox
        ├── Email notification
        ├── Mobile push
        ├── In-app notification
        └── Audit event

We should not make the agreement API depend directly on an email provider.

Instead:

API
 ↓
Database transaction
 ↓
Outbox event
 ↓
Worker
 ↓
Email / Push / WebSocket

That prevents notification failures from corrupting agreement transactions.

View private legal notes	party only	party only	✗
View other party's private notes	✗	✗	✗

The exact permissions will become database/configuration-driven, not hardwired into every endpoint.

Milestone 1.12 — Negotiation & Redline Engine

This is the core of the lawyer-to-lawyer workflow.

The system must never overwrite the previous legal text. Every material change produces a new version and an explicit change record.

The model becomes:

Agreement
   │
   ├── Version 1
   │
   ├── Version 2
   │      ├── Clause 4 changed
   │      └── Clause 8 added
   │
   ├── Version 3
   │      └── Clause 4 counter-proposal
   │
   └── Version N
          └── final agreed text
1. The fundamental rule

A lawyer does not directly mutate:

agreement_versions.content

Instead:

Existing Version
      ↓
Create negotiation proposal
      ↓
Create clause changes
      ↓
Review
      ↓
Accept / reject / counter
      ↓
Create new version

This gives us a complete legal history.

2. Clause-level structure

We need to stop treating the agreement as one giant string.

Add:

agreement_clauses
agreement_change_sets
agreement_clause_changes
agreement_comments

The logical structure becomes:

Agreement
 ├── Version
 │    ├── Clause
 │    ├── Clause
 │    └── Clause

 ├── Change Set
 │    ├── Clause Change
 │    ├── Clause Change
 │    └── Clause Change
 │
 └── Comments

4. Why clause keys matter

Suppose Version 1 says:

Payment must be made within 30 days.

Version 2:

Payment must be made within 45 days.

The system knows both are:

clause_key = payment_terms

Therefore it can display:

PAYMENT TERMS

Version 1
Payment must be made within 30 days.

Version 2
Payment must be made within 45 days.

CHANGE
30 days → 45 days

This is much better than trying to compare entire documents blindly.

7. Never trust submitted previous text

This is extremely important.

The lawyer sends:

{
  "clause_id": "...",
  "proposed_content": "Payment within 60 days"
}

They do not send:

{
  "previous_content": "Payment within 30 days"
}

The server obtains the original from the database.

Otherwise a malicious client could falsify the negotiation history.

The server creates:

previous_content =
database version content

proposed_content =
lawyer submitted content

10. Server-side validation

Before accepting the proposal:

Authenticated user
       ↓
Agreement membership
       ↓
can_propose_changes
       ↓
Party membership
       ↓
base_version belongs to agreement
       ↓
base_version is current negotiable version
       ↓
clauses belong to agreement
       ↓
change types valid
       ↓
proposed content valid
       ↓
create change set

If the lawyer is looking at Version 7 but Version 8 was already created:

409 CONFLICT

The system must not allow a stale version to overwrite newer negotiations.

11. Optimistic concurrency

This is essential when both lawyers work simultaneously.

Example:

             Current Version 7
              /            \
             /              \
       Lawyer A            Lawyer B
       edits V7            edits V7
           │                  │
           ↓                  ↓
       Proposal A          Proposal B

Neither proposal automatically destroys the other.

Instead the system detects:

base_version = 7
current_version = 8

and requires reconciliation.

That prevents hidden overwrites.

12. Redline generation

We need explicit redline information.

For a modified clause:

Previous:
Payment shall be made within 30 days.

Proposed:
Payment shall be made within 45 days.

The backend calculates a diff.

For example, internally:

import difflib


def build_word_diff(
    old_text: str,
    new_text: str,
) -> list[dict]:
    old_words = old_text.split()
    new_words = new_text.split()

    matcher = difflib.SequenceMatcher(
        None,
        old_words,
        new_words,
    )

    result = []

    for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in matcher.get_opcodes():
        result.append(
            {
                "operation": tag,
                "old": old_words[i1:i2],
                "new": new_words[j1:j2],
            }
        )

    return result

This is only the computational diff.

The UI should render:

Payment shall be made within
[30 days]
[45 days]

with deleted/inserted styling.

Later we can use a document-aware diff engine for DOCX/PDF formats.

13. The system must distinguish proposals from accepted text

This is critical.

Current official agreement
        ≠
Lawyer proposal

Until accepted:

Current Version = V7
Proposed Change = Pending

Only after the appropriate workflow accepts it:

V7
 ↓
Accepted Change Set
 ↓
V8
14. Accept / reject / counter

Endpoints:

POST /api/v1/agreements/{id}/change-sets/{change_set_id}/accept

POST /api/v1/agreements/{id}/change-sets/{change_set_id}/reject

POST /api/v1/agreements/{id}/change-sets/{change_set_id}/counter

But there is an important distinction:

Accept

The other side accepts the exact proposed changes.

Reject

The other side rejects that proposal.

Counter

The other side creates a new proposal based on the current negotiated version.

A counter should not modify the original proposal.

Example:

A Proposal #14
  30 → 45 days

B Counter #19
  30 → 40 days

Both remain permanently recorded.

15. Negotiation state machine

Do not allow arbitrary status changes.

DRAFT
 ↓
PROPOSED
 ↓
UNDER_REVIEW
 ├───────────────┐
 ↓               ↓
ACCEPTED       REJECTED
 ↓
NEW_VERSION

UNDER_REVIEW
 ↓
COUNTER_PROPOSED
 ↓
UNDER_REVIEW

The actual workflow state will later be integrated with Milestone 1.13 approval workflows.

System

The exact number of rounds is unlimited.

17. Notifications

Every material event emits an internal event.

For example:

agreement.change_set.created
agreement.change_set.accepted
agreement.change_set.rejected
agreement.change_set.countered
agreement.version.created
agreement.clause.added
agreement.clause.modified
agreement.clause.removed

Then:

Event
 │
 ├── in-app notification
 ├── email
 ├── push notification
 ├── WebSocket live update
 └── audit event

Example:

Party B's counsel proposed changes to:

• Payment Terms
• Limitation of Liability
• Termination

Agreement: MSA-2026-001

Action required: Review counterproposal.

Only users authorized for that agreement receive it.

18. No notification leakage

This is especially important.

Suppose Party A's lawyer writes a private note:

"Client is willing to accept 60 days if liability cap remains."

Party B must receive nothing from that private note.

But when the lawyer officially proposes:

Payment shall be made within 60 days.

that proposal becomes shared with the other party according to the negotiation workflow.

Therefore:

PRIVATE INTERNAL DISCUSSION
            ≠
FORMAL NEGOTIATION CHANGE

backend/app/services/

async def create_change_set(...):

This keeps the legal workflow out of the HTTP layer.

20. Materializing a new version

When a change set is finally accepted:

Current V7
   ↓
Copy clauses
   ↓
Apply accepted changes
   ↓
Build V8
   ↓
Calculate content hash
   ↓
Lock V8 metadata
   ↓
Create version record
   ↓
Record accepted change set
   ↓
Audit event
   ↓
Notify authorized participants

The old V7 remains untouched.

21. Hash the version

Use SHA-256:

import hashlib


def calculate_content_hash(content: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(
        content.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()

For production, the hash should be generated from a deterministic canonical representation of the agreement, not an unstable serialization.

Eventually we'll hash:

agreement metadata
+
ordered clauses
+
approved version content

rather than relying solely on rendered HTML.

24. What we have now

The platform has three important security boundaries:

Organization boundary
       ↓
Agreement boundary
       ↓
Party/private-work-product boundary

And three different representations of legal text:

CURRENT AGREED VERSION
        ↓
FORMAL PROPOSAL / REDLINE
        ↓
PRIVATE DRAFT / INTERNAL NOTES

That separation is what prevents lawyers on one side from accidentally exposing their internal strategy to the other side.

Milestone 1.13 — Multi-Stage Approval & Confirmation Engine

This milestone turns the negotiation engine into a controlled legal decision workflow.

The important distinction is:

LAWYER REVIEW
≠
LAWYER APPROVAL OF CLIENT
≠
PARTY APPROVAL
≠
SIGNATURE

A lawyer can recommend and negotiate terms, but the system must know whether they are actually authorized to bind the represented party.

The workflow therefore becomes:

Draft
 ↓
Party A Lawyer Review
 ↓
Party A Lawyer Confirmation
 ↓
Party A Authorized Representative Confirmation
 ↓
Released to Party B
 ↓
Party B Lawyer Review
 ↓
Party B Lawyer Confirmation
 ↓
Party B Authorized Representative Confirmation
 ↓
FINAL NEGOTIATED
 ↓
Signature Workflow
 ↓
ACTIVE

And the order must be configurable per agreement type/workflow.

1. New workflow entities

Add:

workflow_definitions
workflow_steps
workflow_instances
workflow_step_instances
workflow_actions

Conceptually:

Agreement Type
     ↓
Workflow Definition
     ↓
Workflow Steps
     ↓
Workflow Instance for Agreement
     ↓
Current Step

3. Why actor_type matters

We do not hardcode:

if step == 1:
    lawyer()
elif step == 2:
    party()

Instead the workflow definition describes the required actor.

Examples:

LAWYER
PARTY_REPRESENTATIVE
SIGNATORY
APPROVER
LEGAL_REVIEWER

This lets the same engine support different agreement types.

For example, an NDA might require:

Lawyer → Representative → Lawyer → Representative

while an internal procurement agreement might require:

Legal → Finance → Executive

A definition is a reusable configuration.

        ),
        nullable=True,
    )

    started_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        nullable=True,
    )

    completed_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        nullable=True,
    )

    workflow_instance = relationship(
        "WorkflowInstance",
    )

    workflow_step = relationship(
        "WorkflowStep",
    )

    assigned_member = relationship(
        "AgreementMember",
    )
6. Why we snapshot the workflow

Imagine an organization changes its default approval workflow tomorrow.

An agreement already being negotiated today must not suddenly acquire a different process.

Therefore:

Workflow Definition V3
       ↓
Agreement A123
       ↓
Workflow Instance
       ↓
Step instances frozen for A123

Future agreements can use V4.

Existing agreements remain governed by their original workflow instance unless explicitly amended through a controlled process.
