29. Important architectural improvement

At this point, several modules are converging:

Negotiation
Approval
Signature
Notification
Obligation
Amendment
Termination

They should not remain isolated modules.

The domain is now better represented as:

                    Agreement
                       │
                ┌──────┴──────┐
                │             │
             Lifecycle      Documents
                │
       ┌────────┼─────────┐
       │        │         │
   Negotiation Approval Execution
       │        │         │
       └────────┼─────────┘
                │
             Events
                │
       ┌────────┼────────┐
       ▼        ▼        ▼
 Notifications Audit  Automation
                │
          Obligations
                │
      Renewal / Termination

Amendments participate in all of these rather than reinventing them.

30. Final amendment lifecycle
ACTIVE AGREEMENT
       ↓
AMENDMENT REQUEST
       ↓
ELIGIBILITY CHECK
       ↓
PARTIES / COUNSEL ASSIGNED
       ↓
AMENDMENT DRAFT
       ↓
REDLINES
       ↓
COUNTERPROPOSALS
       ↓
LAWYER CONFIRMATION
       ↓
PARTY CONFIRMATION
       ↓
OTHER SIDE CONFIRMATION
       ↓
AMENDMENT FINAL
       ↓
EXECUTION REQUIREMENTS
       ↓
SIGNING
       ↓
AMENDMENT EXECUTED
       ↓
EFFECTIVE DATE
       ↓
CURRENT TERMS RECALCULATED
       ↓
OBLIGATIONS UPDATED
       ↓
RENEWAL / TERMINATION RULES UPDATED
       ↓
AUDIT + NOTIFICATIONS

This is where the platform starts understanding the agreements rather than merely storing and routing them.

The goal is not:

PDF → LLM → "looks good"
The production architecture is:

Real agreement/document
        ↓
Secure ingestion
        ↓
Text + structure extraction
        ↓
Clause segmentation
        ↓
Entity / obligation / date extraction
        ↓
Rules + legal knowledge
        ↓
AI analysis
        ↓
Evidence-backed findings
        ↓
Human legal review
        ↓
Approved intelligence
The AI must never become the authoritative legal source by itself.

The system reports what it actually finds.

7. Don't trust LLM-generated citations
The model should not be allowed to say:

"According to section 8.3..."
and have the system blindly trust it.

Instead the application should identify the source passage itself.

Better:

AI
 ↓
candidate clause ID
 ↓
server retrieves exact source
 ↓
server verifies correspondence
 ↓
finding created
The source belongs to the document extraction system, not to the model's imagination.

8. Contract findings
Create:

class ContractFinding(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,

13. AI must not silently become legal advice
For example, rather than:

"Clause 9 is illegal."
the system should produce:

Potential issue detected.

Reason:
The provision may conflict with the configured jurisdiction rule
for this agreement type.

Relevant source:
Clause 9.2

Confidence:
0.86

Recommended action:
Legal review required.
This is a much safer product behavior.

14. Rule engine + AI engine
The strongest architecture is:

                  AGREEMENT
                      │
             ┌────────┴────────┐
             ▼                 ▼
        Deterministic       AI analysis
           rules                │
             │                  │
             └────────┬─────────┘
                      ▼
                Finding Fusion
                      │
                      ▼
                 Evidence
                      │
                      ▼
                Human Review
Rules are good at:

date consistency
required fields
jurisdiction conditions
workflow requirements
formal execution requirements
explicit thresholds
known contractual policies
AI is good at:

semantic comparison
ambiguous language
unusual wording
clause classification
risk prioritization
summarization
relationship discovery
Do not make the LLM the sole decision maker for deterministic checks.

15. Missing-clause detection
Suppose an agreement type has required provisions configured in the agreement schema/rules.

The system can calculate:

Required:
✓ Parties
✓ Payment
✓ Term
✓ Confidentiality
✓ Governing law
⚠ Termination provision
Then:

Finding:
Potential missing termination provision.
It should identify the rule that expected it.

rule_version_id
agreement_type_id
jurisdiction_id
becomes part of the evidence.

16. Cross-clause inconsistency
Example:

Clause 4:

Term: 24 months
Clause 17:

Termination: Agreement expires after 12 months
The AI/rules engine can identify:

INCONSISTENCY
Evidence:

Clause 4
Clause 17
This is much more useful than just saying:

"The contract may have inconsistencies."

17. Date consistency
Another deterministic check:

execution_date
effective_date
expiry_date
renewal_date
termination_notice_date
For example:

expiry_date < effective_date
is a data integrity error.

The system should catch this without AI.

18. Financial consistency
Suppose:

Invoice schedule:
Monthly

Payment:
Quarterly
The platform can flag a review item if those provisions conflict or appear ambiguous.

For numerical calculations:

decimal.Decimal
should be used rather than floating-point arithmetic.

19. Cross-document analysis
An agreement may have:

Main Agreement
Schedule A
SOW
SLA
DPA
Pricing Appendix
The intelligence engine should analyze relationships:

Main Agreement
      │
      ├── Schedule A
      ├── SOW
      ├── SLA
      └── DPA
For example:

Main Agreement:
payment = 30 days

SOW:
payment = 45 days
→

CROSS_DOCUMENT_CONFLICT
with both sources displayed.

20. Document hierarchy
We need a proper relationship model.

Eventually:

agreement_documents
can represent:

primary agreement
schedule
appendix
statement of work
amendment
annex
exhibit
policy
Then the AI engine knows which documents are related.

21. Retrieval layer
Don't send entire 100-page contracts into every AI call.

Use:

Document
 ↓
Sections
 ↓
Clauses
 ↓
Embeddings / search index
 ↓
Relevant context
 ↓
AI
The retrieval layer can initially use PostgreSQL full-text search.

Later:

PostgreSQL
   +
vector database/search
as scale increases.

22. Citation-first AI
For every analysis:

question
 ↓
retrieve source
 ↓
source IDs
 ↓
model analysis
 ↓
finding
 ↓
verify source
 ↓
persist finding
The model should receive structured context like:

{
  "source_id": "clause-uuid",
  "section": "8.2",
  "text": "..."
}
and return references to those source IDs.

The backend validates that those IDs were actually supplied.

23. Structured AI output
Do not parse free-form model prose.

Require structured output conceptually like:

{
  "findings": [
    {
      "type": "inconsistency",
      "severity": "high",
      "title": "Conflicting payment periods",
      "summary": "...",
      "evidence": [
        {
          "source_id": "..."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "..."
        }
      ],
      "confidence": 0.91
    }
  ]
}
The server validates this against a schema.

Invalid output is rejected.

24. AI provider abstraction
Create:

backend/app/ai/providers/base.py

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class AIProvider(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def analyze(
        self,
        *,
        system_instructions: str,
        input_data: dict,
    ) -> dict:
        raise NotImplementedError
Then:

AIProvider
   ├── configured provider A
   ├── configured provider B
   └── internal/local model
The contract system doesn't depend directly on one vendor.

25. Extraction provider abstraction
Likewise:

class DocumentExtractor(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def extract(
        self,
        document_path: str,
    ) -> dict:
        raise NotImplementedError
Possible implementations:

DOCX extractor
PDF text extractor
OCR provider
image/document parser
The system selects the actual configured provider based on document characteristics.

26. OCR should not be the default
First attempt:

native PDF/DOCX text
Then:

if text quality insufficient:
    OCR
This reduces cost and improves accuracy.

For scanned contracts, OCR output should carry page/source references and extraction confidence.

27. Analysis pipeline
Create:

backend/app/services/contract_intelligence_service.py

class ContractIntelligenceService:

    async def analyze(
        self,
        agreement_id,
        version_id,
    ):
        document = await self.load_authorized_document(
            agreement_id,
            version_id,
        )

        extraction = await self.extract_document(
            document
        )

        clauses = await self.identify_clauses(
            extraction
        )

        obligations = await self.extract_obligations(
            clauses
        )

        rule_findings = await self.run_rules(
            agreement_id,
            version_id,
            clauses,
        )

        ai_findings = await self.run_ai_analysis(
            agreement_id,
            version_id,
            clauses,
            obligations,
        )

        findings = await self.merge_findings(
            rule_findings,
            ai_findings,
        )

        await self.persist_findings(
            findings
        )

        return findings
This is intentionally orchestration only.

Each stage remains independently testable.

28. Finding fusion
Suppose:

Rule engine:
"Expiry date conflicts with term."

AI:
"This clause appears inconsistent with the stated term."
Don't show users two duplicate findings.

Merge them:

ONE FINDING
   │
   ├── deterministic evidence
   └── AI supporting analysis
The final finding remains explainable.

29. Risk scoring
Do not let an LLM arbitrarily produce:

risk = 9.7
without defined semantics.

Use a configured risk framework.

For example:

severity:
low
medium
high
critical
and factors such as:

financial exposure
legal exposure
operational impact
data/privacy impact
termination impact
jurisdictional sensitivity
The scoring model itself should be versioned.

30. Risk score history
If a clause changes:

Version 8
Risk = high

Version 9
Risk = medium
retain both analyses.

Do not overwrite Version 8's result.

31. AI analysis triggered by changes
This is where the previous milestones become powerful.

When a lawyer modifies a clause:

change_set.created
        ↓
impact analysis
        ↓
affected findings
        ↓
affected obligations
        ↓
affected deadlines
        ↓
affected renewal/termination terms
Example:

Lawyer changes Termination clause
        ↓
AI detects affected termination rule
        ↓
existing renewal/termination workflow marked for review
32. Amendment impact analysis
When Amendment #4 changes:

payment term
the AI engine asks:

Which obligations depend on this clause?
Which deadlines depend on it?
Which schedules mention the old term?
Which other clauses reference the old provision?
Then:

IMPACT REPORT

3 obligations affected
1 payment schedule affected
2 documents contain references
1 workflow rule requires review
This is a major differentiator for the platform.

34. Don't hide uncertainty
Instead of:

"This contract violates the law."

Uncertainty should be explicit.

35. AI audit
Every analysis stores:

agreement_id
version_id
model_version_id
analysis_type

Do not store sensitive prompts or outputs unnecessarily if your retention policy doesn't permit it.

36. Sensitive information
The AI pipeline should use data minimization.

Depending on the configured architecture:

document
 ↓
authorized processing boundary
 ↓
redaction/minimization
 ↓
AI provider
Avoid sending unnecessary:

personal data
bank information
government identifiers
credentials
private internal notes
to external AI services.

The organization should control what AI providers are allowed to receive.

37. AI data governance
Configuration should include:

AI enabled
external provider allowed
data retention mode
training-use restrictions
allowed document classes
jurisdiction restrictions
human review requirement
The product should not assume an external model may retain or train on customer contract data.

That must depend on the actual provider's contractual/privacy configuration.

40. Do not automatically change agreements because of AI
This is a strict boundary.

AI may produce:

suggested clause
suggested correction
risk finding
missing-clause warning
obligation candidate
but it cannot do:

AI
 ↓
modify legal agreement
 ↓
send to other party
without the existing human-controlled workflow.

The correct flow is:

AI suggestion
 ↓
Lawyer reviews
 ↓
Lawyer explicitly proposes
 ↓
Redline
 ↓
Negotiation
 ↓
Party confirmation
 ↓
Execution
That preserves the control model we've built since 1.11.

42. Testing requirements
This milestone needs significantly stronger testing.

Source-grounding test
Given a known source clause:

Clause 8.2
the resulting finding must point to the correct clause.

Hallucination test
If the text does not contain a termination right, the model must not fabricate one.

Version test
Analysis of Version 7 must never appear as analysis of Version 8.

Authorization test
Party A must not retrieve Party B's private AI findings.

Reproducibility test
Same input hash + same model/configuration should identify the same analysis run.

Stale-analysis test
If Version 12 is analyzed and Version 13 becomes current, Version 12 findings remain associated with Version 12.

45. What remains before calling the core platform complete
The major next stages are:

1.20 — Legal Audit & Evidentiary Record
1.21 — Enterprise Integrations
1.22 — Security Hardening & Data Governance
1.23 — Production Deployment & Reliability
1.24 — Billing & SaaS Administration
1.25 — End-to-End Lifecycle Integration + Testing
But there is an important architectural step before integrations and production hardening:
Milestone 1.20 — Legal Audit & Evidentiary Record

This milestone makes the entire agreement lifecycle tamper-evident and independently verifiable.

The objective is not merely to keep application logs. We need a dedicated legal/audit record that can answer:

Who did what, to which agreement/version, when, under which authority, what exact content existed at that point, and what happened afterward?

The resulting chain is:

Agreement created
      ↓
Party assigned
      ↓
Lawyer assigned
      ↓
Draft generated
      ↓
Clause changed
      ↓
Redline proposed
      ↓
Counterproposal
      ↓
Approval
      ↓
Signing
      ↓
Execution
      ↓
Obligation event
      ↓
Amendment
      ↓
Renewal / termination
      ↓
ONE CONTINUOUS AUDIT HISTORY
1. Audit architecture

We now separate four concepts:

DOMAIN STATE
    ↓
"What is the current state?"

AUDIT EVENT
    ↓
"What happened?"

EVIDENCE
    ↓
"What exact artifact/content supports it?"

OUTBOX EVENT
    ↓
"What downstream systems need to react?"

These should not be merged into one table.

2. Immutable audit event

You already have an audit_events concept from Milestone 1.

Now we make it substantially stronger.

Create:

backend/app/models/audit.py

import uuid

3. Why the hash chain matters

Suppose:

Event 1
hash = AAA

Event 2
previous_hash = AAA
hash = BBB

Event 3
previous_hash = BBB
hash = CCC

If somebody alters Event 2:

Event 2
hash = XXX

then Event 3 contains:

previous_hash = BBB

and the chain no longer validates.

That gives us tamper detection.

4. Hash construction

Never hash a Python dictionary directly because serialization can vary.

Create a canonical representation.

backend/app/services/audit_service.py

import hashlib
import json
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID


def canonicalize(value) -> str:
    return json.dumps(
        value,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=False,
    )


def calculate_event_hash(
    *,
    organization_id: UUID,
    agreement_id: UUID | None,
    actor_user_id: UUID | None,
    action: str,
    resource_type: str,
    resource_id: UUID | None,
    occurred_at: datetime,
    metadata: dict,
    previous_event_hash: str | None,
) -> str:

    payload = {
        "organization_id": str(organization_id),
        "agreement_id": (
            str(agreement_id)
            if agreement_id
            else None
        ),
        "actor_user_id": (
            str(actor_user_id)
            if actor_user_id
            else None
        ),
        "action": action,
        "resource_type": resource_type,
        "resource_id": (
            str(resource_id)
            if resource_id
            else None
        ),
        "occurred_at": occurred_at.isoformat(),
        "metadata": metadata,
        "previous_event_hash": previous_event_hash,
    }

    canonical = canonicalize(payload)

    return hashlib.sha256(
        canonical.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()
5. Important: event order

A hash chain requires deterministic ordering.

Within an agreement, we should use:

occurred_at
+
database insertion sequence

But timestamp alone isn't enough because two events may occur within the same timestamp resolution.

Add:

sequence_number: Mapped[int]

to AuditEvent.

Use:

agreement_id
+
sequence_number

with a unique constraint.

For example:

Agreement A123

1 → created
2 → lawyer assigned
3 → version created
4 → change proposed
5 → lawyer confirmed
6 → party confirmed

The sequence must be generated transactionally.

6. Never generate audit sequence in application memory

Do not do:

sequence = existing_count + 1

because two concurrent requests can both obtain the same number.

Use a database-backed mechanism.

For PostgreSQL, one practical approach is a dedicated agreement audit sequence table:

agreement_audit_sequences
agreement_id
next_sequence

and lock the row:

SELECT next_sequence
FROM agreement_audit_sequences
WHERE agreement_id = :agreement_id
FOR UPDATE;

Then increment it inside the same transaction.

7. Create the audit service
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.models.audit import AuditEvent


class AuditService:

    @staticmethod
    async def record(
        db: AsyncSession,
        *,
        organization_id,
        agreement_id,
        actor_user_id,
        action,
        resource_type,
        resource_id,
        metadata,
        ip_address=None,
        user_agent=None,
    ) -> AuditEvent:

        occurred_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

        previous_result = await db.execute(
            select(AuditEvent)
            .where(
                AuditEvent.organization_id
                == organization_id,
                AuditEvent.agreement_id
                == agreement_id,
            )
            .order_by(
                AuditEvent.occurred_at.desc()
            )
            .limit(1)
            .with_for_update()
        )

        previous = previous_result.scalar_one_or_none()

        previous_hash = (
            previous.event_hash
            if previous
            else None
        )

        event_hash = calculate_event_hash(
            organization_id=organization_id,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            actor_user_id=actor_user_id,
            action=action,
            resource_type=resource_type,
            resource_id=resource_id,
            occurred_at=occurred_at,
            metadata=metadata,
            previous_event_hash=previous_hash,
        )

        event = AuditEvent(
            organization_id=organization_id,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            actor_user_id=actor_user_id,
            action=action,
            resource_type=resource_type,
            resource_id=resource_id,
            occurred_at=occurred_at,
            ip_address=ip_address,
            user_agent=user_agent,
            metadata=metadata,
            previous_event_hash=previous_hash,
            event_hash=event_hash,
        )

        db.add(event)

        return event

This is the basic implementation, but we'll strengthen it with the dedicated sequence mechanism before calling the audit layer production-complete.

10. Audit event vs user activity

Not every UI interaction needs a legal audit event.

For example:

opening the dashboard
scrolling
changing browser tab

doesn't belong in the contractual legal history.

But:

viewed confidential agreement
downloaded executed document
approved version
proposed amendment
signed agreement

may be security/activity events depending on policy.

We therefore need:

LEGAL_AUDIT
SECURITY_AUDIT
ACTIVITY_TELEMETRY

Do not mix high-volume telemetry with the immutable legal chain.

11. Document evidence snapshots

For critical events, create evidence snapshots.

Example:

Party confirmed Version 18

The audit event references:

version_id
content_hash

not just:

"version 18"

This lets verification later prove which exact content was involved.

14. Evidence hash

For a version:

Version ID
+
canonical content
→ SHA-256

For a file:

document bytes
→ SHA-256

For an approval:

approval facts
+
confirmed version hash
→ SHA-256

This creates a chain of references.

15. Merkle-style batching

At larger scale, maintaining an enormous chain can become expensive to externally verify.

A useful later optimization is periodic audit batching:

Event 1
Event 2
Event 3
...
Event 10,000
       ↓
batch root hash
       ↓
external timestamp/evidence

The product can then verify:

        ↓
batch root
        ↓
external timestamp

This should be introduced after the core audit chain is correct.

16. External timestamping

For stronger evidentiary integrity, the system can support an RFC 3161-compatible trusted timestamp service.

Architecture:

Audit batch
    ↓
hash
    ↓
timestamp authority
    ↓
timestamp token
    ↓
private evidence storage

The timestamp token should be stored as evidence.

This does not replace the internal audit chain; it anchors it externally.

17. Verification service

Create:

backend/app/services/audit_verification.py

from sqlalchemy import select


async def verify_agreement_audit_chain(
    db,
    agreement_id,
):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(AuditEvent)
        .where(
            AuditEvent.agreement_id == agreement_id
        )
        .order_by(
            AuditEvent.sequence_number.asc()
        )
    )

    events = list(result.scalars().all())

    previous_hash = None

    for event in events:
        if event.previous_event_hash != previous_hash:
            return {
                "valid": False,
                "failed_event_id": str(event.id),
                "reason": "previous hash mismatch",
            }

        calculated = calculate_event_hash(
            organization_id=event.organization_id,
            agreement_id=event.agreement_id,
            actor_user_id=event.actor_user_id,
            action=event.action,
            resource_type=event.resource_type,
            resource_id=event.resource_id,
            occurred_at=event.occurred_at,
            metadata=event.metadata,
            previous_event_hash=event.previous_event_hash,
        )

        if calculated != event.event_hash:
            return {
                "valid": False,
                "failed_event_id": str(event.id),
                "reason": "event hash mismatch",
            }

        previous_hash = event.event_hash

    return {
        "valid": True,
        "events_verified": len(events),
    }

This gives us a real verification function rather than simply trusting database rows.

21. Access control for audit records

The audit trail is often more sensitive than the agreement itself.

Therefore:

Agreement member
    ↓
may see allowed agreement audit history

but internal security events may be restricted further.

For example:

Legal user
→ contractual history

Organization security administrator
→ authentication/security history

System administrator
→ infrastructure audit

A normal agreement participant should not automatically get every platform security event.

22. Prevent audit deletion

Application users should never have:

DELETE /audit-events/{id}

There should be no normal application service method that deletes audit events.

Database privileges should reinforce this.

The API's database role should ideally have:

INSERT audit
SELECT audit

and no routine:

DELETE
UPDATE

authority over finalized audit rows.

23. Database permissions

For production PostgreSQL, separate database roles:

application_runtime
migration_admin
audit_verifier
backup_role

The normal application runtime should not have unrestricted DDL privileges.

This greatly reduces the impact of a compromised application server.

24. Trigger-based protection

Application-level protection isn't enough.

We can add PostgreSQL triggers that prevent changes to finalized audit records.

Conceptually:

CREATE FUNCTION prevent_audit_mutation()
RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'Audit records are immutable';
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Then:

CREATE TRIGGER audit_immutable
BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON audit_events
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION prevent_audit_mutation();

We must be careful to allow controlled maintenance/migrations through separate privileged roles.

25. Audit the audit system

Security-sensitive administrative actions must themselves be auditable.

For example:

audit verification requested
audit export created
audit export downloaded
privileged audit access
audit configuration changed

This creates:

Agreement audit
      +
Security audit
26. Event-to-evidence linkage

For a signature:

signature.completed
       │
       ├── signature request
       ├── signer
       ├── execution package
       ├── document hash
       └── evidence ID

For a clause change:

change_set.accepted
       │
       ├── base version
       ├── change set
       ├── changed clauses
       ├── resulting version
       └── version hash

For termination:

termination.completed
       │
       ├── termination request
       ├── notice
       ├── settlement
       ├── effective date
       └── post-termination obligations

This is the evidentiary graph.

27. Build an evidence graph

At this stage, a relational model alone becomes harder to reason about.

We can maintain explicit references:

EVENT
 │
 ├── caused_by_event
 ├── references_version
 ├── references_document
 ├── references_user
 ├── references_party
 └── references_evidence

This gives investigators a way to reconstruct:

"What caused Agreement A123 to become ACTIVE?"

Answer:

Negotiation completed
→ execution package created
→ signer A completed
→ signer B completed
→ execution evidence sealed
→ executed
→ effective date reached
→ active
28. Chain of custody for files

For uploaded/generated files:

uploaded
 ↓
malware scanned
 ↓
stored
 ↓
hashed
 ↓
processed
 ↓
versioned
 ↓
used in execution
 ↓
retained

Every significant transition should have:

timestamp
actor/system
file hash
storage reference
action

This becomes especially important for:

executed documents
termination notices
evidence submissions
signed artifacts
29. Retention

Do not make one global:

delete_after = X years

The platform should support retention policies by:

organization
agreement type
jurisdiction
document type
regulatory category
legal hold

For example:

LEGAL HOLD
     ↓
normal deletion suspended

This is also important for privacy compliance.

Sri Lanka's current personal-data framework includes the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 and later amendments/guidance, so the retention architecture should support purpose limitation, controlled retention and deletion rather than keeping everything forever by default.

       ↓

An audit export itself is sensitive.

Therefore:

Request export

Don't generate huge exports synchronously from an API request.

Milestone 1.21 — Enterprise Integrations & External Systems

Now we connect the platform to the systems companies already use while preserving the security model we built in 1.11–1.20.

The key rule is:

An integration is another principal with explicitly scoped access. It never becomes a superuser.

So the architecture is:

External System
      ↓
OAuth / API credentials
      ↓
Integration Identity
      ↓
Tenant Boundary
      ↓
Permission Scope
      ↓
Integration Service
      ↓
Agreement / Lifecycle APIs

Create:

backend/app/integrations/base.py

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class IntegrationProvider(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def connect(self, authorization_data):
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    async def disconnect(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    async def refresh_credentials(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    async def test_connection(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

Specific providers implement this interface.

The agreement domain never directly calls vendor SDKs.

Don't automatically send the full contract when the HR system only needs:

agreement_id
status
effective_date
expiry_date
14. Calendar integration

For obligations:

Contract deadline
      ↓
Calendar event

But calendar synchronization should be controlled.

A user might choose:

sync my assigned deadlines

rather than:

sync every organization contract

This respects agreement confidentiality.

15. Email integration

The notification system already has an email abstraction.

The integration architecture should allow:

organization email provider

to be configured rather than forcing every organization to use a single platform mailbox.

Examples of configuration:

sender identity
reply address
provider connection
allowed domains
email templates

Secrets remain in secure secret storage.

16. Cloud storage

We can support:

documents
       ↓
platform object storage
       +
optional external storage synchronization

Important:

The external storage connector should not turn into an alternate authorization system.

The platform determines:

who may access document

and generates authorized access to the external location.

17. E-signature integrations

The signature abstraction from Milestone 1.15 can now connect to external providers.

SignatureRequest
      ↓
SignatureProvider
      ↓
External execution service
      ↓
Webhook
      ↓
Signature event
      ↓
Execution verification
      ↓
ACTIVE

The external provider is not allowed to directly update agreement status.

Its webhook is treated as an external event that must be verified and processed.

20. Outgoing webhook architecture

The event engine from 1.14 already produces:

    ↓
Outbox
    ↓
Webhook Dispatcher
    ↓
External System

Example:

        ↓
CRM webhook
        ↓
ERP webhook
        ↓
customer automation

The agreement system remains the authoritative source.

21. Webhook signatures

Outgoing webhooks should be cryptographically authenticated.

Conceptually:

payload
+
timestamp
+
endpoint secret
        ↓
HMAC

The external recipient verifies the signature before trusting the event.

Never send an unsigned mutable payload and expect the recipient to trust it.

22. Incoming webhook security

For incoming events:

External provider
       ↓
HTTPS webhook
       ↓
signature verification
       ↓
timestamp validation
       ↓
event ID
       ↓
idempotency check
       ↓
authorized integration
       ↓
domain event

Reject:

invalid signature
expired timestamp
unknown integration
malformed payload
duplicate event
23. Idempotency

External providers can retry webhooks.

Suppose:

signature.completed

arrives three times.

The platform must generate only one domain outcome.

Store:

provider
integration_id
external_event_id
received_at
processed_at
status

with a unique constraint:

integration_id
+
external_event_id

25. Integration mapping

Different systems represent the same entity differently.

Example:

Platform:
agreement_id = UUID

CRM:
contract_id = "CTR-8271"

ERP:
document_id = 984432

HR:
employment_contract_id = "EMP-..."

Create a mapping layer:

integration_entity_mappings

integration_id
local_entity_type
local_entity_id
external_entity_type
external_entity_id

This prevents external identifiers from leaking into the core agreement schema.

26. Sync direction

Every integration should explicitly define:

PLATFORM → EXTERNAL
EXTERNAL → PLATFORM
BIDIRECTIONAL

For each data field:

source of truth
sync permission
conflict strategy

Example:

Agreement status
→ Platform is authoritative

Customer name
→ CRM is authoritative before contract creation

Payment status
→ ERP is authoritative

This avoids uncontrolled synchronization loops.

27. Conflict handling

Never do:

external_value = incoming_value

without checking the source of truth.

Example:

Platform:
Agreement expiry = 2027-09-30

External:
Expiry = 2027-12-31

Result:

INTEGRATION_CONFLICT

Then route to:

authorized user review

rather than silently changing legal data.

28. Integration permissions

Example:

CRM integration:

agreements.read
agreements.status.read
counterparties.read
agreements.write = NO
documents.read = NO
private_notes.read = NO
audit.read = NO

This is exactly the principle from 1.11 applied to external systems.

29. External system must not see private legal work

For your lawyer workflow:

       ↓

But:

       ↓

       ↓

if the organization granted that scope.

31. API key handling

Display the actual secret only once at issuance.

32. Rate limiting

per:

34. Integration failure behavior

External systems can be unavailable.

Example:

Agreement executed
       ↓
CRM unavailable

The agreement must still become:

EXECUTED

The CRM sync becomes:

PENDING

and retries later.

External system availability must not determine whether the core legal transaction succeeds.

36. Integration disconnect

When an organization disconnects a provider:

CONNECTED
   ↓
DISCONNECTING
   ↓
REVOKE CREDENTIALS
   ↓
STOP NEW SYNC
   ↓
DISCONNECTED

Existing agreement records remain.

Disconnecting Salesforce, an ERP, storage, or an e-signature provider must never delete agreements.

37. Data deletion behavior

Integration deletion should remove:

tokens
credentials

provider configuration

but retain:

legal audit records
agreement history

compliance evidence

according to the organization's retention/legal-hold policies.

Milestone 1.22 — Security Hardening & Data Governance

At this point the platform holds:

Contracts
Lawyer communications
Private negotiation notes
Identity information
Signature evidence
Financial obligations
Compliance evidence
Audit history

So security can no longer be treated as middleware around the API. It becomes part of the domain architecture.

The security model should now be:

Identity
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Tenant authorization
   ↓
Agreement authorization
   ↓
Party isolation
   ↓
Resource authorization
   ↓
Data minimization
   ↓
Audit
1. Zero-trust access model

Every sensitive request must independently establish:

Who is requesting?
        ↓
Is the account active?
        ↓
Which organization?
        ↓
Which agreement?
        ↓
Which party?
        ↓
Which agreement role?
        ↓
Which permission?
        ↓
Which exact resource?

Never assume:

"authenticated user = trusted user"

or:

"organization member = agreement member"
2. Strong authentication

The authentication system should support:

Password + MFA
OIDC/SSO
Session management
Recovery flow
Email verification
Account lockout/risk controls

For users with privileged capabilities:

organization administration
legal administration
member management
signing
security administration

require stronger authentication according to organization policy.

3. MFA model

Create:

user_authenticators
user_sessions
recovery_codes
authentication_events

Example:

backend/app/models/authentication.py

import uuid
from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import (
    DateTime,
    ForeignKey,
    String,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.models.base import (
    Base,
    TimestampMixin,
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,

class UserAuthenticator(
    UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin,
    TimestampMixin,
    Base,
):
    __tablename__ = "user_authenticators"

    user_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        UUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "users.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,

    authenticator_type: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(50),
        nullable=False,

    credential_reference: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(1000),

    )

        nullable=True,
    )

    verified_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    last_used_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

    revoked_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

For modern MFA, prefer phishing-resistant authenticators such as WebAuthn/passkeys where supported.

Do not store raw authenticator secrets in ordinary application tables.

4. Session management

Do not treat a JWT as a permanent identity.

Use:

short-lived access token
+
rotating refresh token
+
server-side session record

Only the hash of the refresh token is stored.

5. Refresh-token rotation

Correct flow:

Login
 ↓
Refresh Token A
 ↓
Use A
 ↓
invalidate A
 ↓
issue B
 ↓
Use B
 ↓
invalidate B
 ↓
issue C

If an already-used refresh token appears again:

TOKEN REUSE DETECTED
       ↓
revoke token family/session
       ↓
security event
       ↓
force reauthentication

That protects against stolen refresh tokens.

6. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security

Application checks are necessary.

They should not be the only tenant boundary.

PostgreSQL Row-Level Security can provide defense in depth.

Conceptually:

Application
    ↓
organization context
    ↓
PostgreSQL
    ↓
RLS
    ↓
only rows for current tenant

For tenant tables:

ALTER TABLE agreements ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

Then establish policies based on a transaction-local tenant context.

Conceptually:

CREATE POLICY agreement_tenant_isolation
ON agreements
USING (
    organization_id =
    current_setting(
        'app.current_organization',
        true
    )::uuid
);

The exact implementation needs careful connection-pool handling.

Never allow a pooled connection to retain the previous request's tenant context.

7. Transaction tenant context

Before tenant-scoped DB operations:

SELECT set_config(
    'app.current_organization',
    :organization_id,
    true
);

The third argument must be transaction-local.

Use:

SET LOCAL

semantics wherever appropriate.

Then:

Request A
organization X
   ↓
transaction
   ↓
RLS = X
   ↓
COMMIT

Request B
organization Y
   ↓
new transaction
   ↓
RLS = Y

This reduces tenant-crossing risk.

8. Defense in depth

We now have:

Application authorization
          +
Agreement membership
          +
Party-level authorization
          +
PostgreSQL RLS
          +
Object-storage authorization

A developer accidentally forgetting one application filter should not automatically expose the entire tenant.

9. Object-storage security

Documents are among the most sensitive resources.

Use:

private bucket
server-side encryption
versioning
short-lived presigned URLs
malware scanning
access logs
retention rules
legal holds

Never:

public-read bucket

for agreements or evidence.

10. Presigned URL flow

Don't return permanent storage URLs.

Instead:

GET /agreements/{id}/documents/{document_id}
        ↓
authorization
        ↓
document authorization
        ↓
generate short-lived URL
        ↓
return URL

The URL should expire quickly.

The storage system should also use a bucket policy preventing public access.

11. Encryption strategy

Use encryption at:

transport
storage
database/backups
secrets

Transport:

TLS

Storage:

managed encryption keys

Highly sensitive fields may additionally require application-level encryption.

12. Field-level encryption

Some fields may warrant additional protection:

tax identifiers
government identifiers
private credentials
certain identity information
sensitive legal metadata

Architecture:

Application
 ↓
KMS key
 ↓
encrypt value
 ↓
database stores ciphertext

Never place:

ENCRYPTION_KEY = "..."

into source code.

13. Key management

Use a key-management system rather than one static encryption key.

Architecture:

Application
     ↓
KMS
     ↓
Data encryption key
     ↓
Ciphertext

Support:

key rotation
key versioning
key revocation
access logging
environment isolation

Production and development keys must never be the same.

14. Secret management

All external secrets go into secret management:

database credentials
JWT signing secrets
OAuth secrets
email provider credentials
signature provider credentials
storage credentials
KMS references
AI provider credentials

The application should obtain them from:

environment / secret manager

not Git.

15. Secret scanning

CI should fail if source contains:

API keys
private keys
passwords
cloud credentials
tokens
connection strings

Use a secret-scanning stage in CI.

Also scan:

git history
docker layers
configuration files
logs
16. Password security

Use an adaptive password hashing algorithm such as Argon2id.

Example:

from argon2 import PasswordHasher

password_hasher = PasswordHasher()


def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return password_hasher.hash(password)


def verify_password(
    password: str,
    password_hash: str,
) -> bool:
    try:
        password_hasher.verify(
            password_hash,
            password,
        )
        return True
    except Exception:
        return False

Never log a password.

17. Login rate limiting

Protect:

/login
/password-reset
/email-verification
/MFA
/signing

against brute-force abuse.

Rate limits should be based on multiple factors:

IP
account
device/session
endpoint

Avoid relying only on IP because organizations may share addresses.

18. Account lockout behavior

Permanent account lockouts can themselves become a denial-of-service mechanism.

Prefer:

failed attempts
 ↓
progressive delay
 ↓
risk evaluation
 ↓
MFA / reauthentication

and administrator/security notification when appropriate.

19. CSRF

If authentication uses cookies:

HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
CSRF protection

must be configured correctly.

For state-changing requests:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

validate appropriate CSRF protections when cookie-based authentication is used.

20. CORS

Never deploy:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

for a private authenticated application.

Use explicit configured origins:

web application origin
mobile deep-link configuration
authorized administrative origins

Production and development origins should differ.

21. Content Security Policy

The web frontend should use a restrictive CSP.

Conceptually:

default-src 'self'
script-src ...
style-src ...
img-src ...
connect-src ...
frame-ancestors 'none'

The actual policy must be based on the technologies and third-party providers actually used.

Don't simply copy a generic CSP without testing the application.

22. Security headers

Configure reverse proxy/application security headers including appropriate:

Strict-Transport-Security
Content-Security-Policy
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy

Avoid deprecated or ineffective headers just for appearance.

23. SSRF protection

This platform will eventually fetch:

external documents
webhooks
legal sources
AI provider URLs
integration endpoints

Any user-controlled URL is a potential SSRF vector.

Never blindly:

httpx.get(user_url)

Implement:

URL validation
scheme allowlist
DNS resolution checks
private-network blocking
redirect validation
egress restrictions
timeouts
response-size limits

Pay particular attention to cloud metadata endpoints.

24. Document security

Uploaded files must not be trusted.

Pipeline:

Upload
 ↓
File size/type validation
 ↓
Hash
 ↓
Malware scan
 ↓
Safe storage
 ↓
Parsing sandbox
 ↓
Text extraction
 ↓
Analysis

Don't determine file type using only:

filename.endswith(".pdf")

Inspect actual content/type.

25. PDF/DOCX parser isolation

A malicious document could exploit a parser.

Don't process arbitrary uploaded documents directly inside the core API process.

Prefer:

API
 ↓
quarantine storage
 ↓
isolated worker/container
 ↓
parser
 ↓
sanitized extracted content
 ↓
analysis

The worker should have limited:

network access
filesystem access
CPU
memory
execution time
26. Malware scanning

Before a document becomes available to other participants:

uploaded
 ↓
QUARANTINED
 ↓
scan
 ├── clean → AVAILABLE
 └── malicious → BLOCKED

The notification engine should not notify users that a document is ready until the security state is acceptable.

27. DLP layer

Because agreements may contain sensitive information:

PII
financial data
credentials
health information
government IDs
trade secrets

introduce configurable DLP policies.

For example:

Detected sensitive data
        ↓
policy evaluation
        ↓
allow
warn
mask
block
review

Do not silently redact the legal document itself.

DLP should distinguish:

display protection
export protection
external sharing protection
AI-provider transfer protection
28. AI data boundary

Before contract data reaches an external AI service:

Agreement
 ↓
authorization
 ↓
AI policy
 ↓
data minimization
 ↓
optional redaction
 ↓
provider

Store which provider/data policy was used in the analysis record.

This allows an organization to answer:

Was our contract sent to an external model?
Which configured provider?
For what analysis?
When?
29. No training leakage

The platform should provide an explicit policy:

customer contract data
        ↓
AI processing

does not automatically imply:

customer contract data
        ↓
provider model training

The actual provider terms/configuration need to support the organization's selected policy.

This should be part of integration/AI configuration rather than an undocumented assumption.

30. Security event architecture

Use the event system:

authentication.failed
authentication.success
mfa.enabled
mfa.disabled
session.created
session.revoked
refresh_token.reuse_detected

permission.denied
agreement.access.denied
document.downloaded
document.exported

integration.connected
integration.disconnected

admin.permission.changed
security_policy.changed

Security events should be separated from ordinary contractual events where appropriate.

31. Suspicious behavior detection

The system can detect signals such as:

many failed logins
new country/device
impossible travel pattern
rapid downloads
mass contract exports
unusual API activity
repeated authorization failures
mass document access

But don't automatically label every anomaly as an attack.

Use:

signal
 ↓
risk score
 ↓
policy threshold
 ↓
security action

Possible actions:

allow
step-up authentication
temporarily restrict
notify security administrator
revoke session
32. Mass-download protection

For example:

normal:
5 documents/day

sudden:
2,000 documents in 3 minutes

The system can detect the behavior and trigger:

additional authentication
temporary export restriction
security alert

without deleting or modifying legal records.

33. Export controls

Legal history exports need separate permission:

agreement.view

does not automatically imply:

agreement.export

Similarly:

document.view

does not imply:

document.bulk_download

Use dedicated permissions.

34. Screenshot / screen protection

You cannot reliably prevent somebody from photographing a screen.

So don't pretend a UI control makes content impossible to copy.

Instead protect against practical leakage with:

short sessions
watermarking where appropriate
download controls
access logging
DLP
export permissions
35. Watermarking

For sensitive exports, optionally generate:

CONFIDENTIAL
Downloaded by: authorized user
Date/time
Agreement reference

The watermark should not modify the authoritative executed legal document.

It applies to a derived viewing/export copy.

36. Data classification

Every major resource gets a classification:

PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
RESTRICTED
LEGAL_PRIVILEGED / PRIVATE

For this platform:

Executed agreement
→ CONFIDENTIAL / configured

Private lawyer notes
→ RESTRICTED

Signature credentials
→ highly restricted

Audit evidence
→ RESTRICTED

Policies can then operate against classification.

37. Retention engine

Connect this to Milestone 1.20.

Create:

retention_policies
retention_assignments
retention_events

A policy can be based on:

agreement type
jurisdiction
organization policy
document type
termination state
legal hold

Never implement:

delete_after_years = 7

as a global hardcoded rule.

38. Legal hold

The hold system must override normal deletion.

Retention due
   ↓
Legal hold?
   ├── YES → retain
   └── NO  → eligible for deletion

But:

eligible for deletion

doesn't mean:

physically deleted immediately

There should be controlled deletion workflows and audit records.

39. Backup security

Backups must have:

encryption
access restrictions
retention policy
integrity checks
restore testing
region strategy

A backup that has never been restored successfully isn't a proven recovery mechanism.

40. Disaster recovery

Define:

RPO
Recovery Point Objective

RTO
Recovery Time Objective

For example, actual values are selected based on business requirements rather than invented by the application.

Architecture:

Primary DB
   ↓
replication / backups
   ↓
backup storage
   ↓
restore environment
   ↓
periodic restore test
41. Database backup principle

Do not rely solely on:

daily SQL dump

Use an appropriate PostgreSQL backup strategy with point-in-time recovery where required.

Test:

database lost
 ↓
restore
 ↓
verify migrations
 ↓
verify audit integrity
 ↓
verify document references
42. Dependency security

CI should run:

dependency vulnerability scanning
container scanning
secret scanning
static analysis
software composition analysis

Pin dependencies through a reviewed lock/constraints strategy.

Regularly update:

Python packages
Node packages
Docker base images
system packages
43. Container security

Containers should:

run as non-root
use minimal images
drop unnecessary Linux capabilities
read-only filesystem where practical
limit CPU/memory
avoid privileged mode
use pinned base images

Especially isolate:

document processing
OCR
AI workers
webhook processing

from the main API.

44. Network segmentation

Production architecture:

Internet
   ↓
WAF / CDN
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
API
   │
   ├── PostgreSQL private network
   ├── Redis private network
   ├── object storage
   ├── worker network
   └── secret/KMS services

PostgreSQL should not be directly reachable from the public internet.

45. Egress control

Workers that process documents or AI requests should not have unrestricted outbound internet access.

Use an allowlist where practical:

approved AI providers
approved storage
approved email
approved integrations
approved legal sources

This reduces SSRF and data-exfiltration risk.

46. Webhook security

Incoming webhook handling must verify:

provider identity
signature
timestamp
event ID
integration
schema

Then:

idempotency
+
rate limit
+
authorization
+
processing

Never let an external webhook directly execute arbitrary application behavior.

47. Security incident process

Create:

security_incidents
security_incident_events
security_incident_actions

Example:

Suspicious mass download
        ↓
Incident opened
        ↓
risk evaluation
        ↓
session revoked
        ↓
security administrator notified
        ↓
forensic audit
        ↓
containment
        ↓
recovery
        ↓
incident closed

The incident record itself should be tightly restricted.

48. Security API

Administrative endpoints:

GET  /api/v1/security/events
GET  /api/v1/security/sessions
POST /api/v1/security/sessions/{id}/revoke

GET  /api/v1/security/incidents
POST /api/v1/security/incidents

GET  /api/v1/security/policies
PATCH /api/v1/security/policies

These require security/admin-specific permissions.

49. Tenant isolation test suite

This deserves dedicated automated tests.

Test:

Tenant A → Tenant B agreement
Tenant B → Tenant A agreement

Party A → Party B private notes
Party B → Party A private notes

User without agreement assignment
→ agreement

Revoked member
→ agreement

Removed lawyer
→ old documents

Expired session
→ agreement

Revoked API key
→ agreement

Every one must fail.

50. IDOR testing

Test attacks such as:

GET /agreements/{other-agreement-id}

and:

GET /documents/{other-document-id}

while authenticated as another user.

Result must be:

404

or another carefully chosen non-disclosing response.

Never leak:

agreement title
party name
document existence
status
metadata

before authorization.

51. Object-storage IDOR testing

Even if:

API access denied

test whether a previously generated document URL still works after permission removal.

Therefore presigned URLs should have short lifetimes, and sensitive workflows should consider additional access controls.

52. Revocation propagation

When a lawyer is removed:

AgreementMember
    ↓
status = revoked

immediately prevents:

WebSocket
new download URLs
new signing sessions
new actions

Existing sessions/tokens may need revocation depending on their authorization scope.

53. Signing security

For a signing workflow:

 ↓
current session
 ↓
MFA / required authentication
 ↓
current signing session
 ↓
exact execution package
 ↓
consent
 ↓
signature

A user who previously had agreement access but lost signing authority must not be able to finish an old signing session.

54. Approval security

Likewise:

      ↓
participant removed
      ↓
approval invalidated

A previous authentication state shouldn't allow an ex-member to complete a pending approval.

55. Security headers + reverse proxy

Nginx or the production ingress should handle:

TLS termination
request size limits
rate limiting
basic bot filtering
security headers
connection timeouts

Application-level rate limits remain necessary for identity and domain-specific abuse.

56. Request correlation

Every request gets:

request_id

and ideally:

trace_id

Then a single user operation can be tracked:

request
 ↓
service
 ↓
DB transaction
 ↓
audit
 ↓
outbox
 ↓
worker
 ↓
notification

without putting contract content into logs.

57. Structured logging

Logs should be:

{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "level": "INFO",
  "request_id": "...",
  "actor_id": "...",
  "organization_id": "...",
  "action": "agreement.change_set.created"
}

Never log:

password
JWT
refresh token
private key
contract body
private lawyer notes
signature secrets
58. Privacy-aware telemetry

Observability systems can become an accidental data leak.

Therefore:

metrics → aggregate values
traces → IDs/metadata
logs → sanitized metadata

rather than:

full contract text in traces
59. Security migration

Add:

from app.models.authentication import (
    UserAuthenticator,
    UserSession,
)

from app.models.security import (
    SecurityEvent,
    SecurityIncident,
    SecurityIncidentEvent,
)

Then:

alembic revision --autogenerate \
  -m "add authentication and security hardening"

Review and apply:

alembic upgrade head

Before production launch:

[ ] PostgreSQL private

[ ] Agreement isolation tested

[ ] Strict CORS
[ ] CSP
[ ] SSRF protection

[ ] AI data policy
[ ] Audit integrity verification
[ ] Webhook signature verification
[ ] Dependency scanning
[ ] Container scanning
[ ] Incident process
[ ] Security monitoring
61. Final security architecture
                         INTERNET
                            │
                       WAF / TLS
                            │
                     Reverse Proxy
                            │
                     Authentication
                            │
                         API
                            │
              ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
              │                           │
        Authorization                 Security
              │                           │
      ┌───────┼────────┐           ┌──────┴──────┐
      ▼       ▼        ▼           ▼             ▼
   Tenant  Agreement  Party      Audit        Detection
    RLS      ACL       ACL
      │       │        │
      └───────┼────────┘
              ▼
          PostgreSQL
              │
      ┌───────┼────────┐
      ▼       ▼        ▼
    Redis   Workers   Storage
              │          │
       ┌──────┼──────┐   │
       ▼      ▼      ▼   ▼
      AI    Parser  Notify Documents

The critical point is that security is now enforced at multiple independent layers, not just in FastAPI.

62. Where the platform stands

The core is now:

1.10  Legal knowledge + jurisdiction rules
1.11  Party/lawyer access control
1.12  Negotiation + redlines
1.13  Multi-stage confirmation
1.14  Event + notifications
1.15  Signature + execution evidence
1.16  Obligations + compliance
1.17  Renewal + termination
1.18  Amendments
1.19  Contract intelligence + AI review
1.20  Audit + evidentiary record
1.21  Enterprise integrations
1.22  Security + data governance

So the next stage is infrastructure rather than adding another isolated business feature.
Milestone 1.23 — Production Deployment, Reliability & Observability

Now we take everything from 1.01–1.22 and make it deployable, monitorable, recoverable, and safe to operate in production.

The target topology is:

                         INTERNET
                            │
                       DNS / CDN / WAF
                            │
                         HTTPS/TLS
                            │
                     Load Balancer
                            │
                 ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                 │                     │
             API Servers          WebSocket
                 │                     │
                 └──────────┬──────────┘
                            │
                    Internal Network
                            │
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       │                    │                    │
   PostgreSQL              Redis              Object Storage
       │                    │                    │
       │               ┌────┴────┐               │
       │               │         │               │
       │             Celery    Scheduler          │
       │               │                         │
       └───────────────┼─────────────────────────┘
                       │
            AI / Document / Integration
                  Worker Processes
1. Separate runtime workloads

Do not put everything into one FastAPI process.

Use:

api
worker
scheduler
websocket
frontend
postgres
redis
object-storage
reverse-proxy

A practical first production deployment can still use containers on a few machines. Kubernetes is optional; separation of responsibilities is the important part.

2. Docker architecture

Repository:

infrastructure/
└── docker/
    ├── api.Dockerfile
    ├── worker.Dockerfile
    ├── frontend.Dockerfile
    └── nginx.conf

For backend:

FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app

RUN useradd \
    --create-home \
    --shell /usr/sbin/nologin \
    appuser

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install \
    --no-cache-dir \
    -r requirements.txt

COPY app ./app
COPY migrations ./migrations
COPY alembic.ini .

RUN chown -R appuser:appuser /app

USER appuser

CMD [
    "uvicorn",
    "app.main:app",
    "--host",
    "0.0.0.0",
    "--port",
    "8000"
]

The process does not run as root.

3. Do not bake secrets into Docker

Never:

ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=...

Secrets arrive at runtime:

Secret Manager
      ↓
runtime environment
      ↓
container

Same for:

JWT secrets
storage credentials
AI credentials
email credentials
integration credentials
KMS configuration
4. Docker Compose for local/staging

A development/staging Compose file can define:

services:
  api:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/api.Dockerfile
    env_file:
      - .env
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  worker:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/api.Dockerfile
    command: celery -A app.workers.celery_app worker --loglevel=INFO
    env_file:
      - .env

  scheduler:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/api.Dockerfile
    command: celery -A app.workers.celery_app beat --loglevel=INFO
    env_file:
      - .env

  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          "CMD-SHELL",
          "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}"
        ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:8
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

For production, use managed/HA infrastructure where appropriate rather than treating this Compose stack as the final HA architecture.

5. Application health endpoints

Create:

GET /health/live
GET /health/ready

live means:

Process is running.

ready means:

This instance can safely receive traffic.

6. Liveness
from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/health/live")
async def liveness():
    return {
        "status": "ok",
    }

Do not query every dependency here.

A liveness probe should remain lightweight.

7. Readiness

Readiness can check:

database connectivity
redis connectivity
required configuration
critical dependencies

Example:

@router.get("/health/ready")
async def readiness(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    await db.execute(text("SELECT 1"))

    redis_ok = await redis_client.ping()

    if not redis_ok:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=503,
            detail="Redis unavailable",
        )

    return {
        "status": "ready",
    }

If the database is unavailable:

503

so the load balancer stops routing traffic to that instance.

8. Graceful shutdown

The API must stop accepting new work before terminating.

SIGTERM
   ↓
stop new requests
   ↓
finish active requests
   ↓
close DB connections
   ↓
close Redis
   ↓
close WebSockets
   ↓
process exits

This is essential for rolling deployments.

9. Connection pool management

PostgreSQL connection counts become important with multiple API instances and workers.

For example:

10 API instances
×
20 DB connections
=
200 connections

Then workers add more.

Configure the pool deliberately:

engine = create_async_engine(
    settings.database_url,
    pool_size=settings.db_pool_size,
    max_overflow=settings.db_max_overflow,
    pool_pre_ping=True,
)

Values come from deployment configuration, not hardcoded assumptions.

10. Database migration strategy

Production deployment should separate:

Application deployment
        │
        ├── migration compatibility check
        │
        ├── database migration
        │
        └── application rollout

Use backward-compatible migrations wherever possible.

For example:

Add nullable column
      ↓
Deploy application using it
      ↓
Backfill
      ↓
Enforce constraint

Avoid destructive migrations during the same release where old application instances are still running.

11. CI/CD pipeline

Use:

git push
   ↓
lint
   ↓
type checking
   ↓
unit tests
   ↓
integration tests
   ↓
security scans
   ↓
build container
   ↓
image scan
   ↓
staging
   ↓
smoke tests
   ↓
production approval
   ↓
production deployment
12. CI checks

Minimum backend checks:

ruff check .
pytest
mypy app

Also:

dependency vulnerability scan
secret scan
container scan
migration check

The exact tools can be configured according to your repository.

13. Testing pyramid

Use:

             E2E
             /\
            /  \
       Integration
         /      \
        /        \
      Unit tests

Unit tests cover:

authorization
state transitions
deadline calculation
redline logic
hashing
workflow logic

Integration tests cover:

PostgreSQL
Redis
object storage
webhooks
event processing

E2E covers:

create agreement
assign lawyers
negotiate
approve
sign
activate
amend
terminate
14. The critical end-to-end test

One automated scenario should execute:

Organization created
    ↓
Users created
    ↓
Legal entities created
    ↓
Agreement created
    ↓
Parties assigned
    ↓
Lawyers invited
    ↓
Lawyers accepted
    ↓
Draft generated
    ↓
Clause modified
    ↓
Counterproposal
    ↓
Both-side confirmation
    ↓
Execution package
    ↓
Signatures
    ↓
ACTIVE
    ↓
Obligation created
    ↓
Amendment
    ↓
Termination

Then verify the audit chain remains valid.

That single test catches a huge class of integration errors.

15. Observability architecture

We need three pillars:

Logs
Metrics
Traces

And a fourth layer:

Audit / security events

Don't treat audit logs as ordinary operational logs.

16. Structured logs

Use structlog.

import structlog

logger = structlog.get_logger()

logger.info(
    "agreement.change_set.created",
    agreement_id=str(agreement_id),
    change_set_id=str(change_set_id),
    actor_user_id=str(user_id),
)

Never log contract content or secrets.

17. Correlation IDs

Every request gets:

request_id
trace_id

FastAPI middleware:

import uuid


@app.middleware("http")
async def request_context(request, call_next):

    request_id = request.headers.get(
        "X-Request-ID"
    ) or str(uuid.uuid4())

    response = await call_next(request)

    response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = request_id

    return response

In production, validate externally supplied IDs rather than blindly trusting arbitrary strings.

18. Metrics

Track:

HTTP latency
HTTP errors
request rate
DB latency
DB pool exhaustion
Redis latency
queue depth
worker failures
notification delivery
webhook failures
AI processing time
document processing time
signing failures
agreement workflow failures
19. Business metrics

Also track domain metrics:

agreements_created
agreements_active
agreements_pending_signature
average_negotiation_rounds
average_execution_time
obligations_overdue
renewals_upcoming
termination_requests
amendments_created
ai_findings_reviewed

These are operational/business metrics, not raw contract contents.

20. Prometheus-style metrics

For example:

from prometheus_client import Counter


agreement_created = Counter(
    "agreements_created_total",
    "Number of agreements created",
)

Then:

agreement_created.inc()

Metrics should never include high-cardinality identifiers such as:

agreement_id
user_id
email

as labels.

That can destroy metrics-system performance.

21. Queue observability

Celery/Redis workloads need:

queue depth
active tasks
failed tasks
retry count
task age
dead-letter count
processing duration

Example alert:

notification queue age > configured threshold

This is far more useful than simply knowing the worker process is alive.

22. Dead-letter handling

Messages that repeatedly fail shouldn't disappear.

Use:

FAILED
 ↓
retry
 ↓
retry
 ↓
max attempts
 ↓
DEAD_LETTER

Then administrators can inspect:

task
error
attempts
first failure
last failure
related integration
related agreement

without exposing contract contents unnecessarily.

23. Distributed tracing

For a complex request:

HTTP request
   ↓
FastAPI
   ↓
PostgreSQL
   ↓
Outbox
   ↓
Celery
   ↓
AI provider
   ↓
Notification

A trace connects those operations.

Use an OpenTelemetry-compatible architecture.

The trace should contain:

service
operation
duration
status
trace_id

not full legal documents.

24. Error handling

Create consistent API errors.

Example:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "AGREEMENT_VERSION_CONFLICT",
    "message": "The agreement changed before this action was completed.",
    "request_id": "..."
  }
}

Don't expose Python tracebacks to clients.

25. Exception taxonomy

Create:

AuthenticationError
AuthorizationError
ResourceNotFoundError
ValidationError
ConcurrencyError
WorkflowStateError
ExecutionError
IntegrationError
DocumentProcessingError
ExternalProviderError

Then map them to stable API codes.

26. Circuit breakers

External providers can fail.

For example:

Email Provider
      ↓
5 consecutive failures
      ↓
OPEN
      ↓
stop immediate calls
      ↓
cooldown
      ↓
test
      ↓
CLOSED

Use this for:

email
AI provider
external signature provider
CRM
ERP
storage

This prevents one failing dependency from causing cascading failures.

27. Timeouts

Every external call must have a timeout.

Bad:

await client.post(url)

Better:

await client.post(
    url,
    timeout=10.0,
)

But actual timeout values should come from environment/configuration.

28. Retry only when safe

Do not retry every operation.

Safe candidates:

GET
idempotent webhook processing
notification delivery
status retrieval

Potentially dangerous:

create payment
create signature
send legal notice
create external record

unless an idempotency key exists.

29. Idempotency keys

For critical external actions:

Idempotency-Key: <unique-client-generated-value>

Store:

key
user
organization
endpoint
request hash
response
status

Then retrying the request doesn't create a duplicate action.

Especially important for:

signature requests
payment actions
external CRM creation
external webhooks
termination notices
30. Blue/green or rolling deployments

Use:

Version A
   ↓
Version B deployed
   ↓
health checks
   ↓
traffic shifts
   ↓
A drains
   ↓
A removed

Do not take the entire platform offline for every deployment.

31. Deployment sequence

A safe release looks like:

Build image
   ↓
Security scan
   ↓
Deploy migration-compatible code
   ↓
Run migration
   ↓
Deploy new workers
   ↓
Deploy API
   ↓
Readiness checks
   ↓
Smoke tests
   ↓
Traffic increase
   ↓
Monitor

Rollback needs to be designed before deployment.

32. Rollback

Suppose release B has a bug.

You need:

B
 ↓
error rate increases
 ↓
stop rollout
 ↓
rollback application
 ↓
preserve compatible database state
 ↓
retry after fix

This is another reason migrations should be backward-compatible.

33. Database HA

For serious production workloads:

Primary PostgreSQL
      │
      ├── replica
      └── backup/PITR

Automatic failover can be managed by a suitable managed PostgreSQL service or a proven HA architecture.

Don't invent your own failover mechanism.

34. Redis HA

Redis becomes infrastructure for:

rate limiting
cache
distributed coordination
Celery broker
real-time events
temporary session state

For production, use a highly available managed/service deployment appropriate to your workload.

Do not make the system depend on one unprotected Redis container.

35. Caching strategy

Cache only data that can safely be cached.

Good candidates:

agreement type definitions
published workflow definitions
legal rules
notification templates
non-sensitive configuration

Use caution with:

private contract content
private lawyer notes
signing sessions
sensitive evidence

If sensitive data is cached, it needs the same authorization/security standards as the primary store.

36. Cache invalidation

When a rule/workflow/template changes:

database update
 ↓
cache invalidation event
 ↓
Redis cache removed
 ↓
next request reloads authoritative value

Don't leave old legal/workflow definitions indefinitely cached.

37. Object storage reliability

Use:

versioning
durability controls
server-side encryption
lifecycle policies
replication where required
access logs

Critical executed artifacts should have stronger retention than temporary processing files.

38. Temporary file lifecycle

Uploaded/processing documents should move through:

quarantine
 ↓
processing
 ↓
validated
 ↓
permanent storage

Temporary files must eventually be cleaned up.

Don't leave raw uploaded files indefinitely on worker disks.

39. Scheduler reliability

There should be only one logical scheduled action even if multiple scheduler instances exist.

For deadline processing:

Scheduler A
Scheduler B
      ↓
distributed lock / idempotency
      ↓
ONE deadline event

Otherwise users could receive duplicate reminders.

40. Exactly-once illusion

Distributed systems generally cannot guarantee true exactly-once processing end-to-end.

Design for:

at-least-once delivery
+
idempotent processing
+
deduplication

This principle should be applied to:

webhooks
notifications
queue jobs
integration events
deadline reminders
41. Backup verification

Don't stop at:

backup succeeded

Run actual restore tests:

Backup
 ↓
restore isolated environment
 ↓
run migrations/compatibility checks
 ↓
verify DB
 ↓
verify document references
 ↓
verify audit chain
 ↓
verify hashes

Record the result.

42. Disaster recovery drill

Periodically test:

database failure
storage failure
Redis failure
API node failure
worker failure
external provider failure

The system should degrade gracefully.

Example:

Email provider unavailable
      ↓
agreement negotiation still works
      ↓
notification queued
      ↓
email delivered later
43. Rate limiting at production edge

Use multiple layers:

WAF/edge
      ↓
reverse proxy
      ↓
Redis application rate limit
      ↓
endpoint-specific controls

Examples:

login
password recovery
signing
bulk export
document download
webhooks
public API

Each has different abuse characteristics.

44. Production config validation

At startup, validate required configuration.

required = [
    settings.database_url,
    settings.jwt_secret_key.get_secret_value(),
    settings.redis_url,
]

if any(not value for value in required):
    raise RuntimeError(
        "Required production configuration missing"
    )

For production, also reject unsafe configuration such as insecure cookie settings or development origins.

45. Environment separation

Use:

development
testing
staging
production

Separate:

databases
storage buckets
encryption keys
OAuth credentials
AI providers
email configuration
signing providers

Never connect staging to production legal documents.

46. Production hostname structure

Typical conceptual setup:

app.example.com
api.example.com
ws.example.com

Internal:

postgres.internal
redis.internal
worker.internal

Only required services are internet-facing.

47. Database connection security

Use TLS for database connections where supported/required by the deployment environment.

The production connection string should include appropriate SSL verification settings.

Do not disable certificate validation just to make deployment work.

48. WebSocket reliability

The client needs:

connect
 ↓
authenticate
 ↓
subscribe to authorized scope
 ↓
heartbeat
 ↓
reconnect
 ↓
resume

The server needs:

connection authentication
authorization
connection limits
idle timeout
heartbeat
disconnect

After reconnect, the client should fetch missed authoritative state from the API rather than assuming every event was received.

49. Event ordering

WebSocket messages can be delayed.

Therefore, include:

event_id
event_sequence
created_at

Clients should be able to detect:

sequence 101
sequence 103

and then fetch missing state/events.

The database remains authoritative.

50. Production monitoring dashboard

At minimum:

SYSTEM

API availability
API error rate
P95/P99 latency
DB health
Redis health
worker health
queue depth
storage failures
webhook failures
notification failures
AI failures

Business:

active agreements
pending approvals

upcoming renewals

Security:

failed logins
authorization failures
suspicious downloads
token reuse
security incidents
51. Alerting

Alerts should be tied to action.

Examples:

API availability breach
DB unavailable
queue stuck
audit verification failure
backup failure
certificate expiry approaching
mass document export anomaly
signature provider failing
storage capacity threshold

Avoid alerting on every small transient error.

52. Production logging retention

Operational logs should have a finite retention policy.

Legal audit records follow the separate legal/audit retention policy.

This distinction is critical:

Application log
      ≠
Legal audit record

Don't use Elasticsearch/Loki/etc. as the legal system of record.

53. Deployment artifact provenance

Every production deployment should identify:

git commit
container image digest
build timestamp
dependency lock version
migration version

Then an incident can answer:

Which exact software version processed this agreement event?

54. Application version endpoint

Internal/admin:

GET /health/version

Response:

{
  "version": "configured-release-version",
  "commit": "configured-commit",
  "migration": "configured-schema-version"
}

These values should come from the build/deployment system.

57. What 1.23 accomplishes

The system is now designed so that:

API failure
    ≠
lost agreement

Worker failure
    ≠
lost event

Email failure
    ≠
failed approval

Redis failure
    ≠
lost legal record

External provider failure
    ≠
corrupted agreement

Deployment
    ≠
unplanned downtime

Database failure
    ≠
permanent data loss

The legal database, immutable evidence, document storage, event system, and external integrations have separate failure boundaries.

Milestone 1.24 — SaaS Billing, Plans, Entitlements & Organization Administration

Now we add the commercial SaaS layer without contaminating the legal domain.

The important architectural rule is:

Billing
   ↓
Entitlements
   ↓
Feature access

BUT

Billing
   ≠
Legal authority
   ≠
Agreement permissions
   ≠
Signing authority

A company running out of AI credits must not accidentally lose access to its executed contracts. Billing controls product capabilities; it does not rewrite legal state.

1. Commercial architecture
Organization
     ↓
Billing Customer
     ↓
Subscription
     ↓
Plan
     ↓
Entitlements
     ↓
Usage
     ↓
Invoices / Payments

Feature requests become:

API request
    ↓
Authentication
    ↓
Agreement authorization
    ↓
Entitlement check
    ↓
Operation

Both authorization and entitlement must pass.

2. What can be metered

The system should meter actual usage, not artificial counters.

Possible dimensions:

organization seats
active agreements
agreements created
document storage
document processing
AI analysis
AI tokens/compute
signature transactions
external integrations
API requests
webhook volume
audit exports

A plan may limit or include any of these.

14. Example real usage

    ↓
